title: Solar module manufacturing in Europe: Ideal factory capacity ranges from 1 GW to 3 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Global solar supply chains are undergoing a profound transformation, driven by growing protectionism and industrial policies aimed at supporting domestic manufacturing. This is the key takeaway from an interview with
pv magazine
featuring Laura Sartore, CEO of Ecoprogetti, an Italian company specializing in machinery and production lines for solar module manufacturing.
According to Sartore, this trend is increasingly evident across major international markets. “All the world’s primary supply chains, with the exception of China’s, are shifting toward a form of protectionism and price floors,” she said, citing the United States as one of the most prominent examples.
pv magazine Session @ NetZero Milan Expo Summit 2026
The dynamics shaping global PV supply chains – including solar modules, inverters, and battery energy storage systems – will be discussed during the “
Decoding solar supply chains
” session at the NetZero event in Milan on Oct. 21.
The session will examine the forces reshaping clean energy supply chains, from manufacturing and sourcing strategies to shifting trade and regulatory requirements. It will also explore what these developments mean for companies procuring solar and energy storage equipment in an increasingly complex global market.
Join us in Milan to hear from industry experts and take part in the discussion on the future of solar supply chains.
The US market shows that introducing minimum price thresholds, even above the prices charged by Chinese manufacturers, does not necessarily slow demand. On the contrary, according to Sartore, the sector continues to grow despite rising component costs, supported by the development of a domestic supply chain.
In China, prices are also gradually rising across the supply chain following government efforts to curb overcapacity, a trend that was expected to continue into 2025. According to Sartore, this shift reflects a growing focus on the economic viability of manufacturing in a market where solar technology has already firmly established its competitiveness against other energy sources.
India: An industrial policy covering the entire supply chain
Among international markets, Sartore identifies India as one of the most compelling examples of industrial policy in the solar sector.
The Indian government is progressively expanding protectionist measures and domestic manufacturing requirements beyond modules to include cells, wafers and ingots, aiming to reduce dependence on Chinese imports and strengthen local production capacity.
“In my view, India has the most serious industrial policy. They have observed Europe’s mistakes, and they continue to monitor developments in the United States,” Sartore said, highlighting the clear industrial strategy pursued by Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government.
A key element of this strategy is industry consolidation. Production capacity exceeding domestic demand is not necessarily seen as a problem. Instead, it can encourage mergers and direct investment toward segments of the supply chain that remain underdeveloped.
“The days of small-scale factories with a capacity of 200–500 MW are over; we are now seeing multi-gigawatt-scale facilities. And that is how it had to be—that is the only way forward for a continent-sized nation like India,” Sartore said.
This consolidation is helping create larger, more financially robust manufacturers capable of investing not only in solar cell and module production but also in the materials and components needed for manufacturing, including glass, encapsulants, backsheets and junction boxes.
According to Sartore, India now has the most comprehensive solar manufacturing supply chain outside China. However, domestic polysilicon production, a technically complex industrial process, remains underdeveloped.
“It will certainly be more challenging, because, beyond the raw material extraction phase, polysilicon production requires specialized technological expertise, capital-intensive facilities, and competitive access to energy. These industrial capabilities are currently lacking and must be developed and solidified; yet, India possesses the potential to scale them up,” Sartore explained.
Beyond technical expertise and investment, the environmental impact of manufacturing presents another challenge. Sartore stressed that developing a domestic polysilicon supply chain must also account for emissions from industrial processes.
“As India develops its polysilicon production, it must aim for high environmental standards and low-emission processes from the very outset. It is not enough to simply replicate production capacity—as seen in China—without prioritizing emissions; the goal must be to build an industrial supply chain that is competitive in terms of both energy efficiency and environmental impact,” Sartore added, noting that these requirements could lengthen the timeline for developing India’s domestic supply chain.
Europe: The medium-sized manufacturing model should not be abandoned
While India and the United States are focusing on large-scale factories and highly integrated supply chains, Sartore advocates a different approach for Europe.
She argues that Europe’s industrial model cannot be assessed using the same criteria as those applied in the United States or Asia. The continent’s manufacturing sector has historically been built around small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), industrial clusters and networks of specialized manufacturers.
“In Europe, we lack the ‘gigafactory’ or ‘mega-factory’ structure seen in India or the United States. Historically, our industrial fabric has been composed of small and medium-sized enterprises, across all sectors and fields,” she said.
Sartore points to Italy and Germany, where numerous industries have achieved international leadership through networks of relatively small but highly competitive companies.
According to Sartore, Europe’s solar manufacturing sector should build on this strength rather than attempt to replicate production models dominated by a handful of large manufacturers.
“The European multi-factory, network-based model is one that should not be abandoned,” she said.
However, this does not mean that small module assembly lines can remain competitive regardless of their production capacity. Manufacturers need to achieve a minimum production scale and invest in adequate levels of technology and automation to justify Capex and maintain competitive costs.
“A scale of 800 MW to 1 GW is the minimum threshold—necessary to make an investment sustainable—otherwise, the Capex burden becomes too heavy, making it impossible to reach competitive module price points,” Sartore explained.
Optimal production scale
Factory size is a key factor in the future of European solar module manufacturing.
According to Sartore, a production capacity of 1 GW to 3 GW offers an optimal balance between economies of scale, financial viability and operational complexity.
“A capacity of 1 to 3 GW is manageable,” she said, explaining that facilities of this size typically correspond to companies with annual revenue of €100 million ($112.2 million) to €200 million and approximately 150 to 300 employees.
Such companies are large enough to support industrial-scale manufacturing while remaining compatible with Europe’s existing industrial structure.
The challenge goes beyond the initial capital investment required to build a factory. Once production begins, manufacturers face substantial operating costs, particularly for raw material procurement.
Although increasing production capacity initially reduces module production costs per unit, there is a point beyond which the financial burden of operating a larger facility can offset these savings.
“In the European context, the 1 GW to 3 GW range captures the benefits of economies of scale. Beyond 3 GW, additional management costs and financial charges come into play; these weigh on the bottom line and do not necessarily lead to lower raw material procurement costs,” Sartore said.
For a 5 GW factory, working capital requirements can become particularly significant. Procuring and managing large volumes of raw materials requires substantial credit lines, bank guarantees and careful financial planning. These costs must be weighed against potential economies of scale, as greater production capacity does not necessarily translate into lower unit costs. Larger facilities also face greater financial exposure if demand falls short of production capacity.
“In Europe, without supply chain integration, if I need to purchase 5 GW worth of raw materials, I require structured bank collateral. There are high costs for credit guarantees and interest on cash flow—all of which weigh on the purchase price of the raw materials and on the company itself—potentially making the resulting photovoltaic module no more cost-effective than one produced by a smaller-scale manufacturer,” she explained.
As a result, a larger factory does not necessarily have lower production costs than a medium-sized facility, particularly when financing expenses and operating overheads are taken into account.
For medium-sized European manufacturers, a more moderate production scale can help limit financial exposure and make working capital requirements easier to manage, particularly given the financing conditions in Europe’s banking sector.
Flexible production for the European market
Production capacity should also reflect the characteristics of market demand.
According to Sartore, Europe’s solar market has a more fragmented structure than other major international markets, with projects generally smaller than gigawatt-scale installations and manufacturers required to handle a wider range of order sizes.
European solar projects often range from a few megawatts to several tens of megawatts, while installations approaching or exceeding 1 GW remain relatively rare.
Sartore argues that this further supports the development of a network of manufacturers capable of adapting production to individual customer requirements.
“There won’t be many gigawatt-scale solar power plant projects in Europe,” Sartore said. “The European market is defined by diverse requirements and local conditions, making the development of numerous medium-to-large-scale plants more likely than the creation of a large number of mega-installations.”
Production flexibility therefore becomes a key competitive factor alongside manufacturing costs and supply chain capabilities.
According to Sartore, this model is better suited to Europe’s industrial structure and the specific characteristics of its solar market.

title: Italy allocates €770 million for 505 MW of agricultural rooftop solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Italy has allocated all available funding under the latest round of its Agrisolare scheme, awarding €770.4 million in grants to 7,409 projects for approximately 505 MW of rooftop solar capacity on agricultural, livestock and agro-industrial buildings.
The Gestore dei Servizi Energetici (GSE), Italy’s energy services manager, published the list of approved projects under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) measure, which implements a decree issued by the Ministry of Agriculture on Dec. 17, 2025.
Three additional lists published by GSE show that 1,863 eligible applications were not funded because the budget had been exhausted. These applications represent €187.3 million in requested grants and approximately 170 MW of solar capacity.
A further 7,610 applications were deemed ineligible, representing €775.4 million in requested grants. Another 37 applicants withdrew, accounting for €3.9 million.
In total, the scheme received 16,919 applications seeking approximately €1.74 billion in grants — more than twice the amount awarded. Around 45% of applications failed the eligibility checks, and the value of grants sought by ineligible applicants exceeded the amount allocated to successful projects.
In May, Agriculture Minister Francesco Lollobrigida told the Senate that approximately 16,000 businesses had applied, with around 8,000 expected to receive funding in an initial phase. He said the government hoped to find additional resources for the remaining applicants.
Lombardy received the largest allocation, with 884 projects awarded €145.2 million, representing 18.8% of the total funding, for 92 MW of solar capacity. Veneto followed with 735 projects and €99.5 million, while Emilia-Romagna received €84.6 million across 633 projects. Piedmont had 664 projects awarded €72.5 million.
Sicily was the leading region in southern Italy, with 617 projects and €58.3 million in grants, followed by Puglia with €55.1 million and Campania with €48.9 million.
The largest individual grant, at €1.54 million, went to Società agricola Dossi di Franguelli Eugenio & C. in Costa de’ Nobili, in the province of Pavia, for an 847 kW installation. A pig farm in Roncade, in the province of Treviso, received €1.38 million for a 764 kW system, while a poultry farm in Scandolara Ravara, in the province of Cremona, was awarded €1.24 million for a system of approximately 1 MW.
The average grant was approximately €1,500 per kW of solar capacity.
Applications were submitted through the GSE platform between March 10 and April 9, 2026. Successful applicants have 18 months from the grant award to complete construction, subject to justified extensions. Final reporting must be completed by Dec. 31, 2028.
The earlier version of the Agrisolare scheme approved approximately 23,000 projects representing 1.7 GW of solar capacity.

title: Dominican Republic to introduce grid usage fee for distributed PV - pv magazine Global
content:
Dominican Republic’s national utility Edesur has announced that it will introduce a new billing charge for certain customers with rooftop solar installations in the Dominican Republic from Nov. 1, 2026, under the country’s distributed generation regulations.
According to a notice sent by the utility to its self-generation customers, the measure will initially apply to those who joined the net metering program before October 2021 and are subject to the BTS-1 and BTS-2 low-voltage tariffs, which cover residential and commercial electricity consumers, respectively.
The change is based on Resolution SIE-007-2026-REG, issued by the Superintendency of Electricity (SIE) in January 2026. Article 19(1)(e) of the resolution establishes a distribution network usage charge for customers on single-part electricity tariffs.
The charge will be calculated by multiplying the electricity injected into the grid, measured in kWh, by 25% of the energy component of the customer’s applicable tariff. It therefore does not represent a 25% increase in the total electricity bill or a charge on all electricity generated by the PV installation. Instead, it applies only to electricity exported to the grid.
Affected customers will continue to pay their usual fixed charges and electricity consumption charges, with the new distribution network usage fee added to their bills.
The new charge follows earlier regulatory measures introduced in 2026. Under Resolution SIE-103-2026-TF, the SIE established distribution network usage charges for distributed generation customers served by Edesur, Edenorte and Edeeste for the April-to-September period.
However, the scope of Edesur’s announcement must also be considered in light of the transitional provisions established by the regulator.
When introducing the new regulations in January, the SIE stated that existing interconnection contracts would retain their terms until their expiration. It also indicated that the network usage charge would apply to new installations with demand below 10 kW and to existing installations once their contracts expire.
As a result, enrollment in the net metering program before October 2021 does not necessarily mean that all contracts in that category have expired. Edesur’s announcement does not specify how many customers will be affected or provide details of the contractual conditions determining their inclusion.
The new distributed generation regulations, introduced in February 2026, also reduce the maximum approval period for installations to 45 days and eliminate the previous 15% PV penetration limit per distribution circuit. They also introduce changes to the compensation mechanism for accumulated annual energy credits.
According to the SIE, the network usage charge is intended to account for the costs of maintaining electricity distribution infrastructure used by distributed generation customers and support the financial sustainability of the electricity system.

title: Non-destructive testing tracks polymer degradation in PV modules - pv magazine Global
content:
A research team in Germany has investigated whether compressive stress relaxation measurement (CSRM) can be used to monitor polymer degradation in aging photovoltaic modules. The technique is typically used in manufacturing quality control to assess the degree of encapsulant cross-linking after lamination.
“This publication uses the CSRM not only for lamination control, but also to monitor the mechanical response of the mini-modules’ rear side,” the researchers explained. “To achieve a higher resolution and sample throughput, the cross-linking density will be used to calibrate the CSRM. The influence of encapsulants and backsheet degradation on the CSRM during weathering is of interest. Therefore, the degradation of the encapsulant and the backsheet will be decoupled.”
CSRM is a non-destructive technique commonly used to assess encapsulant curing after PV module lamination. It involves pressing a tip into the rear surface of a module and measuring how the force decreases while the indentation depth remains constant. The response reflects the mechanical properties of both the encapsulant and the backsheet.
To evaluate CSRM as a method for monitoring aging, the researchers fabricated 200 mm × 200 mm mini-modules incorporating passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC) solar cells, ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) encapsulants, and polyethylene/polyethylene terephthalate (PET) backsheets. They varied lamination times at 155 C to achieve different degrees of cross-linking.
For each CSRM measurement, they heated the test location to 89 C, pressed a 4 mm steel tip approximately 100 µm into the module’s rear surface, applied a force of less than 20 N, and recorded the decline in force while holding the tip in place.
The modules were subjected to damp heat (DH) testing at 85 C and 85% relative humidity for up to 3,500 hours, or combined heat and ultraviolet (UV) irradiation at 85 C, 60% relative humidity, and an irradiance of 227 W/m2 for up to 2,000 hours. At 250-hour intervals, the team used CSRM to monitor mechanical changes and measured the modules’ electrical performance. Additional solvent tests and thermal analyses helped distinguish changes in encapsulant cross-linking from backsheet degradation.
“After the first 250 h of the DH test, the encapsulants showed an increase in the degree of cross-linking but maintained differences between the samples throughout the test,” the researchers said. “As a result, the PV module power degradation correlated with the initial cross-linking state. By the end of the test, the encapsulant and the backsheet had degraded, resulting in a drop in the CSRM response.”
The results also showed that the encapsulant’s cross-linking density subsequently decreased, while the backsheet underwent post-crystallization and exhibited chain scission.
“The combined DH+UV weathering test caused post-cross-linking within the first 250 h, leading to leveling of the cross-linking states,” the researchers concluded. “The canceled chemical differences in the encapsulants became reflected in a similar module power degradation. Thus, overacceleration shall be avoided by all means to deliver realistic reliability predictions.”
The findings are presented in the study, “
Non-destructive monitoring of polymer degradation in PV modules by compressive stress relaxation measurement and implications for the PV module reliability
,” published in
Polymer Testing
. The research team included scientists from Germany’s
Anhalt University of Applied Sciences
Fraunhofer CSP

title: JinkoSolar unveils 510 W rooftop solar module with 25.5% efficiency, 40-year warranty - pv magazine Global
content:
Chinese solar module manufacturer JinkoSolar has unveiled a 510 W all-black residential solar panel based on its newly introduced
TOPCon-based Amorphous-Si Passivating Cell (TAC) technology
, which combines TOPCon electron-selective contacts, amorphous silicon heterojunction passivation and a back-contact electrode architecture.
The JKM485–510T series targets premium residential applications, including villas and homes with limited rooftop space, where power density, aesthetics and long-term reliability are key considerations.
The company said the 48-cell Tiger Neo 5.0 module has a maximum power conversion efficiency of 25.52% and a monofacial, dual-glass design. It measures 1,762 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm, weighs 22 kg and offers a maximum power density of approximately 255 W/m².
JinkoSolar said it has integrated several technologies to increase module power density and improve aesthetics. Its Gapless Cell Array (GCA) technology eliminates conventional gaps between cells, while concealed interconnections and busbars reduce inactive areas. According to the company, the design increases the effective light-receiving area by approximately 2%, resulting in an additional 10 W of module output.
The module also features Uniform Matrix Interconnection (UMI) technology, which replaces conventional printed main busbars with distributed electrical connections. JinkoSolar said the architecture shortens current paths, reduces resistive losses and enables interconnection processes that place less mechanical stress on the cells.
For improved aesthetics, the manufacturer has incorporated its All Consistent Color (ACC) technology, which combines precise control of coating thickness and refractive index with AI-assisted cell sorting. The process is designed to minimize visible color variations between cells, encapsulation materials and the frame, resulting in a more uniform black appearance.
The panel also uses Full-Spectrum Light Trapping (FLT) technology, combining surface texturing, antireflective coatings and rear-side reflection to improve light utilization under oblique sunlight and low-irradiance conditions.
The module features a power temperature coefficient of -0.24%/C, compared with approximately -0.26%/C for JinkoSolar’s previous TOPCon products. The manufacturer also claims the new panel delivers around 30 W more power than conventional back-contact modules of comparable dimensions.
For reliability, JinkoSolar has integrated a Perimeter Moisture Barrier (PMB) featuring butyl-based edge sealing to reduce moisture ingress and the associated risk of corrosion. The module also incorporates an optimized current-shunting design intended to limit power losses and reduce hot-spot risks under partial shading.
JinkoSolar offers a 40-year product warranty and a 40-year linear power output warranty for the module, according to its technical documentation.
“Our vision for Tiger Neo 5.0 was to develop a panel tailored to premium residential rooftops,” said JinkoSolar CEO Charlie Cao.
The new residential panel expands JinkoSolar’s Tiger Neo 5.0 portfolio, which includes larger-format TOPCon modules introduced in June 2026, with power outputs exceeding 700 W and efficiencies of up to 25.91%.
JinkoSolar has identified Europe and Australia as target markets for residential applications. The company has not yet disclosed commercial availability, pricing or production volumes for the new TAC-based module.

title: China proposes stricter efficiency standards for solar manufacturers - pv magazine Global
content:
China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has proposed stricter efficiency requirements for photovoltaic manufacturers, raising minimum average conversion efficiencies for solar cells and modules and introducing separate thresholds for TOPCon, heterojunction (HJT) and back-contact (BC) technologies.
The draft 2026 Photovoltaic Manufacturing Industry Specifications, released for public consultation on Oct. 16 alongside proposed revisions to the system for listing compliant manufacturers, would replace the 2024 rules. The consultation period runs until Nov. 15.
For new and expanded solar cell production lines, the proposed minimum average conversion efficiencies are 26.2% for n-type TOPCon, 26.0% for HJT and 26.6% for BC technologies. The 2024 rules set a uniform 26.0% threshold for new n-type cells. Existing production lines would need to achieve efficiencies of at least 25.3% for TOPCon and HJT and 25.6% for BC, compared with the previous 25.0% requirement for n-type cells.
For new and expanded module production, the proposed minimum efficiencies are 24.2% for TOPCon, 24.0% for HJT and 24.4% for BC, up from a uniform 23.1% threshold for n-type modules under the 2024 rules. Existing module production would face minimum efficiency requirements of 23.4% for TOPCon and HJT and 23.7% for BC. All thresholds refer to average conversion efficiency, with bifacial modules assessed on front-side performance.
The draft also removes separate performance categories for multicrystalline and p-type crystalline silicon products while introducing requirements for emerging photovoltaic technologies. New tandem solar modules would need to achieve at least 27% efficiency, compared with 25% for existing tandem modules. New perovskite modules would face a minimum efficiency threshold of 20%.
The proposed revisions would also tighten requirements for upstream manufacturing. New polysilicon projects using the trichlorosilane process would face a comprehensive electricity consumption limit of less than 37 kWh/kg, compared with the previous general polysilicon benchmark of 53 kWh/kg. The draft separately proposes a 15 kWh/kg ceiling for new silane fluidized-bed projects and limits water consumption at new polysilicon facilities to 30 cubic meters per metric ton.
Manufacturers would continue to be required to spend at least 3% of annual sales on research, development and process improvements, but the minimum absolute expenditure would double to CNY 20 million ($2.94 million), from CNY 10 million. The existing minimum equity-capital ratio of 30% for new and expanded projects would remain unchanged.
The proposal also introduces a maximum degradation limit of 8.6% under combined environmental stress testing for crystalline silicon modules. It would strengthen oversight of manufacturers included on MIIT’s published compliance list through regular reviews and the removal of companies that no longer meet the requirements. Industry self-regulation would also be considered when evaluating applications.
MIIT states that the specifications are guidance rather than mandatory conditions for administrative approval. Their impact on investment decisions and efforts to reduce excess manufacturing capacity would therefore depend partly on how local authorities, financial institutions and industry participants apply the compliance criteria.
The proposed manufacturing standards were released on the same day that China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology proposed adding 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies to a catalogue of restricted or prohibited technology exports. Under the separate proposal, exports of certain advanced perovskite and tandem manufacturing technologies would be prohibited.
The proposed export-control revisions are also subject to public consultation, although a temporary pre-export registration requirement for the listed technologies has already taken effect. The measures target technology transfers and certain associated equipment rather than imposing a blanket ban on solar product exports.
Together, the proposals signal increased government scrutiny of domestic photovoltaic manufacturing standards and the overseas transfer of advanced production technologies. Whether the revised efficiency requirements accelerate the phaseout of excess manufacturing capacity will depend on their final wording and implementation.

title: Holosolis secures EU Innovation Fund support for 5 GW solar factory - pv magazine Global
content:
French solar manufacturer
Holosolis
has been selected for funding under the EU Innovation Fund for its Solar4EU project, which aims to establish an integrated 5 GW solar cell and module manufacturing facility in Hambach, France.
The company is advancing plans to begin production in 2027, with a gradual ramp-up to full capacity by 2030. The project has already secured more than €220 million in initial financing, including €200 million through France’s C3IV tax credit scheme. Holosolis has also brought in Chinese solar manufacturer Trina Solar as a strategic technology partner.
Solar4EU is among 12 clean-tech manufacturing projects selected under the latest Innovation Fund call. Together, the projects are requesting almost €895 million ($1.05 billion) in support for manufacturing facilities covering solar modules, heat pumps, electrolysers, electric-vehicle batteries and rare-earth permanent magnets.
Other solar-related projects include Belgium’s ReGAIN Pilot, which aims to establish a circular production line for reusable germanium substrates for solar panels.
Battery manufacturing projects selected for funding include PowerCo Spain, which plans to develop a gigafactory for prismatic lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells for electric vehicles, and Poland’s ArisEU project, which aims to establish a 9 GWh LFP battery cell manufacturing facility.
The European Commission has selected 77 net-zero technology projects to receive €3.4 billion ($3.98 billion) under the Innovation Fund, financed through revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS).
The selected projects span 23 European Economic Area countries and cover industrial decarbonisation, renewable energy, energy storage, clean-tech manufacturing, low-carbon mobility, critical raw materials and carbon management.
According to the Commission, the projects could avoid approximately 290 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent during their first 10 years of operation.
The selected projects will now enter grant agreement preparations with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA). The Commission expects the process to be completed in the first quarter of 2027.

title: The rapidly growing business of solar grazing - pv magazine Global
content:
The business of solar grazing, using animals to manage vegetation at solar sites, has taken off in along with the growth of solar in the U.S. According to Stacie Peterson, executive director of the American Solar Grazing Association (ASGA), solar grazing became a business in 2018. This was one year before the U.S. achieved two million solar installations.
United States Solar Grazing 2024 Census
was the first to attempt to capture the full scope and scale of U.S. solar grazing. Conducted by ASGA in conjunction with U.S. Department of Energy National Lab of the Rockies (NREL), the census found that over 113,000 sheep grazed through fields of solar panels on 129,000 acres of land. The 2025 census has not yet been released, but Peterson told
pv magazine USA
that she believes the numbers have greatly increased.
The ASGA Solar Grazing Map is a resource for solar grazers and solar site operators and developers to connect with each other and build partnerships. Credit: American Solar Grazing Association
What solar grazers bring to solar sites is expertise in agriculture, land stewardship, vegetation management, soil health knowledge and forage and weed knowledge, according to Peterson. Graziers provide additional benefits to solar developers or owners including their connections within the local community and their deep understanding of the land.
Having a regular physical presence at the site is another plus, which Rebekah Pierce, solar grazer and owner of New York-based J&R Pierce Family Farms said has great value to O&M teams. “It’s hard to quantify on paper what being on site means to the O&M team, but we’re there every other day. If we see an issue that needs to be addressed like a loose wire or a hole in a fence, we let them know and that issue is addressed.”
While most solar grazing is done with sheep, J&R Pierce Family Farm raises cows as well as sheep. Pierce proposed a cattle-grazing pilot to Nexamp, a solar developer that grazed livestock at 89 sites this past season across five states for a total of almost 2,000 acres, according to Keith Hevenor, communications manager.
“We began our grazing program in 2019 with just one site and have been expanding significantly each year since,” Hevenor said. “We are looking forward to even more progress next year and love that our grazing partners are able to continue an agricultural application on these solar farms while providing a necessary service for us in a safer and more sustainable way.”
The cow pilot began last summer on two of Nexamp’s solar sites in Fort Covington, New York. Five cattle, including one bull, grazed among the solar modules mounted on trackers, and it was a success with the cows showing “no unusual behavior,” according to Pierce. She said that sheep remain the most flexible option for solar sites, especially those that were not designed for grazing larger animals. Pierce noted, however, that grazing cattle is worth consideration, especially when looking at market potential and the fact that Americans consume far more beef than lamb.
J&R Pierce Family Farm grazed cattle on two of Nexamp’s solar projects in New York state. Credit: J&R Pierce Family Farm
The arrangement between the solar grazer and the developer are different depending on region and for different graziers, Peterson said. In addition to signing an agreement that works for both parties, Pierce stressed that communication is key, so it’s important to have a connection with the right person in the company, especially in light of the fact that solar projects are commonly acquired and new people take the helm.
Many times, enhancing communication requires dispelling misconceptions. Pierce said that in most cases, livestock are less risky than mechanical mowers and other farm equipment. She said sheep don’t chew on wires and damage things, they don’t kick up rocks, they’re not creating fire risk. These misconceptions, she said, just aren’t true and the benefits are many.
A main challenge for both parties is in educating one another about priorities and how they can work together successfully.
“The more corporate world of solar companies can be quite the dichotomy from the one of farmers/ranchers, and vice versa,” said Matt Kovarik of Maine-based Black Earth Grazing. “Once we both do a little work of educating each other on our systems, the partnership can serve both interests and work out quite successfully.”
ReVision Energy, a renewable energy contracting company based in New England, has partnered since 2024 with Black Earth Grazing on a dual-management solar grazing program. It’s been so successful that the farmers changed the name from Black Earth Forest Farm to Black Earth Grazing. They started with 40 ewes and now manage a flock of several hundred. They’re currently responsible for 11 of ReVision’s community solar sites, and the flock keeps growing as more solar sites become available.
The many benefits of solar grazing for solar companies include vegetation management that requires fewer fossil fuels than mechanical methods, a human presence on site and a connection to local graziers who provide products to the community pay taxes, support local services and more.
“We are there to provide vegetation management, but we are a bit more invested in the land and its productivity than a mowing crew would be, as we are deriving benefits from a healthy well-managed pasture that feeds our sheep,” said .
For the grazier, the benefits include the pay they receive for performing land stewardship and vegetation management and access to a greater land area that enables them to expand the size of their operations.
Solar grazing offers a cost-effective solution to land stewardship and vegetation management, with many other tangible benefits as a bonus. For solar developers interested in solar grazing, ASGA offers a
one-day workshop
for site operations and management teams, developers, asset managers and sustainability teams. Participants receive a Level 1 Solar Grazing Management Certification.
Register for
pv magazine USA week
to learn more about solar grazing October 22 in a keynote fireside chat with Silicon Ranch, one of the leading solar grazing installers in the U.S.

title: A 50-Year-Old Mystery: Scientists Discover What May Have Killed Brazil’s Frogs
content:
A wild clay robber frog (Haddadus binotatus) seen near the Boracéia Biological Station, São Paulo, Brazil. Credit: Jack Boyette, Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute
Museum specimens are helping scientists trace a deadly fungus linked to mysterious frog disappearances in Brazil nearly half a century ago.
Frog species that escaped a wave of population declines in Brazil carried widespread infections with a deadly fungus. Yet museum specimens from the species that suffered the steepest losses showed no detectable infection.
These findings come from an investigation that points to amphibian chytridiomycosis, commonly called chytrid, as the likely cause of die-offs at Boracéia Biological Station between 1979 and 1982.
Caused by the microscopic fungus
Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis
, the disease can have very different consequences for different species. Scientists at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU) reported their findings in
Molecular Ecology
The preserved amphibians came from collections made at Boracéia by William Ronald Heyer, a former curator of amphibians and reptiles, and held at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Natural History. The researchers suspect that differences in susceptibility could explain why the species hit hardest left no detectable infections in the specimens available for testing.
“It’s important to keep in mind that not all species suffered catastrophic losses at Boracéia,” said Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the study. “The species that didn’t decline may have naturally tolerated the fungus, allowing them to become infected without suffering mass mortality. By contrast, the species that declined most dramatically may have been so susceptible that infected frogs died before Heyer could collect them.”
The timing points to chytrid
Comparing collection dates revealed a different pattern. Tests detected no chytrid infection in specimens collected before 1979, whereas more than half of those collected during the 1980s tested positive. Evidence of the fungus therefore appeared around the period when amphibians were disappearing.
The comparison covered more than 370 museum specimens representing 17 species. Heyer had collected them during five field campaigns, two in the 1970s before the sudden declines and three in the 1980s afterward. That record allowed the NZCBI researchers to investigate both the pathogen’s arrival and changes in how commonly it infected amphibians.
Climate change and extreme weather had previously been proposed as explanations for Boracéia’s losses.
“While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances,” Boyette said.
The infection timeline, considered alongside the differences among species, suggests that the fungus spread rapidly through a community of amphibians that had not previously encountered it. Establishing such a history is difficult when the suspected pathogen was unknown at the time of the deaths.
Researchers began observing drastic amphibian declines across Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, a global hotspot of frog biodiversity, in the 1970s. Chytrid is believed to have originated in Asia and likely spread worldwide during the 1970s and 1980s, but scientists did not formally describe the fungus until 1999. By then, catastrophic population losses had pushed hundreds of amphibian species around the world to the brink of extinction or beyond.
“After almost 50 years, we still aren’t confident what caused many historical amphibian die-offs, making these declines some of the most enduring cold cases in wildlife epidemiology,” Boyette said.
Signs of recovery despite persistent chytrid
To see how Boracéia’s amphibians were faring decades later, the team made six visits between 2022 and 2024, working with researchers from the University of São Paulo. They located 12 of the 17 species represented in Heyer’s collection. The other five remain unaccounted for. Their absence raises the possibility that they have disappeared locally, although their fate is still uncertain.
Most amphibian species at the station now appear to have recovered since the early 1980s, despite continued chytrid infections. The researchers interpret modern infection patterns as evidence that widespread tolerance has evolved among species that previously declined, likely helping them persist and recover. DNA collected from museum samples is now being used to investigate the genomic mechanisms that shaped these amphibians’ historical responses to the fungus.
Filling gaps in chytrid’s history
Boracéia provides evidence from one site, and the researchers caution against extending its findings to the Atlantic Forest as a whole. The approach nevertheless offers a model for investigating other historical outbreaks, particularly those that unfolded before scientists recognized the disease involved.
“Museum collectors could not have anticipated how important their collections would be to our modern conservation challenges, but without them, we would never be able to detect pathogens that went unnoticed for decades and reconstruct disease outbreaks that would otherwise remain a mystery,” said Michael Campana, a genomicist at NZCBI who participated in the study.
Other ongoing projects aim to fill gaps in historical specimen records using ancient environmental DNA, genetic material preserved in the environment. Together with research on museum samples, these efforts seek to reconstruct chytrid’s emergence, spread, and effects over the past century, building a clearer picture of its toll on biodiversity.
Reconstructing past outbreaks may also help researchers anticipate the consequences of emerging fungal threats. Another pathogen,
B. salamandrivorans
, is already threatening salamanders in Europe and could pose a serious risk to salamander populations in North America.
Reference: “Overcoming Detection Lag in a Cryptic Panzootic: Chytrid Invasion Linked to Historically Enigmatic Amphibian Declines in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest” by Jack L. Boyette, Tamilie Carvalho, David Rodriguez, Wesley J. Neely, Daniel Medina, Renato A. Martins, Robert J. Ossiboff, Zaira Gomez, William C. Vuyk, Shannon M. Buttimer, Karen A. Paniagua Torres, Ananda Brito de Assis, Carlos A. Navas, Carly R. Muletz-Wolz, Michael G. Campana, Corinne L. Richards-Zawacki and C. Guilherme Becker, 14 October 2026,
Molecular Ecology
DOI: 10.1111/mec.70573

title: Scientists Solve a 30-Year Biological Mystery and the Discovery Could Change How We Treat Inflammation
content:
Tiny, transparent, fast-growing — zebrafish are an ideal model organism for studying some biological processes. Credit: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Scientists have solved a decades-old biological mystery, revealing an unexpected dual role for a key inflammatory signaling pathway.
Scientists have uncovered a surprising function of a molecule that controls inflammation: It not only recruits immune cells to fight infections but also helps protect healthy tissue from damage. The discovery, published October 7 in
, solves a biological mystery that puzzled researchers for more than 30 years.
The findings from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) could advance research into cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma.
An Unexpected Cause of Inflammation
The molecule, called 5-oxoETE, summons white blood cells to infection sites, where they attack harmful microorganisms.
“They flood the site with toxic substances to kill the bacteria,” says MSK cell biologist Philipp Niethammer, PhD. “But this can cause damage to healthy cells if it gets out of control.”
When researcher Miklos Lengyel, MD, PhD, disabled hcar1-4 (the zebrafish version of the human gene OXER1), which allows cells to detect 5-oxoETE, the fish unexpectedly developed intestinal inflammation without an infection.
“So if you remove the receptor that detects the signal, you’d expect less inflammation, not more,” Dr. Lengyel says.
“It made absolutely no sense,” he says. “I had to prove using several different methods before the rest of the lab was convinced.”
A Hidden Cellular Defense
Further experiments revealed that 5-oxoETE activates a protective process involving NUDIX hydrolases, enzymes that remove damaged DNA building blocks. Without this protection, intestinal cells became vulnerable to chemical stress from normal gut bacteria, leading to cell death and inflammation.
“As it turns out, this signal isn’t just an alarm, it’s also a shield,” Dr. Niethammer says.
“This makes sense when you think about it,” he adds. “These immune cells unleash chemical warfare against a pathogen, and organisms have evolved an elegant way of protecting healthy cells at the same time.”
Left to right: Zaza Gelashvili, Dr. Miklos Lengyel, Dr. Philipp Niethammer, and Dr. Yanan Ma Credit: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center
Solving a 30-Year Mystery
In a separate investigation, Yanan Ma, PhD, identified DHRS7 as the gene responsible for producing the enzyme that generates 5-oxoETE. Scientists had observed this enzyme’s activity in 1992 but had never identified its genetic source.
“Typically, when you have a paper with two first authors like Yanan and Miklos, there is just one story that two people contributed to equally,” Dr. Niethammer says. “But this paper is not like that. In this paper, there are two separate projects led by two different authors that came together as one larger discovery. And I think that’s extremely important to note.”
Zebrafish were crucial because mice lack a known immune cell receptor for 5-oxoETE.
“Mice and rats are the primary model used in biomedical research,” Dr. Ma says. “It makes sense, they’re mammals, and there’s about an 80% overlap between their genes and ours.”
“This means that you can’t study the pathway in mice,” she explains. “But the pathway is intact in fish. So picking the right alternative model was critical to advancing our understanding of how the human body responds.”
Implications for Cancer and Inflammatory Disease
Mutations affecting DHRS7 and OXER1 have been identified in certain cancers, while disrupted 5-oxoETE signaling has also been associated with inflammatory bowel disease and asthma.
“More research is needed, but there’s a possibility that activating the pathway could increase the resilience of the gut to oxidative stress, which might help counteract damage caused by radiation therapy or chemotherapy,” Dr. Lengyel says.
The researchers also connected the pathway to physical injuries. Mechanical stress releases arachidonic acid, a molecule used to produce 5-oxoETE.
“There’s a mechanical component to the pathway that’s upstream of what Yanan and Miklos have been studying,” explains doctoral student Zaza Gelashvili, MS. “You can think of it as the first step in a chain reaction: Physical stress unlocks the raw material, oxidative stress drives the conversion, and DHRS7 amplifies the signal.”
“What we are really studying is a pathway that integrates two completely different kinds of stress, mechanical and metabolic, and converts them into a single, coordinated, protective response,” Dr. Niethammer says.
Reference: “5-oxoETE links redox control of epithelial damage detection and resilience” by Yanan Ma, Miklós Lengyel, King Lam Hui, Yohannes A. Ambaw, Zaza Gelashvili, Leehyeon Kim, Ritchie Ly, Siyang Peng, Meysoon Quraishi, Tobias C. Walther, Robert V. Farese Jr and Philipp Niethammer, 7 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11121-2
The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (R35GM140883); an MSK Basic Research Innovation Award; a Starr Foundation Program for Discovery Science grant; a Tow Foundation fellowship; a Marie-Josée Kravis Women in Science Endeavor (WISE) fellowship; a Crohn’s Colitis Foundation Research Fellows Award (1268111); an Experimental Immuno-Oncology Scholars fellowship; and core facility services funding in part by MSK’s National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support grant (P30CA008748).

title: Scientists Discover Exercise Changes the Body in Ways We Never Fully Understood
content:
Exercise affects far more than muscle, but its molecular effects vary across the body. By mapping changes across 22 tissues in mice, scientists uncovered a complex network of responses that could offer new insights into training, recovery, and long-term health. Credit: Shutterstock
Salk Institute researchers have created a molecular map of how healthy mice respond to exercise, offering clues that could help improve performance and reduce injury risk.
Exercise can help the body resist disease and dysfunction and recover from illness. Studies have also linked it to more than 30 percent lower mortality from all causes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Explaining those benefits is harder, partly because studies in people generally rely on blood and muscle samples, leaving researchers with an incomplete picture of how exercise changes other organs.
Researchers at the Salk Institute turned to mice to follow those changes through more of the body. They compared young male and female mice that ran voluntarily on a wheel for eight weeks with mice that remained sedentary, creating a first-of-its-kind molecular atlas spanning 22 tissues. The study was published in
on October 15, 2026.
No single gene responded everywhere
Exercise altered the activity of nearly half the genes examined in at least one tissue, yet no single gene’s activity changed in all 22. Those comparisons came from bulk RNA sequencing, which measures gene activity across whole tissue samples. Rather than revealing one response shared everywhere, the analysis showed that tissues adapted in different ways.
The researchers also cataloged the small molecules that cells use and produce during metabolism in eight tissues and plasma, the liquid part of blood. Alongside this metabolomics analysis, they used proteomics to measure protein levels in four specific leg muscles, examining a hamstring muscle, two calf muscles, and the quadriceps.
Manoj Hariharan (left), Geraldine Maier (center), and Ramesh Ramasamy (right) debuted a molecular atlas of exercise-associated changes in mice, defining the healthy, exercised-trained state, which could help improve performance and prevent injury. Credit: Salk Institute
“Exercise doesn’t just change our muscles, it changes many of our organs and cells at different levels—some short-term, some long-term,” says co-first and co-corresponding author Geraldine Maier, PhD, a staff scientist at Salk. “Our experimental setup allows us to capture that detail across tissues, and sexes, and in muscle, down to the individual cell types.”
Training changes DNA marks in muscle
Skeletal muscle accounted for most of the changes in gene activity, and the strong responses in leg muscles prompted the researchers to examine three of them more closely. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing, they could distinguish neighboring cell types and compare their gene activity instead of averaging their responses together. They also conducted the first single-cell analysis of DNA methylation in muscle after exercise.
In some muscle cell types, training changed chemical marks on DNA that help regulate gene activity, while other cell types showed no such changes. These marks are added through a process called DNA methylation. Changes in their pattern can be more persistent than shifts in RNA or protein levels, allowing this form of epigenetic regulation to have lasting effects on how particular cell types and whole tissues behave.
“Exercise impacts the whole body, not just your muscles, so an atlas like ours that looks more holistically at many tissues is key to understanding the true impact of exercise,” says co-first author Manoj Hariharan, PhD, a former senior staff scientist at Salk. “That’s also why single-cell studies are so important—there are so many cell type-specific changes that get lost in bulk sequencing. I hope our work highlights that and encourages more single-cell atlases, and especially multi-omic single-cell atlases, moving forward.”
Exercise responses vary by sex and time
Female mice showed broader changes in gene activity and distinct expression patterns compared with males. The epigenetic response to training also differed strongly by sex.
To capture variation across daily biological rhythms, the researchers collected tissues during both the active and resting phases of the mice’s circadian cycle. Most tissues showed greater exercise-related changes when sampled during the active phase, with the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung as exceptions.
“Our atlas provides a comprehensive resource for understanding the systemic molecular adaptations to endurance exercise,” says co-first author Ramesh Ramasamy, PhD, a former computational biologist at Salk. “Now that we have all this data, researchers can begin developing strategies that harness exercise—either alone or in combination with other interventions—to ensure we all live long, healthy lives.”
51 genes distinguish trained muscle
The researchers have already used the gene activity dataset to develop a 51-gene exercise signature, a pattern that distinguishes exercise-trained muscle from sedentary muscle in both mice and humans. It could help identify biomarkers, measurable indicators of a biological state, and support research into muscle disuse and dysfunction.
“Now that we have the data,” adds Maier, “labs can identify one gene or metabolic pathway they find interesting, then dissect that mechanism. Our atlas gives the field a shared foundation to build on.”
How long those molecular changes last remains unresolved. Researchers still need to determine how long training must continue before lasting changes develop and whether cells retain a memory of exercise for months or years.
Reference: “Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise” by Geraldine Maier, Manoj Hariharan, Ramesh K. Ramasamy, Aidan Glina, Laura van Rosmalen, Suraj J. Pathak, Shaunak Deota, Sahil Patel, Terry Lin, Michael Tun Yin Lam, Hiep D. title: Scientists Unlock the Secret of One of the World’s Smallest Flowering Plants
content:
Duckweed is one of the smallest flowering plants in the world, forming tiny green fronds that float on the surface of freshwater ponds and lakes. Credit: Shutterstock
Tiny aquatic plants are attracting scientific attention for their untapped potential as future food sources, including for space missions.
Some of the world’s smallest flowering plants have found a way to fit the basic architecture of much larger species into a body just a few millimeters (about 0.1 inch) across. Researchers at the University of Nottingham discovered that duckweed retains essential structures found in larger plant shoots, but these components are tightly compressed and fused rather than lost.
Using advanced microscopy and gene expression analysis, the scientists examined how duckweed organizes its remarkably compact body. Their findings, published in
Current Biology
, challenge the assumption that extreme miniaturization necessarily involves losing parts of a plant’s original structure.
Duckweed on end of pencil. Credit: University of Nottingham
How Duckweed Shrinks Without Losing Its Blueprint
Dr. Anthony Bishopp, who led the research, explained: “We were interested to find out how a complete plant body plan can be packed into such a tiny space. While miniaturization in animals is often associated with the loss of organs or body structures, we have revealed that duckweeds have taken a different route.”
“What surprised us is that, when we looked closely, the basic organization of the shoot was still there. Rather than throwing away parts of the blueprint, duckweed appears to have compressed and fused its components into an incredibly compact plant. That gives us a new way of thinking about how plants can evolve to become so small.”
Tiny Plants With Potential for Future Food Production
Despite their miniature size, duckweeds belong to a group of flowering plants whose relatives include some of the largest herbaceous species. Scientists are increasingly investigating duckweed as a potential source of food and protein, both on Earth and during future space missions.
Unlike major agricultural crops, which have undergone thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding, duckweed remains largely unexplored as a cultivated food source. Its unusual anatomy has also been poorly understood, making it difficult to fully explain how the plant grows and develops. The new findings provide a foundation for investigating these processes and identifying traits that could eventually be improved for cultivation.
Dr. Alex Ware, a co-author of the study, said: “Duckweeds are astonishingly small, so it is tempting to think of them as either primitive plants or simply as having lost parts, but this is not the case. Our research adds to growing evidence from across the research community about this plant and will help efforts to turn them into a future crop.”
Reference: “Miniaturization of duckweeds occurred through compression of the angiosperm body plan” by Alexander Ware, Emily Chan, Rahul Bhosale and Anthony Bishopp, 7 October 2026,
Current Biology
DOI: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.035

title: Antarctica’s Sea Ice Has Gone From Record Highs to Near-Record Lows
content:
Antarctic sea ice reached its annual maximum extent on September 14, 2026—the third-lowest maximum in the satellite record. Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison
Antarctica’s sea ice has plunged from record highs to its third-lowest winter peak, revealing a dramatic reversal in the frozen continent’s recent history.
Antarctic sea ice reached one of its lowest winter peaks ever recorded in 2026, continuing a striking shift in ice coverage around the frozen continent. Its annual maximum was the third lowest since satellites began tracking sea ice in the late 1970s.
Antarctica and the Arctic have very different geographies. The Arctic is an ocean surrounded by land, while Antarctica is a massive continent encircled by ocean. This allows Antarctic sea ice to spread across a much larger area during winter. However, as the ice extends into warmer waters farther from the continent, it becomes more vulnerable to melting when summer arrives. Antarctic sea ice typically reaches its greatest extent in September, near the end of the Southern Hemisphere’s winter, before shrinking to its annual minimum in February.
NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) reported that Antarctic sea ice likely reached its annual maximum on September 14 (above). At its peak, the ice covered approximately 17.59 million square kilometers (6.79 million square miles). That made 2026 the year with the third-lowest winter maximum in the satellite record.
Antarctic Sea Ice Shifts From Record Highs to Historic Lows
For decades, Antarctic sea ice appeared to be moving in the opposite direction of Arctic sea ice. Between 1979 and 2014, the total extent of Antarctic sea ice grew by approximately 1 percent per decade. However, scientists remain uncertain whether this increase reflected a significant underlying trend, since ice coverage around Antarctica can fluctuate substantially from one year to the next.
The growth was particularly notable between 2012 and 2014, when Antarctic winter sea ice set new records for three consecutive years. During the same period, Arctic sea ice was experiencing a steep decline.
That pattern changed dramatically after 2014. Antarctic sea ice stopped expanding in 2015, and substantial declines began appearing in 2016. Although ice coverage has occasionally recovered somewhat, it has generally remained below normal in the years since.
The most extreme conditions occurred in 2023, when Antarctica recorded both its lowest summer minimum and lowest winter maximum in the satellite record. Researchers are continuing to track these changes to determine whether the persistent decline represents a lasting transformation in Antarctic sea ice or could still be explained by statistical fluctuations.
How Satellites Monitor Antarctic Sea Ice Through Clouds
Scientists track the extent of Antarctic sea ice using satellites equipped with passive microwave sensors. These instruments detect microwave energy naturally released by Earth’s surface. Because frozen sea ice emits more microwave energy than open ocean water, researchers can distinguish between the two and calculate how much of the ocean is covered by ice.
One major advantage of this technology is its ability to detect sea ice through clouds. Unlike conventional optical imagery, microwave observations are not blocked by cloud cover, allowing scientists to monitor Antarctica’s frozen waters consistently even when weather conditions are poor.
The continuous satellite record began in late 1978 with measurements from NASA’s Nimbus-7. Observations later came from satellites operated under the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP), beginning in 1987, and NASA’s Aqua satellite from 2002 through 2011.
In 2025, researchers began incorporating observations from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s GCOM-W satellite, helping maintain the long-running record of Antarctic sea ice changes.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using data from the
National Snow and Ice Data Center

title: The Amazon Is Burning Again, and NASA Warns the Worst Is Yet To Come
content:
A dangerous chain reaction of wildfires is unfolding across the tropics, and the Amazon rainforest is now caught in its path.
A dangerous El Niño-driven wildfire cascade has reached the Amazon, and NASA scientists warn that the worst may still be ahead as hidden fires spread beneath the rainforest canopy.
El Niño is fueling a chain reaction of wildfires across the tropics, with fires first emerging in equatorial Asia before spreading to the central and eastern Amazon rainforest.
While tornadoes and thunderstorms can cause widespread damage in a matter of minutes, El Niño influences weather conditions over the course of months. In 2026, the climate pattern has intensified drought across the Amazon, leaving vast areas of rainforest increasingly vulnerable to fire. Scientists warn that the region is only beginning what could become an unusually long and destructive fire season.
Satellite observations have revealed a dramatic increase in fires and smoke emissions across the central and eastern Amazon since September 2026. The surge is apparent in several monitoring systems, including NASA’s
Fire Information for Resource Management System
(FIRMS), the
Global Fire Emissions Database
(GFED), and
NASA Worldview
. The affected area extends from the forests surrounding Manaus and Santarém, two important commercial and transportation hubs, eastward toward the mouth of the Amazon River.
Thick Wildfire Smoke Blankets the Amazon
On October 12, 2026, NASA’s Aqua satellite captured an image showing enormous plumes of smoke rising from fires on both sides of the Amazon River. The image was recorded by MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer), one of the satellite’s Earth-observing instruments.
That same day, Manaus, the capital of Brazil’s Amazonas state, was engulfed in dense smoke. City officials
reported
dangerously polluted air, with concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exceeding 135 micrograms per cubic meter. That level placed air quality in the second-worst category of a regional
air quality index
The smoke brought significant disruptions to the city of more than 2 million residents. Schools shut down, public events were called off, and children’s sports leagues suspended activities as authorities issued warnings about unhealthy air conditions, according to
news reports
Scientists Warn of an El Niño Wildfire Cascade
According to Douglas Morton, an Earth system scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, the fires around Manaus and Santarém are part of a much larger pattern. He describes it as a “cascade” of tropical wildfires driven by changes in rainfall associated with El Niño.
The sequence typically begins near the equator, where dry conditions contribute to
peat fires in Indonesia
. Increased burning then develops in the central and eastern Amazon. Morton and researchers from the University of California, Irvine; Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam; and the University of Maryland documented this connection in a
2017 study
examining the devastating wildfire season associated with the
2015–2016 El Niño
. A similar sequence occurred in 2023.
The wildfire activity unfolding in 2026 appears to be following that same progression. Since August, parts of Indonesia have experienced persistent drought, widespread fires, and heavy smoke. In October, wildfires
destroyed hundreds of homes
, while thick smoke
covered entire islands
on most days.
“Now, in the Amazon, we’re seeing the second domino in the cascade fall,” Morton said, referring to the growing number of fires in the Brazilian states of Pará and Amazonas.
More Amazon Wildfires Could Be Coming
Scientists expect the next phase of the wildfire cascade to develop farther north during November and December. Areas at risk include the Brazilian states of Roraima and Amapá, northern Pará, and parts of Venezuela, Guyana, and Suriname.
The danger could then shift southward. Morton predicts that drought and wildfire risk will reach their highest levels in the southern Amazon regions of Brazil and Paraguay around August and September 2027.
“It’s so striking—and frustrating—that this is happening all over again,” said Morton.
One particularly troubling aspect is that many of the forests now burning were also damaged during the El Niño events of 2015 and 2023. Fire can be especially destructive in tropical rainforests because most native plants and animals have not evolved to withstand frequent burning.
Previous wildfires have also weakened parts of the forest, leaving behind damaged and partially charred trees. Morton explained that these changes make the remaining vegetation more vulnerable, potentially allowing some fires to burn with greater intensity than before.
For communities around Manaus and Santarém, relief may not arrive until seasonal rains return in December 2026 or January 2027. However, Morton emphasized that regions farther north and south still have an opportunity to reduce their risk.
“Given the intensity of this El Niño, this really is the year for people to avoid burning at all costs,” Morton said.
Extreme Drought Turns Human-Started Fires Dangerous
Despite the enormous number of wildfires affecting the Amazon, lightning is responsible for very few of them. The Brazilian Amazon is normally so wet that lightning starts
less than 1 percent
of fires. According to Morton, human activity is responsible for the overwhelming majority of the fires currently burning there.
What makes 2026 especially dangerous is the severity of the drought, which has been intensified by El Niño. Brazil’s National Institute of Meteorology reported that rainfall in Manaus was 95 percent below normal in
and 60 percent below normal in
September
Many of the major fires began as controlled burns used to manage agricultural land, such as clearing unwanted vegetation from pastures or removing crop remnants from fields. But with the forest floor unusually dry, some of those fires escaped their intended boundaries and spread into the rainforest’s understory.
Shane Coffield, an assistant research scientist at the University of Maryland who works at NASA Goddard, said satellite analysis suggests that between 50 and 70 uncontrolled fires are currently burning in the Santarém area alone.
NASA Discovers Hidden Amazon Fires That Satellites Miss
The true extent of the burning may be even greater than official fire monitoring systems suggest.
Through a
NASA Earth Action project
, Coffield is examining observations from VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) to find fires that fall below the detection thresholds used for official FIRMS fire data.
These additional detections, referred to as “candidate fires,” could help researchers build a more complete picture of wildfire activity. Coffield intends to provide their locations to scientists at
MapBiomas
, a collaborative network of universities, nongovernmental organizations, and technology companies that tracks fires and changes in land use throughout the Amazon.
“For the area around Santarém, we’ve identified about 40 percent more fires than you’ll see in active fire counts from FIRMS,” said Coffield.
Detecting every fire from space is difficult, particularly in dense tropical forests. Heavy smoke, cloud cover, and thick tree canopies can interfere with satellite sensors by obscuring the infrared heat signals emitted by flames. Smaller, less intense fires moving through vegetation beneath the forest canopy are especially easy to overlook.
This means that some of the days with the thickest smoke can produce surprisingly few satellite fire detections, even when extensive burning is taking place.
“On some of the smokiest days, we have very few detections from MODIS and VIIRS, and we know that isn’t right.”
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data from NASA

title: OpenAI’s ‘Pacing 2.0’ Problem: How Smart Is Too Smart?
content: OpenAI is bound to get a reality check soon, if it hasn’t already, on how difficult it is to “pace” AI technology, let alone getting all the frontier AI developers to agree on how to do so together. CEO Sam Altman last week walked employees through three proposals the industry has discussed for how to safely develop AI, we reported yesterday. Those options included plans for developing an international organization akin to the International Atomic Energy Agency ; merging the frontier labs into a single entity that would develop, test and distribute models; or a scenario, however far-fetched, in which one lab races ahead of the others and literally crushes their GPUs, ending their ability to catch up. It goes without saying that each of those options has major issues. But we’ll say it anyway. An IAEA-esque organization would require international cooperation from countries developing state-of-the-art AI, including China, which likely is wary of slowing down development given the hostile feelings firms like Anthropic have expressed towards it. The second proposal, the “Demis plan,” named after DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis , would be similar to CERN , the physics lab jointly controlled by dozens of countries to pursue cutting edge research. But for now, joint efforts like that might be a tough sell, given that the leading AI developers are for-profit entities, each with different shareholders. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are currently pursuing a self-regulating body that, while much less ambitious than CERN, have already disagreed on important points, my colleague Leo and I reported last month. The third option, the Eliezer plan, named after LessWrong creator Eliezer Yudkowsky , is perhaps the most troubling, though people at OpenAI might jokingly say Anthropic is pursuing it. During Altman’s talk with his employees last week, he also said that OpenAI can’t afford to give up too much ground right now, but within the next year it will need to decide which long-term path to pursue. Altman refers to this decision as “pacing 2.0.” The current approach, “pacing 1.0,” refers to the continued release of frontier models that have passed certain safety tests, while still disclosing any safety concerns associated with the new models, the people who overheard his comments said. As part of pacing 2.0, OpenAI will also need to adopt a “speed limit” on recursive self improvement —AI that can perpetually improve itself—or some sort of criteria that will help it decide when it should stop developing or releasing ultra-advanced AI, Altman said. Developing such criteria would be extremely difficult and somewhat subjective, however. For instance, one might argue that an AI that’s 10 times better than a human scientist is tolerable because it can still be controlled and monitored by existing technology, but not an AI that’s 1,000 times or 10,000 times better than a scientist, which may be able to sidestep those guardrails. But it’s unclear how to even measure such levels of intelligence. It’s safe to say that the industry debates about safety have just begun, and OpenAI and its rivals have their work cut out for them. Here’s what else is going on… AI Deep Dive: Interpretability Could Train Models More Efficiently, Says World Mechanics CEO Earlier this year, a paper called “Interpreting Physics in Video World Models” tackled a key question about how AI models predict the physical world: do they learn separate representations for physical concepts such as velocity and gravity? Or are those concepts lumped together in the patterns the models learn? It turns out that these concepts tend to be “highly entangled” in video models, said Sonia Joseph , the lead author of that paper, and the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics , in the latest episode of The Information’s AI Deep Dive . Joseph argues that separating out these concepts to ensure the model learns a distinct representation for velocity and gravity and so on could help train models with less data and compute. For example, at some point while training an AI model, a researcher could look into the math underlying the model to tell whether it has learned object permanence, and if it has not, add in more training data focused specifically on that capability, she said. Alternatively, scaling up current world models without new approaches could work, she argued. “It'll just take 20 years and be highly inefficient and consume 20 nuclear reactors of compute.”— Rocket Drew Big Number Nscale and Anthropic are in talks for a second compute deal worth roughly $45 billion, on top of the $45 billion, six-year agreement the two companies struck in August for 460 megawatts of Nvidia Vera Rubin chips at Nscale's West Virginia campus.
