title: Forgotten Material From the 1960s Is Hiding Something Unexpected
content:
Dr. Mengke Liu, assistant professor of physics at The University of Texas at Dallas, operates a two-dimensional transfer stage inside a glove box to fabricate atomically thin quantum devices. She and her colleagues discovered an unusual atomic pattern in a uranium-based material that gives it a rare combination of magnetic properties, a finding that could open new pathways for designing advanced electronic and computer memory devices. Credit: University of Texas at Dallas
A long-overlooked material has revealed a hidden atomic pattern that challenges conventional expectations about magnetism.
A uranium compound that has received little scientific attention for decades has been found to contain a previously unknown atomic structure with unusual magnetic properties. The discovery could help researchers identify materials capable of supporting faster, more resilient computer memory.
Scientists discovered a repeating, twisted arrangement of atoms known as a chiral superlattice inside uranium oxytelluride (UOTe). The structure appears to play a central role in how electrons move through the crystal, which exhibits an uncommon combination of two different types of magnetism. The findings were published online October 7 in
A Hidden Atomic Pattern Revealed by Microscopy
Dr. Mengke Liu, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas, discovered the structure while examining crystals synthesized by Dr. Sheng Ran, an associate professor of physics at Washington University in St. Louis. Liu began studying the material while working as a Harvard Quantum Initiative Postdoctoral Fellow, before joining UT Dallas in 2025. Using transmission electron microscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy, she investigated the crystal at atomic resolution.
“I was originally studying this material for an entirely different reason,” Liu said. “When I examined it with high-resolution microscopy, I found a naturally occurring superstructure no one had recognized before.”
The newly identified superlattice consists of a larger, repeating atomic arrangement with a predominantly left-handed or right-handed twist, a property known as chirality. The researchers found that this organization influences electron behavior and is associated with the material’s unusual magnetic characteristics.
Two Forms of Magnetism in One Material
The crystal displays characteristics of both ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. In ferromagnetic materials, atomic magnetic moments align to produce an overall magnetization. In antiferromagnetic materials, neighboring magnetic moments point in opposing directions, typically canceling one another so that the material has no net magnetization.
“Finding a single material that combines both of these properties is interesting fundamentally,” Liu said.
A research team at Harvard University, led by Dr. Suyang Xu, the John L. Loeb Associate Professor of the Natural Sciences and a corresponding author of the study, was independently investigating the same compound. The teams compared results from complementary experiments and conducted additional measurements, confirming that the unusual atomic superstructure is an important factor controlling how electrons travel through the material.
Potential for Faster and More Reliable Memory
Antiferromagnetic materials offer potential advantages for computer memory because they are generally less sensitive to external magnetic fields and can support faster operation than conventional ferromagnets. A material combining characteristics of both could provide new possibilities for magnetic memory technologies, although practical devices based on the discovery have not yet been demonstrated.
“If those advantages can be harnessed, memory devices could potentially become both faster and more robust,” Liu said.
Computational analyses also suggest that hundreds of related compounds might contain comparable superlattice structures. This expands the range of materials researchers can investigate for similar electronic and magnetic behavior.
“This study provides a new way of looking for materials with these unusual properties,” Liu said. “Instead of focusing only on the fundamental atomic arrangement, we can also now explore larger superstructures that might influence how electrons behave.”
A Material Known Since the 1960s Holds New Possibilities
Uranium oxytelluride was first known to scientists decades before the discovery of its unusual superlattice. Modern microscopy techniques have now made it possible to examine structural features that earlier investigations could not resolve.
“Uranium oxytelluride has been known since the 1960s, but it has been largely ignored in research since then. Now, with today’s techniques, we’re able to uncover and study properties that previously were hidden,” Liu said.
Reference: “A chiral superlattice route to spin-split topological antiferromagnetism” by Thao Dinh, Mengke Liu, Jian-Xiang Qiu, Sougata Mardanya, Suk Hyun Sung, Xuan Hoang Le, Christopher Broyles, Chengfeng Zhu, Qiaozhi Xu, Haotian Chen, Zack Rehfuss, Yu-Fei Liu, Xiaoyu Zeng, Houchen Li, Peng Guo, Jinchen Liu, Tianye Huang, Jingtian Shi, Michael Smith, Joanna M. Blawat, John Singleton, Ross McDonald, Iván E. Lukin, Jennifer E. Hoffman, Sugata Chowdhury, Qiong Ma, Kai Sun, Ismail El Baggari, Sheng Ran, Talieh S. Ghiasi, Hongkun Park, Philip Kim and Su-Yang Xu, 7 October 2026,

title: Study Finds the Arctic Could Lose Far More Sea Ice Than Scientists Previously Predicted
content:
Ancient evidence from a warmer Arctic is challenging scientists’ predictions about the region’s future sea ice. Credit: Sarah Das
Clues from a warmer Arctic 6,000 years ago suggest the region could lose a million square kilometers more winter sea ice than scientists previously expected.
The loss of Arctic sea ice has been linked to colder winters and heavier snowfall in the UK, the rest of northern Europe, and North America. The ice regulates how much heat and moisture the ocean releases into the atmosphere, so changes in its cover can influence weather far beyond the polar region.
Climate models disagree most about how much ice will cover the Arctic in winter, making its future particularly difficult to predict. Using evidence from a warmer Arctic 6,000 years ago, researchers have now revised those projections downward by about one million square kilometers, or roughly 386,000 square miles. The findings, published in
Nature Geoscience
, come after the Arctic recorded its lowest maximum sea ice extent since modern measurements began in March 2025, a record tied again this year.
Ancient algae sharpen Arctic ice forecasts
Researchers from the University of Cambridge and the Centro de Investigación en Matematicas (CIMAT) in Mexico compiled the largest-ever database of a key substance produced by algae living in sea ice. Called IP25, this biomarker was measured in ocean sediment cores dating to the mid-Holocene, when subtle shifts in Earth’s orbit contributed to warmer Arctic conditions and reduced ice cover. Alongside IP25, the team measured complementary biomarkers from organisms that live in open water. Together, these traces allowed them to estimate how much sea ice covered the ocean thousands of years ago.
“The scientific community has amassed lots of paleoclimate records over recent decades, but it’s remained a challenge to directly link these records to future projections, since there is uncertainty at both ends,” said lead author Crystal Fu, from Cambridge’s Scott Polar Research Institute.
Arctic sea ice from the air. Credit: Sarah Das
Although the mid-Holocene warming had a different cause from today’s warming, Fu said the ice would respond in the same way. “It doesn’t matter if the warming is natural variation or caused by human activity: if it warms, sea ice is going to melt,” she said.
Less winter ice than previously projected
In the historical simulations, the weighting removed the models’ collective tendency to overestimate winter sea ice, while the range of uncertainty in the projections narrowed by as much as 85%.
“When we apply the model weights to historical simulations, we completely eliminated the positive bias,” said Fu. “The future projections similarly end up being lower than previous estimates, by about a million square kilometers.”
Applying the revised weights to precipitation projections also suggested that snowfall over southeast Greenland and rainfall in the Mediterranean may be underestimated. The researchers described these as hints that effects beyond sea ice could be larger than expected, with possible implications for the Greenland ice sheet’s stability and future flood risk in southern Europe.
“By using evidence from the past, we can now produce more reliable maps of where Arctic winter sea ice is likely to disappear,” said co-author Marco Aquino-López, of CIMAT. “These give us a much clearer picture of what the Arctic might look like in the coming decades, and how much uncertainty remains.”
Reference: “Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections” by C. Y. Fu, M. B. Osman and M. A. Aquino-López, 16 October 2026,
Nature Geoscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02123-w
The research was supported in part by the US National Science Foundation and the Cambridge Trust. Crystal Fu is a Member of Girton College, Cambridge.

title: A Massive Volcanic Eruption Devastated Japan 7,300 Years Ago – but Survivors Found a Way To Thrive
content:
A catastrophic volcanic eruption 7,300 years ago devastated parts of Japan, but its impact on ancient Jomon communities was surprisingly uneven (Artist’s concept). Credit: SciTechDaily.com
Survivors of Japan’s ancient volcanic catastrophe may have found a lifeline along the coast, where communities grew even as more distant populations faltered.
Around 7,300 years ago, the Kikai-Akahoya eruption damaged ecosystems and made parts of Japan uninhabitable for the Jomon people, who lived there by hunting and gathering. Yet some Jomon populations continued to grow through the disaster and its aftermath, while population growth stalled or reversed in more distant areas.
For decades, archaeologists have debated whether the eruption brought an “apocalypse” that abruptly ended all human life closest to its epicenter or whether local populations survived even relatively nearby. A new international study led by Lund University finds that neither total collapse nor simple continuity fully explains what happened.
“This eruption must have been devastating, exploding out of the sea bed with little warning. It battered the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and enormous tsunamis, and then blanketed the landscape with meters of volcanic ash,” explains senior author Peter Jordan, professor of archaeology at Lund University.
Northern Kyushu grew through the disaster
The researchers found that populations declined as ecosystems deteriorated and areas became uninhabitable. In southern Kyushu, however, Jomon populations had been shrinking long before the eruption. The disaster struck a region that was already sparsely populated and visited only by highly mobile groups.
Northern Kyushu had a different population history. Its population was growing before the eruption, and that trend continued through the disaster and its aftermath despite extensive, lasting ecosystem damage. The authors suggest that “refugees” moving out of the worst-hit areas immediately after the eruption may have helped sustain that growth.
Survivors from inland areas appear to have moved away and clustered along northern coastlines, where marine ecosystems recovered quickly. New ways of drawing on the sea’s abundant resources may also have accelerated population growth.
“The disaster caused major loss of life. However, survivors migrated, forged new social relations, innovated new kinds of economy, and appear to have found creative ways to exist and later thrive in the new post-disaster conditions,” says lead author Enrico Crema, professor at Cambridge University.
Population declines farther from the eruption
In more distant parts of Japan, populations that had been growing before the eruption stagnated or declined afterward. These far-reaching effects had not previously been identified. They may have been linked to short-term climate change triggered by the eruption or to extreme tooth wear in the deer and boar that Jomon communities relied on for food. The animals may have suffered that dental damage while grazing in ash-covered landscapes. Other volcanic effects on human health and well-being could also have contributed.
Kikai-Akahoya volcanic deposit in southern Kyushu. This is the “disaster layer” of volcanic ash that runs across the landscape. Archaeologists look at what life was like below this line and also above it to understand human impacts and responses. Credit: Lund University
For Jordan, the contrasting outcomes demonstrate how complex and unpredictable the aftermath of a major disaster can be.
“This study helps in creating a deeper understanding of the contingent ways in which cultures and societies cope with sudden shocks and catastrophes. Even in the most impossible situations, survivors and communities have choices, however limited: they need to act and make decisions, they need to adjust, collaborate and find new connections and social networks,” he concludes.
Reference: “Divergent demographic responses to the Kikai-Akahoya volcanic catastrophe in mid-Holocene Japan” by Enrico R. Crema, Mitsuhiro Kuwahata, Junzo Uchiyama, Ari Junno, Felix Riede and Peter D. Jordan, 14 October 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh7197
This work was supported by the Swedish Research Council (grant no. 2024-00822) (P.D.J.), JSPS KAKENHI (grant nos. JP25K00523) (M.K.), and the European Research Council (grant no. 101224035) (E.R.C. and P.D.J.).

title: James Webb Finds a Tiny World’s Rings Changing in Opposite Ways
content:
Artistic view of the centaur Chariklo and its ring system. The bright point in the upper-right corner represents the Sun as seen from Chariklo’s distance. Credit: L. Maquet, Observatoire de Paris
James Webb has revealed unexpected changes in Chariklo’s two rings, which appear to be evolving in opposite ways over only a few years.
For much of modern astronomy, rings were believed to belong only to the giant planets of the Solar System, including Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. That assumption changed in 2013, when astronomers discovered two dense rings around Chariklo, a small body only about 250 kilometers across that travels between Saturn and Uranus at nearly 17 times the Earth-Sun distance.
On October 18, 2022, researchers led by the Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia (IAA-CSIC) used the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) to examine Chariklo’s rings during a stellar occultation. This method tracks how a star’s light dims as an object passes in front of it. A new study published in Science Advances, also led by the IAA-CSIC, now shows for the first time that Chariklo’s rings can change measurably over the course of only a few years.
“By comparing JWST observations with those obtained during other stellar occultations over the last decade, we discovered opposite changes in the two rings: while the inner ring shows significantly higher opacity, the outer ring shows lower opacity, ” explains Pablo Santos-Sanz, an IAA-CSIC researcher who leads the study.
The contrasting changes suggest that Chariklo’s rings are not static structures. Instead, the system appears to be active and may be influenced by physical processes that are more complicated than astronomers previously realized.
Schematic representation of the stellar occultation by Chariklo’s rings observed with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) on 18 October 2022. Comparison with previous occultations reveals opposite changes in the two rings: C1R shows a stronger signal, while C2R appears much weaker. Credit: Yücel Kılıç, Pablo Santos-Sanz and Celia Navas (IAA-CSIC)
James Webb Achieves a First
The observations also marked an important technical milestone. Chariklo’s passage in front of the star was the first stellar occultation that had been specifically predicted and planned for JWST and then successfully observed by the space telescope.
“Achieving this required knowing with extraordinary precision the orbit of Chariklo, the position of the star—thanks to ESA’s Gaia mission—and the trajectory of JWST itself around the L2 Lagrange point, a region of space located about 1.5 million kilometers beyond Earth, away from the Sun. JWST follows an orbit around this region that requires periodic corrections through station-keeping maneuvers,” notes Yücel Kilic, postdoctoral researcher at the IAA-CSIC and co-author of the study.
During the occultation, Chariklo was moving relative to JWST at only 2.5 kilometers per second. That unusually slow relative motion gave astronomers exceptional spatial resolution, allowing them to probe the fine structure of the rings in greater detail.
Chariklo’s rings are extremely narrow, and the object itself is so distant that the rings cannot be directly photographed, even by JWST or the largest telescopes on Earth. Stellar occultations provide another way to study them. As Chariklo and its rings pass in front of a background star, each ring produces a brief dip in the star’s brightness, revealing information about the ring’s structure and opacity.
Statement by Pablo Santos-Sanz (IAA-CSIC).
Chariklo Challenges Ideas About Ring Stability
Scientists had generally assumed that rings around small Solar System bodies remain relatively stable over time. The newly detected changes in Chariklo call that assumption into question and suggest that such ring systems may evolve much more quickly than expected.
“Our results force us to rethink how they form, how they evolve, and what mechanisms maintain their stability. The ability to detect these changes opens a new window for understanding the evolution of these systems and, possibly, that of other ring systems in the Solar System,” says Santos-Sanz.
Exactly what caused the changes is still uncertain. They may reflect genuine evolution within the rings over time, differences caused by the filters used during separate observations, or some combination of the two.
An International Effort to Understand Chariklo
The Institute of Astrophysics of Andalusia (IAA-CSIC) directed every major stage of the project, beginning with the scientific planning and prediction of Chariklo’s occultation for JWST and continuing through data analysis and interpretation.
Researchers at the IAA-CSIC also played a central role in modeling the rings and carrying out the statistical analysis that confirmed the observed changes are real. The work involved collaborators from Spain, Brazil, France, Hungary, and the United States.
Reference: “JWST stellar occultation reveals unexpected changes in Chariklo’s ring system” by Pablo Santos-Sanz, Altair R. Gomes-Júnior, Bruno E. Morgado, Yucel Kilic, Csilla Kalup, Csaba Kiss, Chrystian L. Pereira, Bryan J. Holler, Nicolás Morales, José Luis Ortiz, Bruno Sicardy, Juan Luis Rizos, John Stansberry, Richard G. French, Heidi B. Hammel, Zhong-Yi Lin, Damya Souami, Josselin Desmars, Stefanie N. Milam, Felipe Braga-Ribas, Marcelo Assafin, Gustavo Benedetti-Rossi, Julio I. B. Camargo, Rene Duffard, Flavia L. Rommel, Estela Fernández-Valenzuela, Noemí Pinilla-Alonso and Mónica Vara-Lubiano, 9 September 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh4794

title: SpaceX Rocket Creates a Spectacular Glowing “Jellyfish” in the Sky
content:
A SpaceX rocket lit up the morning sky with a spectacular glowing “jellyfish” while carrying potentially groundbreaking medical experiments to the International Space Station. (Close view. See wider view below.) Credit: NASA/John Kraus
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a spectacular glowing “jellyfish” in the sky on October 13, 2026, as sunlight lit up its expanding exhaust plumes during an early morning launch. The unusual display, visible across the eastern United States, formed as the rocket carried SpaceX’s Dragon spacecraft toward the International Space Station.
Known as a “jellyfish,” this striking phenomenon occurs when a rocket launches near sunrise or sunset. Sunlight illuminates the spreading exhaust high above Earth, producing a bright, glowing cloud that resembles the shape of a jellyfish.
SpaceX Falcon 9 Launch Lights Up the Morning Sky
The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. It marked SpaceX’s 35th commercial resupply mission for NASA, delivering scientific experiments, essential supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
While the rocket’s illuminated exhaust created a spectacular sight across the eastern United States, its cargo could help support important advances in space technology and medical research.
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket produced a spectacular glowing “jellyfish” across the morning sky, creating an extraordinary light show visible across the eastern United States. Beyond the dazzling display, the mission carried experiments to the International Space Station that could help scientists restore vision, improve drug testing, and uncover new treatments for brain diseases. Credit: NASA/John Kraus
New Solar Arrays and Medical Experiments Head to the Space Station
Among the items aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, or IROSAs. These solar arrays are scheduled for installation later this fall and will help expand the station’s ability to generate electricity.
The spacecraft is also transporting equipment for producing artificial retinas in microgravity, a research effort that could eventually lead to treatments that restore vision on Earth. Another investigation involves 3D heart tissue models, which could help researchers develop methods for conducting drug testing on a larger scale during future space missions.
Additional experiments will explore how a new type of glass forms in the near-weightless conditions of space. Scientists will also study brain organoids, miniature models of brain tissue that could help identify potential treatment targets for neurological diseases, including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis.

title: New Research Reveals a Hidden Weakness Inside Electric Vehicle Batteries
content:
Technology
An illustration of an electric vehicle battery pack powering a car and bus. New research shows that a small number of faster-aging cells can limit the performance and lifespan of an entire battery pack, leaving substantial energy storage capacity unused. Credit: DIC
Researchers analyzing years of EV driving data discovered how differences between individual battery cells can intensify over time.
An electric vehicle (EV) battery can reach the end of its useful life even when many of its individual cells still have substantial capacity remaining. New research shows that a small number of rapidly aging cells can shorten the lifespan of an entire battery pack, leaving a significant share of its potential energy resources unused.
Why a Few Weak Cells Can Limit an Entire Battery
EV battery packs contain numerous cells that must work together to store and deliver energy. In a series-connected battery pack, however, the weakest cells can determine how much of the pack’s total capacity is actually available. During charging, a cell with reduced capacity may reach its maximum allowable voltage before the others. During discharge or high-power operation, a cell with greater internal resistance can reach its operating limits first.
These differences develop for several reasons, including variations in raw materials, manufacturing, cell grouping, temperature, and driving conditions. As cells age at different rates, the pack can eventually reach its retirement threshold even though many of its cells remain functional.
What Years of Real-World Driving Revealed
Led by Zhongwei Chen of the Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics (DICP) at the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) and Changfu Zou of Chalmers University of Technology, the research also involved scientists from Beijing Institute of Technology and Zeekr Technology Europe AB.
The team examined electric passenger cars using nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries and electric buses equipped with lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries. Some vehicles had traveled as far as 300,000 kilometers (about 186,400 miles). Using routinely recorded voltage, current, temperature, and state-of-charge data, the researchers combined battery modeling with neural networks to estimate changes in individual cell capacity and internal resistance. Their approach accounted for differences in operating conditions and seasonal temperatures, allowing more consistent comparisons of battery aging.
In passenger cars, differences in cell health generally remained small at lower mileage. Once vehicles exceeded approximately 170,000 kilometers (about 105,600 miles), however, some cells in many battery packs began aging more rapidly, increasing the gap between stronger and weaker cells. The timing and severity of this deterioration varied among vehicles.
How Much Battery Life Is Being Lost?
Using a common retirement threshold, the researchers calculated that uneven cell aging reduced usable pack-level state of health by 6.2% in passenger cars and 7.5% in buses. Compared with the average potential lifespan of their individual cells, battery packs had lifetimes that were 17.7% shorter in passenger cars and 22.8% shorter in buses.
Differences in internal resistance also reduced available power capability by 12.9% and 15.1%, respectively. By comparison, differences in state of charge typically reduced usable charged capacity by less than 2% under the charging and balancing strategies used in the studied vehicles.
Across their calculated lifetimes, passenger-car battery packs utilized just 80.7% of their potential energy resources, while bus batteries utilized 72.9%. Under the study’s retirement criteria, this meant that approximately 19.3% and 27.1% of potential energy resources, respectively, remained unused when the weakest cells reached their limits.
Extending Battery Life by Addressing Cell Differences
The findings suggest that battery lifespan cannot be accurately assessed using only the average condition of its cells. Comparisons between the vehicle fleets also indicate that battery balancing strategies may influence how differences between cells develop over time.
The researchers identified several potential improvements, including more consistent cell manufacturing, better cell grouping, advanced balancing controls, and improved thermal management. Reconfigurable battery systems, which could adjust how cells are connected and used, may offer another way to reduce the constraints imposed by weaker cells.
“Our findings show that the performance and lifetime of an EV battery pack are not determined solely by the average aging level of their cells, but can be strongly constrained by a small number of faster-aging cells,” said Prof. Chen. “By quantifying this weakest-cell effect under real-world EV operation, our study provides a basis for improving battery utilization, lifetime management, and system-level optimization.”
Reference: “Quantifying the impact of cell-to-cell inconsistency on electric vehicle battery degradation and utilization” by Litao Zhou, Xiaolei Bian, Yizhou Zhang, Zhenpo Wang, Zhongwei Chen, Zhiyu Mao and Changfu Zou, 25 August 2026,
Nature Energy
DOI: 10.1038/s41560-026-02131-5

title: A 58-Million-Year-Old Mammal Is Challenging Long-Held Assumptions About Evolution
content:
Illustration of uintatheres that scientists thought were a prime illustration of sexual dimorphism, or the tendency for males and females of a species to be physically different. Instead, a new study from the University of Kansas shows nuance between males and females. Credit: Wikimedia Commons, Charles Robert Knight
A surprising discovery about ancient horned mammals is challenging long-held ideas about sexual dimorphism.
For decades, scientists have pointed to a group of enormous, horned prehistoric mammals as a classic example of how dramatically males and females can differ in appearance. But a new analysis of fossil skulls suggests that one of paleontology’s most familiar examples of sexual dimorphism may rest on surprisingly weak evidence.
Researchers at the University of Kansas examined approximately 30 skulls belonging to the extinct species
Uintatherium anceps
. Their findings, published in
PLOS One
, challenge the longstanding assumption that males were substantially larger and possessed more prominent horns and canine teeth than females.
“Males have been interpreted as being much larger and possessing far more dramatic cranial features than females,” said study author Kevin Mulcahy, a doctoral student at the KU Biodiversity Institute & Natural History Museum.
A Broken Tooth Leads to an Unexpected Discovery
Uintatheres first appeared around 58 million years ago, less than 10 million years after the asteroid impact that wiped out the nonavian dinosaurs. These large mammals, distinguished by their imposing skulls, horns, and canine teeth, persisted in the fossil record for roughly 20 million years.
The investigation began when Mulcahy and his doctoral adviser, K. Christopher Beard, senior curator at the institute, attempted to identify a broken upper molar recovered during fieldwork in Montana. Suspecting that it belonged to a uintathere, they visited the American Museum of Natural History in New York to compare it with other fossils.
“We had a research visit at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, where our main goal was just to compare that tooth to teeth from other uintatheres and figure out what type of animal we had,” Mulcahy said. “They have this big collection — entire shelves occupied with these skulls, and each one of them is almost a meter long. These are famous specimens that are in the literature, and I was originally just looking at them to compare their teeth, and I noticed a ton of variation in a way that didn’t appear binary.”
The museum’s skulls, some approaching 1 meter (3.3 feet) in length, displayed substantial anatomical variation. However, the differences did not appear to separate neatly into the two groups expected if males and females had dramatically different physical characteristics.
The Skull Measurements Told a Different Story
Mulcahy began measuring the specimens to determine whether their anatomical differences followed the pattern expected from strong sexual dimorphism. In species where males and females differ substantially in size or anatomy, measurements may form two distinguishable statistical groups, known as a bimodal distribution. A unimodal distribution, by contrast, has a single dominant peak.
“I just, really hastily, with a ruler, gathered a bunch of measurements of the skulls while we were there,” Mulcahy said. “I started playing around with statistics, and there are ways you can look at different measurements to see if they’re best fit by a classic unimodal distribution, or if you were to think you’re dealing with something that exhibits strong sexual dimorphism, you’d see something with a bimodal distribution — that there are two means, one for males and one for females.”
Illustration of uintathere skeleton Credit: Wikimedia Commons Marsh, Othniel Charles
The preliminary results showed no clear separation. Mulcahy subsequently expanded the dataset with measurements from other institutions and applied additional statistical techniques, eventually examining approximately 30
Uintatherium anceps
“It wasn’t like there’s one group of specimens that look bigger than another, and then there’s another group that are smaller with smaller horns and canines,” he said. “So I was kind of interested — are these really good examples of sexual dimorphism after all? Is there actual evidence in the morphology of these skulls, in the distribution in particular of the ranges of morphology we’re seeing, that that’s what’s going on?”
Testing the Findings Against Modern Bison
Although the expanded analysis detected some possible signs of sexual dimorphism, the evidence remained inconclusive. Mulcahy considered whether the statistical methods themselves might be unable to detect genuine differences between males and females in fossil populations.
“Maybe there were some little signals of dimorphism here and there, but nothing really concrete,” he said. “I had an idea: Maybe it’s just that the techniques I’m using aren’t robust enough to actually measure sexual dimorphism. With fossil animals, you don’t actually know which specimens are males and which are females. You can guess and then test whether or not the ones you guess are males differ from the ones you guess are females, but that’s super circular, because you could just be picking the most extreme ones to be one sex and the least extreme to be the other. Of course they’re going to differ.”
To evaluate the reliability of his approach, he applied the same statistical techniques to modern bison, large horned herbivores with ecological similarities to those proposed for uintatheres. Unlike the fossil specimens, the bison could be classified by their known sex, allowing the analysis to be checked against actual male and female groups.
“When you’re dealing with living animals, you can just take the males, take the females and compare them,” he said. “Bison are another really big herbivore, with a similar sort of ecology that’s been proposed for uintatheres, and they also have big horns. What I noticed is that the signals of dimorphism I was picking up in bison were a lot clearer. When I was looking at the bison, it was almost perfect that all of the females were most similar to the females, and all the males were most similar to the males.”
How Historical Assumptions May Have Shaped Paleontology
The contrast suggested that the methods could detect pronounced sexual differences when they were present, strengthening the case that
Uintatherium anceps
did not exhibit the degree of dimorphism traditionally attributed to it. The results do not establish that males and females looked identical, but they provide little support for the previously assumed extreme differences.
Mulcahy also suggested that the conventional interpretation of uintathere fossils may partly reflect the scientific and cultural assumptions prevalent when these animals were first studied in the late 19th century. Early paleontologists frequently worked within a framework that expected males to be larger and more imposing than females.
“Back then, this is right when evolutionary theory, sexual selection, natural selection, all of that is kind of coming into play,” he said. “I think it’s really important to remember that these things were first discovered in the late 1800s by a bunch of male paleontologists working in a very Victorian-era mindset. The idea is basically assumed at that point that males are going to be bigger and scarier than females. It’s really interesting: When you step back and actually test that hypothesis, it doesn’t really hold up.”
Rethinking Sexual Dimorphism in Mammal Evolution
The findings also raise questions about other extinct mammals whose presumed sexual differences were inferred primarily from variations in fossil size and anatomy. Without independent evidence of a fossil animal’s sex, distinguishing sexual dimorphism from ordinary variation within a species remains difficult.
Mulcahy argues that pronounced male-biased sexual dimorphism may have evolved independently in different mammalian lineages rather than being an inherited characteristic of early mammals. He points to recent research on living mammals indicating that larger males are far from universal.
“Strong, big male-style sexual dimorphism was probably not ancestral at the root of the mammalian tree, and among the mammals where we do see this pattern today, it’s almost certainly shown up independently several times,” Mulcahy said. “It had long been assumed that sexual dimorphism is the norm, that most species show that males are bigger than females. But just a couple years ago, a paper came out showing that among living mammals, most species either don’t show any dimorphism or actually have larger females. The idea that males are always bigger than females is really just a choice of what animals were people looking at, what are the things that biologists in the past were interested in.”
Reference: “Linear morphometrics fail to support strong sexual dimorphism in Uintatherium anceps” by Kevin D. Mulcahy, 7 October 2026,

title: Power Roll scientist wins £2.7 million fellowship to develop flexible back-contact tandem solar cells
content:
Power Roll scientist wins £2.7 million fellowship to develop flexible back-contact tandem solar cells
Power Roll
, the UK company developing flexible perovskite solar films made in continuous rolls, announced that its Principal Scientist, Dr. Dumitru (Dima) Sirbu, has received a UKRI Future Leaders Fellowship. The award is worth £2.7 million (US$3.6 million) over four years. It will fund a program called Back-Contacted Flexible Tandem Photovoltaics (BaCT-PV).
The program aims to combine the efficiency potential of tandem solar cells with Power Roll’s patented lightweight microgroove architecture and its low-cost, roll-to-roll manufacturing. It targets power conversion efficiencies above 25% while keeping the deployment, cost and sustainability advantages of the company’s technology.
Power Roll says the fellowship brings non-dilutive funding that will help it build new capabilities, generate intellectual property and deepen strategic partnerships. It also supports the company’s goal of establishing next-generation photovoltaic manufacturing in the UK. The company expects a higher-performance product to widen its addressable market for lightweight solar.
The fellowship is part of Round 10 of the UKRI Future Leaders Fellowships, in which Innovate UK announced 28 business and non-academic fellows. Power Roll recently signed an
MOU with Amcor
on solar PV film and is
working with Queen Mary University of London
on quality control for perovskite solar cells.

title: SK Materials JNC to help mass-produce SN Display’s perovskite emitters for displays
content:
SK Materials JNC to help mass-produce SN Display’s perovskite emitters for displays
SK Materials JNC and
SN Display
have signed a memorandum of understanding to build a mass-production system for perovskite nanocrystal materials for displays. The goal is to bring the light-emitting material from the research stage to a level the display industry can use.
Ha Jung-hwan, CEO of SK Materials JNC (left), and Lee Tae-woo, CEO of SN Display. (Photo: SK Materials JNC)
SN Display, a startup founded by Seoul National University professor Tae-Woo Lee, says it can mass-synthesize perovskite nanocrystals at high efficiency. SK Materials JNC already handles synthesis, production, device evaluation and quality control for OLED materials, including boron-based blue dopants. It will take charge of synthesizing and manufacturing SN Display’s materials, and will support process optimization and a quality assurance system.
The companies say perovskite emitters offer high color purity and luminous efficiency that meet the BT.2020 standard, which supports a wider color gamut than HDTV. They see applications ranging from color-conversion films to self-emissive displays, and the material is being discussed as a possible successor to OLED and quantum dots.
SK Materials JNC CEO Ha Jung-hwan said the partnership would “dramatically bring forward” commercialization of next-generation display materials, while Lee said it would expand production and supply capabilities and help secure a stable supply of high-quality materials. SN Display is also behind the
Vision Foundry project
, which aims to make perovskite microdisplays by vacuum deposition.
Earlier this week,
SN Display also signed an MOU with Raontek
to test its perovskite color conversion on microLED and micro-OLED microdisplays for AR/VR.

title: 十五五储能发展研判：支柱产业定位、136项场景、投资红线全解析-索比光伏网
content:
2026年10 月20日，国家发改委召开10月份例行新闻发布会，明确新型储能纳入十五五六大新兴支柱产业，同步对外推出首批136项标志性重大应用场景清单，同时重申对“一哄而上、盲目投资造成重大损失的严肃追究责任”的监管口径，一支持、一约束成为本次发布会最核心的政策信号。
需要厘清的是，新型储能列入六大新兴支柱产业并非本次发布会首次提出，是年内第三次公开重申;本次重大变化在于将支柱产业定位、136项应用场景清单、投资监管追责口径三者结合对外释放。电力能源领域重点提出冀北亿千瓦级新能源、新型储能电力系统两大场景，重点导向构网型柔性直流、风光储主动支撑、柔性负荷调控等技术方向，预示行业竞争逻辑从单纯比拼装机规模，转向系统能力、长时储能、电网支撑能力的综合比拼。
与此同时，“严禁一哄而上盲目投资”的监管信号落地，结合河北、河南、吉林、浙江多地储能项目排查清退、清单制管理的实际动作，意味着储能产业进入“政策扶持升级，粗放扩张受限”的新阶段。支柱产业定位不等于项目收益兜底，过去靠圈指标、简单配储、低水平重复建设的模式生存空间持续收窄，对储能、光伏产业链企业的技术路线选择、系统集成能力、市场化履约能力提出更高要求。
为帮助储能投资商、新能源开发商、EPC服务商完整吃透本次发布会政策信号，分清“六大新兴支柱产业”与“战略性新兴产业”两套政策概念，看懂136项场景技术导向、梳理地方监管案例、找准企业转型方向，索比光伏网结合发布会原文、国家政策文件、地方实操案例，形成深度解读报告，覆盖政策时间线梳理、两套产业概念辨析、场景技术方向拆解、投资监管红线、各地项目案例、企业实操应对、对光伏行业连锁影响等内容。
以下为报告节选内容，完整地方储能项目清退案例汇总、技术路线研判、企业转型实操方案，扫码跳转小程序查看全文完整版报告。

title: 国家能源局：长三角电力市场1-9月减少风光弃电量超过24亿千瓦时-索比光伏网
content:
10月19日，国家能源局在安徽合肥召开长三角电力市场建设推进会，全面总结2026年以来长三角电力市场建设工作成效，系统谋划下一阶段重点任务。国家能源局党组成员、副局长宋宏坤出席会议并讲话。
会议指出，2026年以来长三角电力市场建设工作取得阶段性成效。长三角五省市电力市场全部实现按自然日连续开市，安徽、福建电力现货市场顺利转入正式运行，迎峰度夏期间区域内省间互济电力约4000万千瓦，1—9月减少风光弃电量超过24亿千瓦时，市场交易活跃度持续提升。同时，多部门协同的监管机制加快完善，辅助服务费用向用户侧有序疏导，批发—零售价格传导更加顺畅，适应新型能源体系的市场和价格机制进一步健全。
会议强调，下阶段要全力抓好年度各项任务落地见效。一是进一步推进省级市场建设。推动发用两侧经营主体全面报量报价参与电力市场，加强售电公司规范管理，推动电力辅助服务成本有效传导。二是进一步深化长三角市场建设。整合优化短期互济品种，研究推进区域辅助服务市场建设，推进长三角电力交易平台开发建设与功能升级，推动西北—华东绿电“一次报价、联合交易”落地。三是进一步完善市场治理体系。推动建立零售市场跨部门协同治理机制，加强市场运行风险防控，及时回应社会关切。
会议还对迎峰度冬电力保供工作作出部署，强调要加强供需形势监测预警，充分发挥市场机制保供作用，切实守住民生用能保障底线。
国家能源局监管总监梁昌新主持会议，国家能源局市场监管司及相关派出机构、华东区域五省(市)政府相关部门、相关电力企业等负责同志参加会议。

本文介绍了海南省发展和改革委员会于2026年9月批复的《海南省增量新能源项目可持续发展价格结算机制竞价实施细则（2026年V1.0版）》核心内容。该细则自印发之日起实施，适用于2025年6月1日后投产且未纳入既有机制的风电、光伏等增量新能源项目。明确自2027年1月1日起，新投产的大型工商业分布式光伏项目不再纳入电价竞价主体范围；此前已明确电价的光热项目及竞争性配置的海上风电项目亦不参与。细则规定了竞价组织方式、主体登记、申报与出清规则，并建立严格履约约束：未投产项目若实际并网时间较申报时间延迟超6个月，将作废竞价结果并取消三年内参竞资格。同时配套差价结算机制，强化信用管理与并网保障，旨在通过市场化竞价科学确定机制电价，引导新能源健康有序发展。
2026年9月16日，三峡集团青海能源投资有限公司在青海省西宁市城西区正式成立，注册资本10亿元人民币。该公司由三峡集团主导设立，法定代表人为王清伟，主营业务聚焦风力发电、光伏发电及储能技术服务，旨在加强三峡集团在青海清洁能源领域的布局与协同。股权结构显示，中国三峡新能源（集团）股份有限公司认缴出资3.4亿元，持股34%；中国长江电力股份有限公司与长江三峡投资管理有限公司各认缴3.3亿元，持股比例均为33%。三方共同出资构成公司全部注册资本，体现了三峡集团内部资源整合与多主体协同推进新能源发展的战略安排。
国家能源局于2026年9月23日发布公告，通报2026年8月全国新增建档立卡新能源发电项目（不含户用光伏）情况。当月共新增项目4007个，其中光伏发电项目占绝对多数，达3972个，包括集中式光伏23个和工商业分布式光伏3949个；风电项目29个，生物质发电项目6个。公告明确区分了不同技术类型的项目数量与分类，并指出风电、集中式光伏及生物质发电项目的详细清单以附件形式公布，而工商业分布式光伏项目清单则需通过国家可再生能源发电项目信息管理平台网站查询。该数据反映了当月新能源电力装机建设的结构性特征，凸显分布式光伏在新增项目中的主导地位。
山东电力近日发布2026年8月新能源电力市场结算参考价。数据显示，当月光伏结算参考价为0.306元/千瓦时，环比大幅上涨48%，实现连续四个月上涨；而风电结算参考价为0.358元/千瓦时，环比微降0.15%。从累计数据看，1至8月光伏结算加权均价为131.77525元/兆瓦时（即0.13177525元/千瓦时），风电为305.5075元/兆瓦时（即0.3055075元/千瓦时）。该信息源自山东电力发布的8月电力市场“明白纸”，旨在向市场主体提供透明、可预期的新能源电价参考依据，反映当前省内光伏与风电在电力市场中的差异化价格走势。
山东省八部门联合印发《新能源装备产业高质量发展实施方案（2026—2028年）》，聚焦光伏、风电、核电、锂电池、氢燃料电池、输变电装备六大重点领域，系统部署九项主要任务。方案以构建技术领先、链条完整、集群成势的产业格局为目标，提出到2028年实现产业营收超4700亿元，培育百亿级企业6家以上、“专精特新”小巨人企业100家以上；在光伏领域重点突破HJT、TOPCon、XBC等新型电池及钙钛矿等新材料技术，提升产能利用率至70%以上；同步推进海上风电装备升级、核电关键部件国产化、锂电池全链条发展、氢能“制储输用”协同及特高压输变电装备研制，并强化创新平台建设、市场主体培育、应用场景拓展和金融政策保障，加快打造我国北方重要新能源装备产业基地。
山东省能源局于8月28日公布2026年集中式光伏发电项目建设第二批名单，共纳入20个项目，总装机容量183.3073万千瓦。这批项目经企业申报、市县审核及省级评审等程序确定，须于2027年前实现全容量并网；逾期未投运的将被移出名单，并影响企业后续项目申报及所在市可再生能源消纳责任权重。通知要求各市能源主管部门强化用地、用海等要素保障，落实三级责任人机制，推动项目如期开工投产；国网山东电力需优化电网接入流程，促进接网工程与主体工程同步建设；开发企业须依法合规建设，同步建成配套储能，压实安全主体责任，并及时完成项目建档立卡和绿色电力证书申领工作。（199字）
国家能源局东北监管局出台《东北区域集中式新能源发电企业集中报价工作实施方案（试行）》，规范辽宁、吉林、黑龙江三省集中式风电和光伏企业的市场报价行为。方案明确，仅允许同一集团、同一省份内的新能源企业开展集中报价，严禁跨集团、跨省“抱团”报价，严防垄断协议及价格协同行为。集中报价主体的总装机规模原则上不得超过本省单个最大燃煤电厂装机容量。对装机规模超限的发电集团，允许组建多个独立报价群组，但各群组须在场所、人员、决策、财务等方面严格隔离，禁止集团层面协调或统一指令报价。所有场站仍以注册主体独立申报、出清和结算，确保市场公平竞争与反垄断合规。（198字）
2024年上半年，东北电网新能源发电量达1206亿千瓦时，占总发电量比重超35%，居全国区域电网首位；新能源最大发电电力达5167万千瓦，占总发电电力和用电电力比例分别达68%和73.9%，均创历史新高。为支撑新能源大规模并网消纳，国网东北分部牵头成立专项工作专班，滚动研判消纳形势，优化水电水库调度、安排核电机组调峰、充分调用抽蓄与储能资源，并通过省间现货、中长期交易及互济机制扩大外送与区内调节能力。年初以来，新增1248万千瓦新能源装机并网，总装机达1.4亿千瓦，占比突破50%，在装机快速增长背景下，新能源利用率保持高位稳定。
拉萨市发改委于7月27日印发《拉萨市分布式光伏发电项目备案指南》，明确自2026年7月27日起施行。指南将分布式光伏项目划分为四类：自然人户用（利用自有住宅、接入电压≤380伏）、非自然人户用（利用居民住宅、接入电压≤10千伏、装机≤6兆瓦）、一般工商业（利用公共机构或工商业建筑、接入电压≤10千伏、装机原则上≤6兆瓦）以及大型工商业（接入用户侧电网或专线供电，接入电压≤35千伏且装机≤20兆瓦，或接入110千伏且装机≤50兆瓦）。该指南统一规范了各类项目的适用范围与技术条件，由拉萨市发改委负责解释。
广东省发展改革委于2026年7月23日印发通知，正式公布首批纳入“10千伏及以上新能源可持续发展价格结算机制”的存量项目清单。该机制依据国家及广东省关于深化新能源上网电价市场化改革的系列文件设立，旨在通过规范价格结算方式，支撑新能源高质量发展。清单项目由各地市能源主管部门组织申报，经省、市两级能源部门与电网企业联合核实、公示及异议处理后确认。针对前期漏报项目，相关企业须于8月底前向属地能源主管部门补报材料；各地市需在9月底前完成审核与公示，并将信息报送至省发展改革委（能源局），后续将由省级部门会同广东电网公司、深圳供电局复核，统一印发增补清单。

title: 国家发改委资环司原司长任树本被查！-索比光伏网
content:
中央纪委国家监委网站10月21日消息，据中央纪委国家监委驻国家发展改革委纪检监察组、青海省纪委监委消息：国家发展改革委资源节约和环境保护司原司长、中国招标投标协会原会长任树本涉嫌严重违纪违法，主动投案，目前正接受中央纪委国家监委驻国家发展改革委纪检监察组纪律审查和青海省监察委员会监察调查。
任树本，男，1959年12月生。长期在国家发改委系统工作，曾任重大项目稽察特派员办公室主任、国家投资项目评审中心主任、资源节约与环境保护司司长等职，长期参与国家节能降碳、循环经济、环境保护等领域的政策制定和项目审批，岗位廉政风险较高。
离任发改委后，他出任中国招标投标协会第三届理事会会长，该协会今年9月30日已公告其不再担任会长职务，距此次官宣投案不到一个月。‌‌

title: 工业和信息化部工业软件标准化技术委员会成立-索比光伏网
content:
10月21日，工业和信息化部工业软件标准化技术委员会(以下简称“工业软件标委会”)成立大会在浙江省杭州市召开。工业和信息化部副部长熊继军出席会议并讲话。工业和信息化部有关司局负责同志，工业软件标委会委员代表、相关行业专家等参加会议。
成立工业软件标委会，是深入贯彻落实党中央、国务院决策部署，充分发挥标准的基础性、战略性、引领性作用，加快科技创新成果落地转化与推广应用，引导和推动工业软件产业高质量发展的重要举措。工业软件标委会主要负责关键技术、数据互操作、产品服务、融合应用及生态建设等行业标准制修订工作，秘书处设在工业和信息化部电子第五研究所。
成立大会后，工业软件标委会第一次全体委员会议召开，审议通过了标委会章程、秘书处工作细则、标准制修订工作程序等文件，研究部署了下一阶段重点工作。

title: Germany's BSH proposes offshore wind expansion plan
content:
The Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH) has outlined a pathway
to increase Germany's offshore wind capacity from an estimated 11 GW to
70 GW by 2045.
To support this target, the agency has released a preliminary draft update
to the Area Development Plan 2025, alongside a draft investigation framework
for a strategic environmental assessment.
"The expansion of offshore wind farms and their grid connections must
go hand in hand. Our goal is to give companies long-term planning security
while maintaining flexibility for future developments," said BSH President
Helge Heegewaldt.
According to the agency, the revised plan would reduce the number of required
grid connections, lowering infrastructure costs. By removing five grid
connections that had been included in earlier plans, the BSH expects to
save tens of billions of euros while reducing the number of offshore cable
routes needed.
The draft also proposes greater spacing between wind turbines to reduce
interference and improve electricity generation efficiency. In addition,
the BSH has proposed adjustments to offshore wind development areas to
better protect seabirds and the wider marine environment.
The plan further outlines options for the continued use of existing offshore
wind farm sites and seeks to provide long-term certainty for grid expansion
while retaining flexibility for future planning decisions.

title: Offshore Substation installations completed for Gennaker wind farm
content:
Skyborn Renewables GmbH has announced the successful installation of the
offshore substations (OSS) for the Darß and Zingst offshore platforms,
marking a key milestone for the 976.5 MW Gennaker
Offshore Wind Farm.
According to the company, the two substations form a vital part of the
OST-6-1 grid connection system. They will collect electricity generated
to the onshore grid. The grid connection system is being managed by transmission
system operator 50Hertz.
The milestone follows the successful jacket load-out of the two offshore
substations, which was announced earlier in August.
Installation was carried out by Allseas' offshore construction vessel Pioneering
Spirit. The vessel sits at 382 metres in length and 124 metres in width
and is capable of lifting up to 60,000 tonnes, making it one of the world's
largest construction vessels.
The installation of the substations represents another step forward in
the development of the Gennaker Offshore Wind Farm, which is set to become
one of the largest offshore wind projects in the Baltic Sea.

title: BGS to develop seabed geology data to support offshore projects
content:
BGS to develop seabed geology data to support offshore projects TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
BGS to develop seabed geology data to support offshore projects
The British Geological Survey (BGS) has announced that it is leading a
project to develop seabed geology datasets and reports to support offshore
development.
The three year project is being delivered in partnership with The Crown
Estate, which is providing funding. According to BGS, the data will support
not only offshore wind development but also the wider marine sector, including
linear assets, environmental management and other offshore renewable energy
projects.
Olivia Thomas, Head of Planning & Technical at The Crown Estate, said:
“This project will support the spatial optimisation capabilities of our
Marine Delivery Routemap tool and allow us to bring optimised, lower-risk
project opportunities to market.”
The project will also provide geoscience evidence for The Crown Estate’s
Marine Delivery Routemap, which is designed to dynamically model and map
potential use scenarios and opportunities across the seabed and coastline.
Andrew Finlayson, Head of Marine Geoscience at BGS, said: “During the
scoping phase, we received valuable input from across the marine community,
and we hope the datasets will be a useful resource for a wide range of
stakeholders.”
Once completed, the datasets will be made available through the Marine
Data Exchange and the BGS GeoIndex.

title: Ørsted completes construction large scale BESS for Hornsea 3
content:
Ørstedhave announced
their innovative large-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) has officially
completed construction.
The system is designed to support the Hornsea
3 Offshore Wind Farm,
located off the Norfolk coast. As part of the construction programme, 170
Megapacks have been installed alongside the project’s onshore converter
station.
Once fully operational, the facility, known as Iceni, will have a capacity
of 600 MWh, enough to power an estimated 80,000 UK homes.
Beatrice d’Eufemia, Project Manager for the Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said:
“The system will make the best use of renewable energy produced in the
UK. When electricity generation exceeds demand, the excess can be stored
and then used when demand is greater.”
According to Ørsted, the BESS is located separately from the Hornsea 3
onshore converter station and is connected by 18 x 33 kV cables, each approximately
600 metres long.
Richard Swann, Construction Manager for the Iceni BESS at Ørsted, said:
“It’s a real testament to the hard work, dedication and co-operation
of teams from many different organisations that construction has been completed
successfully.”
The project will now move into the final stages of mechanical and electrical
installation ahead of commissioning.

title: Utopai Becomes a Unicorn as Video AI Takes Off
content: While much of the AI industry has fixated on new personal AI assistants from Meta and OpenAI , video AI is enjoying a quiet renaissance. Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg is teaming up with the former head of OpenAI’s Sora app to launch a new AI film company . Startup Higgsfield quadrupled its valuation to $5.4 billion in August. And Kling AI , the video unit of Chinese social media giant Kuaishou Technology , raised nearly $3 billion at a $15 billion valuation over the summer. The latest video AI company to seize this moment is Utopai Studios , a 4-year-old film startup based in Mountain View, Calif. Utopai closed a funding round for $60 million that valued it at $1 billion and has already received term sheets for a subsequent round that would value the company at $2 billion to $3 billion, according to someone close to the company. The enthusiasm for video AI startups follows improvements in the quality and length of the clips that video AI models can generate. In September, Higgsfield announced that it had crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue, showing that the technology has serious commercial potential. Utopai has more than 20 projects in the works right now, including two TV series and three full-length films that are set to debut in theaters next year, one of which is an animated adaptation of the children’s book “The Most Serious Fart.” Utopai aims to debut its films in about 3,000 theaters in North America. That’s a step up from previous films that have heavily relied on AI, which have tended to be proofs of concept for technology that have been screened in a single theater, Chief Executive Cecilia Shen said in an interview. “We realized that, first of all, there‘s no margin at all for just selling software in the entertainment industry, and secondly, selling good software doesn’t guarantee you to have a good art house film because it's just a part of the process, and it really depends on how humans are leveraging it to produce great content,” she said. Shen previously worked on AI at Google’s X moonshot team before founding Utopai in 2022. While other companies like Kling, Runway and Luma focus on training cutting-edge video and world models, Utopai draws on a variety of models from other providers. It has also customized the open-source video model MiniMax H3 to create its own video AI model, which currently ranks in second place on a leaderboard of text-to-video models compiled by Artificial Analysis, the AI benchmarking firm. Utopai’s strategy of being its own film studio also sets it apart from Higgsfield, which offers a variety of AI models to creators through its application. Utopai also provides its software to outside filmmakers, placing it in a similar lane to Katzenberg’s company, which is in talks with OpenAI to access Sora, tweak it and sell software or other services using it. The excitement over AI-generated video faces hurdles. Many in Hollywood are suspicious of AI due to fears it will encroach on valuable IP and displace human workers. That could advantage Katzenberg’s company thanks to his creative credentials: before launching DreamWorks , he headed Walt Disney Studios . By using AI tools, Utopai can cut the costs that a traditional film would pay for planning out scenes and CGI by 80% to 90%. But Utopai still pays for directors and actors to work on its films, said Shen, and is also raising financing for individual projects, in addition to the company’s funding rounds. In the longer term, Utopai is interested in branching out into new genres, including interactive formats, sports content and animated musicals, she said. In China, AI generated videos have found a broad audience on social media, but in the U.S. people are continuing to stream TV shows on Netflix , and people are going back to movie theaters, said Shen, pointing to the summer box office success of The Odyssey . Still, with “You Can See Everything,” the documentary about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes , captivating audiences across the U.S. in recent days, it’s a reminder that reality can be compelling in ways that AI can never reproduce. Here’s what else is going on… Big Number Microsoft said it has observed cyberattacks by a Chinese state-aligned actor known as Storm-0940 that used a Chinese AI agent called Artex to automate the attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a wide range of industries. Overheard OpenAI would support requirements for AI companies to have shutdown controls for their models, mandated annual independent audits, and stronger cybersecurity practices, a senior company official wrote in a letter to California Gov. Gavin Newsom . Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI agent app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. DeepSeek , the Chinese AI lab, is wrapping up roughly $15 billion (about 100 billion yuan) in new financing led by CATL and Tencent. Nebius , a neocloud, announced on Thursday that it has entered into a $3.5 billion senior secured facility provided by Citi . Flapping Airplanes , a year-old AI research lab, raised $1 billion in a Series A funding round at a $6 billion valuation, led by Index Ventures and Lux Capital. Vegafin Capital , an AI-first lending startup for India's small businesses, raised 10 billion rupees (about $106 million) in a funding round led by Premji Invest . Blacksmith , an AI code-testing startup, raised $66 million in a Series C funding round at a $1 billion valuation, led by Sequoia Capital. Kevel , which builds AI-driven infrastructure for retail and commerce media networks, raised $52 million in new capital from expanded investments by Fulcrum Equity Partners , dunnhumby Ventures , Iberis Capital and ORIX Corporation USA's Growth Capital business. Coherence Neuro , which is developing AI models and a brain implant to detect and treat cancer, raised $45 million in a Series A funding round led by Founders Fund and the OpenAI Startup Fund. Watchtower Labs , a military logistics AI company, emerged from stealth with $35 million in seed financing led by Shield Capital and Conviction Partners , with participation from Founders Fund . Nirva , an AI pendant creator, raised a $25 million pre-Series A round. CapitalOS , a San Francisco-based developer of tech to allow users and agents to issue and use cards, pay bills and manage cash, raised $21.9 million in Series A funding led by LGVP . Longeye , which makes AI-powered evidence-analysis tools for U.S. criminal justice agencies, raised $20 million in a Series A funding round led by N47. Azoma , which makes a platform for AI shopping agents, raised $11.2 million in a Series A funding round led by Puma Growth Partners. Dataline , which connects AI agents to data sources, raised $10.6 million in a seed funding round led by Dispersion Capital and Lattice Fund. Ultra Security, an AI agent security platform, emerged from stealth with $10 million in seed funding from Ludlow Ventures , Hidden Capital , Entrée Capital , Detroit Venture Partners , firedrop and FDVC . Holly , which makes an AI-powered workforce platform for government agencies, and 17A , a government technology firm, were awarded a $1.1 million grant from the Public Benefit Innovation Fund and the Recoding America Fund to help state governments prepare for AI. Nvidia on Wednesday announced new deals with chip substrate suppliers Ibiden , Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Unimicron , to ensure it has enough component materials to produce more of its AI server chips in the coming years. It said the deals, which include a multibillion-dollar reservation with Japan-based Ibiden, would grow substrate capacity for Nvidia products by two and a half times over three years. Substrates bridge compute dies with underlying circuit boards. Meta announced a restructuring Wednesday morning to create a new class of non-voting shares that the company said will allow it to raise new capital for AI investments while preserving CEO Mark Zuckerberg ’s voting control in the firm. The restructuring was partially shaped by concerns that a proposed wealth tax in Meta’s home state of California could prompt Zuckerberg to move away. The creators of PHP , an open source programming language used by the majority of the world’s websites, on Wednesday urged web maintainers across the globe to install a new update after researchers using AI found a flaw that could put those websites at risk of being hacked. OpenAI will make its models available through Google Cloud , the companies announced this morning. The move lessens OpenAI’s reliance on Microsoft , where the companies once shared exclusivity. OpenAI is also expanding ChatGPT ads to 26 more countries as it tries to turn advertising into a bigger source of revenue to help cover its AI costs. Recursive , a neolab founded by You.com CEO Richard Socher , released a free coding model called Flint on Wednesday. The model is small enough to run on a laptop. title: Andreessen Horowitz to Drop ‘Crypto’ From Name of Flagship Blockchain Fund
content: Andreessen Horowitz, which made one of the boldest bets on blockchain investments in the venture world, is dropping the term crypto from the name of its fund focused on the category. A16z crypto, which has raised nearly $10 billion across five funds, has informed some of its limited partners that it plans to change its name to a16z frontier and broaden its investment strategy beyond crypto, according to a person briefed on the matter. One of the firm’s general partners, Ali Yahya, also informed some investors that he is exiting the firm to work on his own startup, the person said. Yahya joined a16z in 2017 as the first full-time member of its crypto team. The decision represents a symbolic shift for one of the most prominent crypto venture operations, which launched its first dedicated fund in 2018. Under general partner Chris Dixon, a16z crypto invested in top blockchain companies including Coinbase, Uniswap and Axie Infinity developer Sky Mavis, raising monster funds that included a $4.5 billion vehicle it launched during the crypto bull market of 2022. Its most recent $2.2 billion fund, announced this May, was less than half the size of the 2022 fund, reflecting a cooldown in enthusiasm around crypto startups. In recent years, a16z crypto has also invested in non-blockchain based startups including Kalshi and Ornn, a financial infrastructure startup focused on AI compute markets. By broadening its investment mandate beyond blockchain startups, the firm will be following in the path of other top crypto venture firms. In May, Haun Ventures, founded by former a16z crypto general partner Katie Haun, announced that it would be looking at financial services startups beyond crypto with  $1 billion in new funds. And in August, Paradigm, started by Coinbase co-founder Fred Ehrsam and former Sequoia partner Matt Huang, said that its new $1.2 billion fund would also invest in AI, robotics and “other frontiers.” A16z crypto has been a particularly outspoken booster of blockchain technology. Dixon was one of the main evangelizers of the web3 investing boom of 2021 and 2022, arguing that much of the internet’s infrastructure and applications should be rebuilt on decentralized rails and governed through digital assets called tokens. His 2024 book Read Write Own aimed to popularize the concept, especially as Andreessen Horowitz broadened its lobbying efforts in Washington, D.C. The firm became a top financial backer of crypto-friendly political candidates, putting tens of millions of dollars into the super PAC network Fairshake ahead of the 2024 election. One of a16z’s founders, Marc Andreessen, also became a vocal booster of then-candidate Donald Trump, who began to voice his support for crypto and won over much of the industry after a perceived crackdown by the Biden administration. Despite a major legislative victory with the Genius Act in mid-2025, which established regulation for dollar-backed cryptocurrencies called stablecoins, the crypto industry has suffered a broad, prolonged downturn in 2026. That includes the recent failure of an a16z-backed bill called the Clarity Act that would have established broader crypto regulation over financial markets, as well as scrutiny into conflicts of interest with the Trump family’s growing crypto business empire. Dixon, meanwhile, acknowledged in a long thread on X earlier this year that it was “fashionable” to say that “non-financial use cases of crypto are dead.” That came as some of its biggest Web3 bets, such as the Axie Infinity and the decentralized social media platform Farcaster, fell far short of their ambitions. Dixon wrote that crypto instead was now in its “financial era,” pointing to the rise of stablecoins and agentic payments. “We play the long game at a16z and a16z crypto,” he wrote.

title: The Closing of the ‘Defenders Window’ Is Nigh
content: At first, the X headlines this morning about the latest AI-powered cybersecurity incident seemed dire. But by the time I had a cup of coffee and began parsing all the cyber jargon, I was reassured that an apparent solution was on its way to plug a major new security hole that could make websites vulnerable to cyberintrusions. Since August, a coalition led by OpenAI has been working to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language that undergirds the web. But there was bad news, too: This type of long-simmering response to the latest AI-discovered vulnerabilities may not be viable for much longer. For months, OpenAI has been harping on what it calls the “ defender’s window ”—the critical period of time when cybersecurity experts, armed with advanced AI models, can identify and patch vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them first. The issue is that the gap is rapidly narrowing between cybercapable models from leading U.S. frontier labs and Chinese open-source models, which lack the restrictions U.S. labs impose on their models’ capabilities. Anthropic said as much in a blog post from late September warning that Chinese lab Z.ai ’s GLM-5.3 model only lags the U.S. frontier models by about four months. The good news: The Trump administration has a shiny new organization created for moments just like these. It’s called the Super Intelligence Force, a name that may elicit eyerolls from some of our more jaded readers. Still, I have heard over and over that all the AI industry wants is coordination and clarity from the White House. That, presumably, is what the SI Force will offer, led by heavy hitters including National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton and senior Defense Department official Emil Michael . An OpenAI spokesperson told me today that they had briefed several agencies, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, about the PHP vulnerability, as well as briefing Clayton and Michael late last week, representing the first “major engagement” between OpenAI and the SI Force. The spokesperson added that the SI Force provided a central point to coordinate their communication across the broader government. According to a White House official, the SI Force’s work involved helping to put pressure on the “relevant parties” to deploy a vulnerability patch. While the SI Force’s coordination function may not seem terribly ambitious, at least it’s a start. It’s worth remembering that the White House essentially had to reorient its entire AI policy in April with the announcement of Mythos. The arrival of Chinese cybercapable open models could represent a Mythos 2.0 moment. I spoke with one former White House official who told me solutions from even a few months ago, like the July Gold Eagle clearinghouse that allows organizations and government agencies to share and fix software vulnerabilities, might already be outdated. It’s up to the SI Force to create a path forward. The next major internet bug likely won’t have the luxury of a two-month-long defender’s window. Meta’s Performance On Sunday, in a preview of this week’s Meta Platforms earnings report, your regular Briefing columnist, Martin Peers, declared: “If Meta can stay on investors’ good sides, an equity offering seems in the cards.” Martin nailed it on both accounts. On Wednesday afternoon, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg delivered a bunch of (mostly) good news that had investors in the company purring like kittens. Meta also announced the creation of a new category of common stock that will allow it to raise capital to fund its hefty AI investments without sacrificing Zuckerberg’s control. The highlights: For the third quarter, its revenue grew 26% to $64.6 billion, slightly above what the company had forecast. It’s trimming the losses from its Reality Labs unit. While it showed negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion rather than the positive free cash flow of $10.63 billion in the year-earlier period, that was due to its AI investments, and the number wasn’t as bad as some analysts had expected. The company’s anticipated capital expenditures of $135 billion to $145 billion for the full year, while eye-popping, were still within the range it had previously forecast. That was reassuring for investors who’ve gotten spooked in the past by sudden leaps in tech company spending on AI. Perhaps equally comforting were Zuckerberg’s reassurances that investors will see a payoff from some of its most expensive AI initiatives. He described Muse, Meta’s new agent app, as a bona fide hit for the company, one that has gained 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada in its first six weeks on the market—a faster pace of growth than for its Threads app. While Zuckerberg said the product will remain free for most people, he described a number of ways Meta plans to eventually get paid for it, including commerce transaction fees paid by businesses and money power users will pay for access to advanced models and extra tokens. Meta shares rose 2% in after-hours trading. Meta also warned of some potentially expensive new legal costs on the horizon, including from lawsuits related to child safety legal cases. During the third quarter, Meta said, its operating income declined 37% from a year earlier to just under $13 billion, due in large part to a nearly $10 billion charge related to legal proceedings. In August, the company settled a child online safety case with 52 attorneys general for $18.59 billion. And on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. Meta did not say when it plans to raise capital through a new equity offering, or how much it might raise. Presumably, that will happen after Jan. 19, the effective date for issuance of the new nonvoting Class C common stock the company announced today. The company’s existing shareholders will receive a dividend of one Class C share for each share of Class A or B common stock they hold. And crucially, when the company raises money in the future with its Class C stock, that won’t dilute Zuckerberg’s voting power. “The creation of the Class C common stock will continue the founder-led model that has driven the company’s success since its inception,” Meta said. —Nick Wingfield Tongue-Tied at Tesla On Tesla’s earnings call, Elon Musk had much less to say on the topic of a potential merger of the EV maker with his other company, SpaceX, than he did Tuesday afternoon on SpaceX’s earnings call. He told investors he had said everything he wanted to on the topic for now. Tesla’s automotive revenues fell 3% to $20.56 billion while its total revenues remained flat at $28 billion compared to a year earlier. Tesla shares fell 3% in after-hours trading. —Nick Wingfield In Other News Electronic Arts plans to shed around 400 jobs, or about 3% of its staff, and shut down its BioWare studio, Bloomberg reported . Microsoft asked shareholders to approve a plan to lower CEO Satya Nadella’s pay by 6% due to falling revenue in its Xbox unit. The company also nominated Stripe co-founder John Collison to its board. Google will stop requiring local government officials to sign nondisclosure agreements when it plans to build data centers in their areas. title: How Thoma Bravo Found a Discount in a Hot Cybersecurity Market
content: Cybersecurity has been a dealmaking bright spot amid the broader software gloom, fueled by bets that AI adoption will boost demand for security products. But it’s been hard for private equity firms to get in on the sizzling sector. Corporate buyers have been snapping up cybersecurity companies, competition that makes it harder for private equity firms to buy at prices that leave room for attractive returns when they eventually sell. Rising interest rates further limit what the firms can pay in debt-heavy buyouts. That makes Thoma Bravo–backed cybersecurity company Proofpoint’s agreement last week to acquire data security company Varonis Systems in a $6.3 billion deal a notable example of how private equity can still find an opening in a hot market. And the tech-focused private equity giant is likely to do at least one more deal around this size in the coming year. The proposed acquisition values Varonis at around six times forward annual recurring revenue, according to a person close to the deal. That’s a discount compared to similar public companies like cloud security and compliance company Qualys, which is trading at around 8 times forward annual recurring revenue. Cybersecurity acquisitions were already booming heading into this year, including Alphabet’s $32 billion agreement to buy Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ roughly $25 billion deal for CyberArk, both announced in 2025. But interest in the sector has intensified amid much-hyped releases of powerful models like Anthropic’s Mythos and a series of hacking incidents and agents gone rogue. It could further increase after Wednesday’s disclosure of AI finding a security flaw in open-source programming language PHP, which most websites use. “People ended up realizing that the…threat vector effectively multiplied to infinity,” said Brian Thom, a managing director at middle market investment bank Brown Gibbons Lang & Co. with a focus on infrastructure software and cybersecurity. Cybersecurity mergers and acquisitions hit a record 170 transactions in Europe and North America during the third quarter, according to an Arrowpoint Advisory report from earlier this month . Corporate buyers have been particularly active, including Accenture, which this summer acquired a majority stake in industrial cybersecurity company Dragos, plus two smaller companies in deals with a combined enterprise value of more than $4 billion. Thoma Bravo, for its part, saw an opportunity as Varonis’ stock price came under pressure. Varonis has spent recent years moving customers from licenses to cloud-based subscriptions, temporarily depressing revenue growth, and announced late last year it would phase out older software by the end of 2026. Its shares had tumbled nearly 50% from last October to around $33 this June, right before reports of a potential takeover surfaced. More broadly, some software-focused private equity firms are hunting for companies with depressed share prices but still-credible growth prospects that can hold up even under threat of AI disruption. And many are still nursing the hangover from a software binge during the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. The Varonis acquisition comes at a critical time for Thoma Bravo, which has owned Proofpoint since taking it over for $12.3 billion in 2021. Proofpoint is generating more than $1 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, excluding the proposed Varonis acquisition, the person said, while five years under Thoma Bravo ownership puts it at the point when private equity firms typically face growing pressure to cash out. Adding Varonis expands Proofpoint’s capabilities beyond its traditional focus of protecting employees from cyberattacks, including phishing and other email threats, to securing sensitive corporate data and controlling who can access it, including employees and AI agents. Though Proofpoint has made previous acquisitions under Thoma Bravo, the Varonis deal is by far its largest and gives it a bigger foothold in AI-related defenses that could arguably help it become a more compelling candidate for an initial public offering. Thoma Bravo could be on the hunt for more multibillion-dollar cybersecurity acquisitions following the Varonis deal, which is set to close in the first half of 2027. “There’s a finite number of very large cybercompanies that we can invest in,” said Andrew Almeida, a Thoma Bravo partner who oversees cybersecurity and infrastructure software investments. The firm is particularly interested in companies that generate revenue from the growing use of AI agents rather than relying solely on traditional pricing models that charge based on the number of human users, he said, and it plans to have another deal similar to the size of Varonis within the next 12 months. “Having agentic revenue, not just an agentic vision, but agentic revenue, is a must. And then having a pricing model that can capture this upcoming and ongoing explosion of agents is also a must,” Almeida added. Wobbly IPO Window All eyes are on when Anthropic will finally make its IPO paperwork public, marking one of the final steps toward its hotly anticipated debut. Anthropic announced it had confidentially filed in June, and by late summer was preparing for an IPO as soon as late September.  Now the latest chatter is that the filing could appear by the end of this week. Other AI-related IPOs that initially looked poised to go ahead of Anthropic’s have been pulled or delayed amid mounting concerns about the costs of financing data centers and chips, while the broader IPO market has lost momentum in the midst of Treasury volatility. That’s raised questions about who will test the market next—and whether Anthropic’s offering could revive IPOs in general. Some IPO advisers, however, say other companies may need to go public first, paving the way for the AI giant. “I don’t think Anthropic going public is going to open the floodgates,” said Edward Best, co-chair of Willkie Farr & Gallagher’s capital markets practice. “I think that Anthropic is going to wait until the water starts moving, and then if Anthropic comes through, it’s just going to widen the river. “They can’t take the risk that they don’t do well. They’re going to wait until they see a better path, and then other people are going to join right afterwards,” he added.
