title: Nearly 20 Years Later, Physicists Finally Detect a Long-Predicted Effect in Graphene
content:
Researchers have shown that tiny wrinkles in graphene can change the material’s electrical properties. By harnessing this characteristic, scientists may one day control electricity in atomically thin materials — such as graphene — by changing their shape instead of adding new chemicals or materials, potentially powering more responsive sensors and ultrathin electronic devices. Credit: Mario Norton / Rice University
A nearly 20-year-old scientific prediction has gained experimental support, revealing how graphene’s atomic structure could unlock new possibilities for advanced sensors and electronic devices.
A wrinkle in graphene just a few atoms wide can dramatically alter how electricity behaves in the material. Scientists have now measured this effect in exceptionally sharp folds, providing experimental evidence for a phenomenon predicted nearly 20 years ago.
The discovery, published in
Advanced Materials
, suggests that researchers could eventually control electrical properties by changing a material’s shape rather than its chemical composition. Graphene, a remarkably strong and conductive material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, is already being explored for batteries, computer chips, and other advanced electronics.
How Tiny Wrinkles Change Graphene’s Electrical Properties
The effect is known as flexoelectricity, which occurs when uneven bending causes electrical charges to separate within a material. In graphene, extreme curvature can shift electrons toward one side of its atomically thin structure, creating an electric dipole with oppositely charged regions.
The researchers examined naturally occurring wrinkles whose sharpest bends were compressed into spaces only a few atoms wide, less than a billionth of a meter (about 0.00000004 inches). They found that the sharpness of a wrinkle mattered far more than its overall height. Their estimates indicated that these highly curved regions produced electrical polarization between 100,000 and 10 million times stronger than that associated with much larger, gentler bends.
“The sharpness of the wrinkle turned out to be much more important than its overall size,” said lead author Sathvik Ajay Iyengar, who earned his doctorate at Rice University and is now at the University of California, Berkeley. “That tells us we can potentially tune electrical behavior by carefully controlling curvature at the nanoscale.”
A Scientific Prediction Nearly 20 Years in the Making
The theoretical foundation for the discovery dates back nearly two decades. Vincent Meunier, now head of Engineering Science and Mechanics at Penn State, and Sergei V. Kalinin, now at the University of Tennessee, predicted in a
Physical Review B
paper that sharply bending graphene could rearrange its electrons and produce an electrical response. At the time, sufficiently clean samples were difficult to fabricate, preventing researchers from directly testing the prediction.
The breakthrough began when Iyengar reexamined experimental data collected with collaborator Manoj Tripathi, now at South Dakota Mines. Their measurements showed unusual electrical signals concentrated around graphene’s sharpest wrinkles. Iyengar brought the findings to Meunier, who had co-advised his doctoral research.
“When Sathvik showed me the measurements he and Manoj had collected, we realized that the unusual signals could provide an experimental connection to an idea we had predicted many years earlier,” Meunier said. “I calculated the effect we had predicted for the specific geometry and compared it to the experiment, and it turns out the fit was almost perfect.”
Measuring Electricity at Atomically Sharp Bends
To investigate the mechanism, the team combined specialized microscopy, laser measurements, and computer modeling. Microscope probes mapped the wrinkles’ shapes, local electrical energy, and current, while Raman spectroscopy revealed where graphene’s atoms were stretched or compressed. Simulations performed using Penn State’s Roar supercomputer helped predict how extreme bending would influence electrons.
Comparing sharply curved wrinkles with nearby flat graphene allowed the researchers to separate the effects of curvature from other influences. The wrinkle tips altered local electrical energy and consistently showed electrical current when approximately one volt was applied. These observations closely matched the team’s calculations and simulations.
The wrinkles effectively acted as microscopic obstacles to electrical transport. Their extreme curvature changed the local electronic environment, providing evidence that flexoelectricity can produce a substantial response even in a material only one atom thick. The measured current required an externally applied voltage, so the results do not demonstrate electricity generation without an external power source.
Toward Electronics Controlled by Shape
The findings point toward a possible method for adjusting the electrical properties of ultrathin materials through precisely controlled bending. Future devices might exploit this behavior to create more sensitive sensors or electronic components whose responses depend on nanoscale geometry.
“Nature already creates these tiny wrinkles for us,” Iyengar said. “Understanding how they influence electrical behavior gives scientists another tool for designing future technologies using the structure of a material itself.”
Reference: “Sub-Nanometer Curvature Unlocks Quantum Orbital Flexoelectricity in Graphene” by Sathvik Ajay Iyengar, James G. McHugh, Jonathan P. Salvage, Robert Vajtai, Venkataramana Gadhamshetty, Alan B. Dalton, Manoj Tripathi, Pulickel M. Ajayan and Vincent Meunier, 25 July 2026,
Advanced Materials
DOI: 10.1002/adma.202518224
The research was supported by the Quad Fellowship, the Sussex Strategy Development Fund, the University of Manchester Dame Kathleen Ollerenshaw Fellowship and the U.S. National Science Foundation under grant numbers OIA-2418752, OIA-1849206 and DGE-2510643. This content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the views of the funders.

title: No Batteries, No Plugs: Scientists Create a Tiny Sensor That Powers Itself
content:
Technology
Soldering a graphene-based sensor. Credit: Russell Cothren
Scientists have developed a tiny temperature sensor that harvests energy from magnetic fields near electrical wiring.
Electrical wiring produces weak electromagnetic fields that typically go unnoticed, but researchers have found a way to turn some of that energy into a power source for tiny electronic devices. Scientists at the
University of Arkansas (U of A)
University of Michigan
have developed a graphene-based energy harvester capable of powering an ultra-low-power temperature sensor without a conventional battery.
The prototype operates using energy collected from its immediate surroundings, consuming power measured in nanowatts, or billionths of a watt. It represents another advance toward the team’s goal of developing autonomous sensors that could function unattended for decades.
Turning Electrical Wiring Into a Power Source
The technology captures energy from magnetic fields generated by electrical wiring carrying alternating current. In the United States, electricity typically operates at 60 hertz, meaning the current changes direction 60 times each second. The researchers designed their sensor to harvest energy from these low-frequency fields.
A graphene inductor collects the energy and sends an alternating electrical signal to a custom circuit, which converts it into direct current. That electricity charges capacitors that store energy for the sensor to use. Unlike a battery, a capacitor stores energy in an electric field rather than through chemical reactions.
“The inductor adds charge to these capacitors at a slow rate,” explained University of Arkansas physics professor Paul Thibado, “but it’s faster than the rate the sensor uses up the charges from the capacitors.”
Because the sensor consumes energy more slowly than the system replenishes it, the capacitors can maintain an electrical reserve. Thibado estimates that this stored energy could keep the device operating for at least 24 hours during a power outage, potentially extending to a week.
Building Sensors That Can Power Themselves
The new device is the second graphene-powered temperature sensor developed by the research team. Their earlier work demonstrated that graphene-based solar cells could supply enough electricity to operate temperature sensors, establishing another possible source of energy for autonomous electronics.
Graphene, a material consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms, has electrical properties that make it useful in energy-harvesting technologies. Thibado has investigated these properties for more than a decade and invented the graphene energy harvesters used in the team’s research.
The researchers ultimately want to combine several methods of collecting environmental energy, including sunlight, heat, sound, motion, and ambient electromagnetic fields. A sensor equipped with multiple harvesting systems could continue operating when one energy source becomes unavailable, reducing its dependence on any single power supply.
Applications Beyond Temperature Monitoring
Although temperature measurement provides a practical demonstration, the technology could eventually support sensors used in agriculture, environmental monitoring, medical tracking, wearable electronics, and supply chain management. These applications often require devices to operate in locations where replacing batteries is expensive, inconvenient, or impractical.
Thibado describes the long-term vision as “set it and forget it,” with sensors designed to operate for extended periods without routine battery replacement. Eliminating disposable batteries could also reduce maintenance demands and electronic waste, although decades of reliable operation have not yet been demonstrated.
The research was published in the
Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology B
, with MD Rezaul Kabir, a doctoral candidate in materials science and engineering at the University of Arkansas, serving as first author. The project also involves researchers at the University of Michigan, including electrical engineering and computer science professor David Blaauw, whose work focuses on low-power wireless sensors and embedded systems.
Commercial Development and Future Possibilities
NTS Innovations, a nanotechnology company, holds the exclusive license to commercialize the graphene energy-harvesting technology. The company has supported patent development, business planning, and efforts to identify potential customers and commercial partners.
More than 60 parties have expressed interest in testing the technology and exploring ways to integrate it into products. Ongoing discussions are helping establish practical requirements, including the minimum electrical power needed for different applications.
The researchers envision networks of self-powered sensors that can collect information for years with little human intervention. Combining graphene-based energy harvesting with electronics that consume extremely small amounts of electricity could help make that goal achievable, particularly as connected devices become more common in homes, industries, and environmental monitoring systems.
Reference: “Graphene powerline energy harvester powers a batteryless sensor” by Md R. Kabir, Ashaduzzaman, T. B. Amin, J. M. Mangum, S. M. Rahman, H. Do, G. Carichner, D. Blaauw and P. M. Thibado, 20 October 2026,
Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology B
DOI: 10.1116/6.0005814

title: Experts Spent Decades Searching for the Secret to Happiness. Here’s What They Found
content:
Scientists suggest that happiness is neither constant nor entirely determined by circumstances. Their findings reveal how everyday choices may shape long-term well-being. Credit: Shutterstock
After decades of studying happiness, some of the world’s leading researchers have changed how they live.
Some of the world’s leading happiness researchers have changed how they live because of what they have discovered. After decades of studying well-being, several have made a conscious effort to spend more time with family and friends, reflecting one of the strongest findings in happiness science.
Their insights come from a discussion involving 13 international experts with a combined 600 years of research experience. The conversation, which explored both scientific evidence and personal experience, led to a new paper published in the
Journal of Happiness Studies
Five Key Lessons From Happiness Research
The key takeaways:
Strong relationships are central to happiness.
Social connections consistently emerge as powerful predictors of well-being. Several researchers have applied this finding by deliberately making more time for the people closest to them.
More money does not guarantee greater happiness.
Financial security helps support a good life, but additional income generally has a smaller effect on happiness once essential needs are met.
Meaningful activities support well-being.
Work and other pursuits can contribute to happiness when they provide purpose and reflect a person’s values.
Daily habits can help cultivate happiness.
Researchers described using strategies supported by scientific evidence, including practicing gratitude, savoring positive experiences, volunteering, strengthening relationships, and becoming more socially involved.
Being happy does not mean always feeling good.
Lasting well-being involves living according to personal values, building supportive connections, and adapting to difficulties rather than avoiding negative emotions altogether.
Why Relationships Matter So Much
“Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it,” says Lara Aknin, a professor of social psychology at Simon Fraser University.
Aknin coauthored the paper with Harvard University’s Säde Stenlund and Kelsey O’Connor, a senior researcher at Luxembourg’s National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies. She emphasizes that social connections are among the most consistently supported findings in happiness research.
“Having relationships is one of the most reliable predictors of happiness that has emerged from a robust body of evidence spanning the social sciences,” says Aknin.
“We know that having just one person you can count on is extremely consequential. Having more relationships and more communities that you feel a part of compounds that sense of well-being.”
How Much Control Do We Have Over Happiness?
Although genetics and life circumstances influence happiness, researchers emphasize that well-being is not necessarily fixed. People who generally consider themselves happy still experience setbacks, stress, and negative emotions. Their overall well-being can depend partly on how they respond to challenges and the activities they choose to pursue.
Some influential models of happiness have estimated that life circumstances, including where someone lives, employment, age, and relationship status, account for roughly 10% of happiness, while voluntary activities may contribute as much as 40%. These figures are model-based estimates rather than fixed proportions that apply to everyone, but they highlight the potential role of personal behavior.
“That leaves a lot of opportunity for people who may be more innately pessimistic to start practising research-backed strategies like meditation or gratitude that might help them see the world in a more positive way,” she says.
Happiness Research Is Still Evolving
The scientific study of well-being has expanded considerably since the 1970s, when the modern field began taking shape. What was once a relatively small area of research now encompasses numerous approaches to understanding happiness, life satisfaction, social relationships, and psychological health.
Aknin, who also coedits the annual
World Happiness Report
, says this expansion has brought challenges. As researchers pursue increasingly specialized questions, some early leaders worry that the field has become fragmented. Despite these differences, the scientists who participated in the discussion shared a commitment to rigorous research that can be translated into practical ways to improve people’s lives.
Why Happiness May Benefit More Than Just the Individual
The researchers also considered how personal well-being affects people’s willingness and ability to support others. Studies have linked happiness with positive outcomes beyond individual life satisfaction, including greater motivation to help other people.
“With many large and threatening realities taking place in the world right now, I sometimes worry that the pursuit of happiness can seem trite. But one reason I remain committed to the scientific study of happiness is that happiness in and of itself predicts a number of valuable outcomes, including the motivation to help other people,” she explains.
“When people feel they are doing well, they have the ability, the capability, and the motivation to engage in world affairs—to take care of the people they love and take care of their communities.”
Aknin describes generosity as a process that can benefit both those who give and those who receive. Supporting others can strengthen relationships and communities, creating opportunities for care and connection to spread.
“Generosity is not zero-sum.”
Reference: “Reflections on the Past, Present, and Future of Well-Being Science from Several of Its Pioneers” by Säde Stenlund, Kelsey J. O’Connor and Lara B. Aknin, 25 August 2026,
Journal of Happiness Studies

title: SunFlex deploys flexible perovskite solar modules on shared bikes and at a smart bus stop in China
content:
SunFlex deploys flexible perovskite solar modules on shared bikes and at a smart bus stop in China
SunFlex New Energy
has deployed flexible perovskite solar modules in two new applications in China: shared bicycles and a smart bus stop.
SunFlex’s flexible perovskite solar applications deployed at smart bus stops. Image Credit: SunFlex New Energy
In a partnership with the bike-sharing company Hello, SunFlex launched what it describes as the world’s first batch of shared bicycles covered with flexible perovskite film. The bicycles are fitted with a lightweight film and an onboard smart positioning system, and have been deployed at the Yangcheng Lake Peninsula tourist resort in Suzhou, where road testing has begun. The company says the film keeps generating electricity in overcast and rainy conditions and is impact-resistant, with stable power supply. No power output or battery details were given.
SunFlex has also installed a basketball-themed smart bus stop in Zhuji, Zhejiang province, tied to the city basketball brand “Zhe BA”. It uses SunFlex’s smart power supply system, and the company says the light weight of the flexible perovskite modules allows direct installation on ordinary structures with low load-bearing capacity. It estimates that the system generates about 1,000 kWh per year, avoids about 0.68 metric tons of carbon emissions per year and saves RMB 700-800 (about US$105-120) a year in electricity costs.
SunFlex points to sites where power connections are hard, such as remote suburbs, scenic areas, new roads and islands. A solar-powered stop there needs no road excavation or long cable runs, and the company says this can save up to RMB 20,000 (about US$3,000) per stop in grid connection and labor costs. It expects to launch a purely solar-powered version of its smart power supply for public facilities in 2027.

title: 新闻联播｜新型电网加快建设 为高质量发展提供坚实支撑-索比光伏网
content:
“六张网”中的电网是经济社会发展的“硬支撑”。从高山到戈壁，从沙漠到深海，各地大型电网加快建设，更绿的电能、更智能的调节正加速升级。
在海拔3600多米的四川阿坝米亚罗山，国家西南立体枢纽大电网重点工程——阿坝至成都东特高压工程进入投运前的冲刺，年底建成后，川西北的水、风、光等清洁能源能直送川渝负荷中心，每年可向川渝地区输送清洁电能超150亿千瓦时，助力成渝双城经济圈发展。
在内蒙古的沙漠边缘，蒙西—京津冀±800千伏特高压直流输电工程进入全线铁塔组立关键节点，这条跨区域的电力“大动脉”输送的主要是库布其1200万千瓦沙戈荒基地的绿电。明年投产后，大漠绿电将点对点直送河北，赋能京津冀绿色低碳发展。
新疆的戈壁风区里，哈密1500兆瓦光热储一体化项目的土建工程日前已完成约95%。项目依托丰富的太阳能资源，创新采用“光伏+光热+储热”一体化协同模式，在夜间或阴天也能持续向电网输出稳定、可调节的绿色电力。
在广东，汇集了4个海上风电场电能的三山岛海上风电柔直输电工程完成建设，进入海上换流站的联调联试。这个被称为“海上电力心脏”的换流站把收集的风电，通过上百公里的海底电缆输送至陆地，并入电网。投产后，每年可向粤港澳大湾区输送清洁电能约60亿千瓦时，满足粤港澳大湾区200万户家庭全年的用电需求。
数字智慧电网建设取得新进展。近日，浙江虚拟电厂完成新一轮与大电网的互动，常态化参与发电端和用电端的市场调节，依托人工智能大模型智能调控，实时预判用电需求变化，快速给出解决方案，以实现富余电力合理调配运用。目前，我国已建成虚拟电厂超530个。预计2030年，全国虚拟电厂最大调节能力将突破5000万千瓦。

title: Boskalis awarded UXO IDC campaign at Gennaker Offshore Wind Farm
content:
Boskalis has secured a second unexploded ordnance (UXO) identification
and clearance (IDC) campaign for the Gennaker
offshore wind farm,
located in the German Baltic Sea.
The award follows the completion of a survey and UXO IDC campaign along
the project's inter-array cable routes .
Boskalis Hirdes EOD Services will use its vessel Kamara to investigate
an estimated 850 additional targets and remove identified UXO where required.
The campaign will prepare seabed corridors that allow the foundation installation
vessel to safely deploy and manoeuvre anchors during foundation installation
at the wind farm.
The company is also responsible for the project's inter-array cable package.
Boskalis Subsea Cables and consortium partner TKF Subsea Solutions were
awarded a contract to supply and install around 130 kilometres of 66 kV
inter-array cables.
Cable Installation is currently scheduled to begin in late 2027 using the
cable-laying vessel BOKA Ocean.
With an installed capacity of up to 976.5 MW, the Gennaker offshore wind
farm is expected to become the largest offshore wind farm in the German
Baltic Sea.

title: Red Eléctrica begins underground cable installation
content:
Red Eléctrica has begun laying underground cable for the electricity interconnection
project linking the Iberian Peninsula and France.
The project is expected to increase electricity exchange capacity between
the two countries from 2,800 MW to 5,000 MW, enhancing energy security
and improving the efficiency and resilience of their power systems.
The high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cables, which measure 13 cm in diameter,
will run for approximately 13 km between the Gatika converter station and
the coast of Lemoiz. Preparatory work for the cable installation has already
been completed, including a land to sea drilling operation.
According to Red Eléctrica, the company has worked closely with local authorities
and the fishing sector throughout the project's development to minimise
impacts on coastal communities and marine activities.
The interconnection has also been designed to reduce environmental impacts.
To support this objective, Red Eléctrica partnered with AZTI, a technology
centre specialising in the marine environment.
As part of the initiative, Red Eléctrica and AZTI have launched Ecos del
Océano (Echoes of the Ocean), a monitoring program that will track marine
mammals and commercially important fish species along the cable route.

title: Encryption Under Siege? OpenAI, Anthropic Disprove Key Cryptography Theorem
content: Cryptographers who develop encryption technologies may not be sleeping very well these days. OpenAI and Anthropic both said Monday that their internal AI models had disproven the Exponential Time Hypothesis , a longstanding computer science theorem that predicts the minimum difficulty of solving a certain category of problems. Cryptographers had long assumed the hypothesis was true, and built other findings on the basis of that assumption. Disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis won’t endanger any current encryption methods, said Matthew Green , professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro . But the finding is a big theoretical step, showing that some problems are easier to solve than cryptographers had thought. That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption , a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure. “Our intuition about what‘s hard is very human, and what human beings think is hard doesn’t matter anymore,” Green said. OpenAI and Anthropic have contacted outside experts to review their results on the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The experts include academics working on complexity theory, a field of research that measures the complexity of certain math or science problems, and thus how difficult they are to solve. Ryan Williams , a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who is one of the outside experts reviewing OpenAI’s research, said the company told him it “didn’t necessarily find anything” that would impact existing encryption systems. But OpenAI’s Exponential Time Hypothesis result is “the kind of finding that would make one wonder about those things,” he said. The fact that a spokesperson for OpenAI did not have a comment to us about whether it’s tried to use its models to solve practical cryptography problems won’t make such researchers wonder any less! Yael Kalai , a professor of electrical engineering and computer science at MIT , said it was possible the finding could prompt the National Institute of Standards and Technology , a U.S. agency governing innovation and tech, to increase its recommended security strength for encryption. That would increase the costs of memory and computation needed for any organization that uses encryption processes, Kalai said. If OpenAI or Anthropic do end up finding flaws in existing encryption algorithms, we would imagine they would probably inform the National Security Agency first, long before disclosing it publicly. In other news… Harvey Acquires AI Sales Startup Aida Legal AI startup Harvey has acquired Aida , which develops AI assistants for sales reps to help them catch deals that may be falling through the cracks, the company told The Information exclusively. The deal, whose terms weren’t disclosed, marks Harvey’s fifth acquisition this year, following its most recent acquisitions of AI security startup Guardrails AI in September and Benchmark , which develops AI for investment firms, in July. With Aida’s tech, Harvey hopes to help its customers better organize their proprietary data, so its legal tools can make use of that data, which may be siloed in different organizations right now. Aida’s leaders have experience in this field, otherwise known as AI for enterprise search; its CEO, Piyush Prahladka , for example, was a cofounder at AI search startup Glean . It’s a sign of how AI application startups are hoping to differentiate themselves from model developers that are also releasing vertical-specific products by leveraging hard-to-access data from their customers.— Stephanie Palazzolo Moonshot’s Influencer Backlash Moonshot AI’s release of a new model last week was supposed to be a much-needed breakout moment for a Chinese firm aiming to go public soon. Instead, it was quickly overshadowed by allegations that the company asked influencers to promote the model without disclosing that it was paying them. Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3.1 Pro last Friday as an upgrade to its popular predecessor, Kimi K3 . Hours later, an X user with the account name of Elshayib , a software developer in Jordan who often comments on AI products, said he had boycotted Moonshot’s paid campaign for the new model because the company told him and other influencers not to label their posts as a paid sponsorship. Elshayib argued that doing so would violate X’s terms of service. Elshayib had the receipts: he posted screenshots that he said showed Moonshot’s instructions for influencers participating in the campaign. The instructions in his screenshots suggested that influencers had to use certain talking points , such as “Kimi K3.1 is literally Opus 5.5 open-source, but 5x cheaper” or “China just made Opus 5.5 free to use for everyone,” referring to Anthropic’s flagship Opus 5.5 closed-source model. Some of the recommended talking points put K3.1 Pro in the context of the U.S.-China tech rivalry. One of them said: “The U.S. cut China off from advanced chips, Kimi trained new [state of the art] model without the compute American labs take for granted.” Moonshot hasn’t addressed the allegations publicly, and a Moonshot spokesperson declined to comment. The PR crisis is the last thing the company, valued at $50 billion in a recent private funding round, needs as it moves toward a public listing in Hong Kong. The exact timeframe for its IPO is unclear, and the market sentiment for publicly traded Chinese AI firms, such as MiniMax and Z.ai , has soured in recent months. The controversy comes as closed-source developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI appear to have maintained their lead against open-source rivals when it comes to capabilities, despite recent rumblings that the gap was closing.— Juro Osawa Government Checks In on Anthropic’s Evaluators The White House has checked in with Anthropic about the company’s work with embedded evaluators, Anthropic head of public policy Sarah Heck said at The Information’s Women in Tech and Finance summit on Wednesday. Current evaluators include employees from AI research nonprofit METR and consulting company Accenture , who work inside the company with “employee-like” access to assess safety risks and practices. “We‘re frankly only a couple weeks into it, and I think we’re all learning,” Heck said at the conference. “I‘ve had many conversations with folks in the administration that want to know how it’s going. They want to know what they're seeing.” Here’s what else is going on… Overheard Areas of weakness are emerging within the broader AI market as the cost of capital is set to continue rising, Kim Posnett , Goldman Sachs ’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. Posnett noted that while she’s “hugely bullish” on AI overall, investors are growing more discerning. Anthropic ’s highly anticipated megalisting has been looming over the broader initial public offering market, holding back other companies gearing up for debuts, Lynn Martin , president of the New York Stock Exchange Group , said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Wednesday. Earnings Report Oracle shares rose more than 10% Wednesday after the company sketched out a timeline for when it would begin to slow its capital spending for data centers and start generating cash again. Microsoft revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion in the September quarter, 1 percentage point faster than the growth it reported in the second quarter. Accelerating sales in its Azure cloud unit, driven in part by server rental revenue from OpenAI, offset the slight revenue decreases in its Xbox and devices units. Google’s cloud sales surged in the latest quarter but overall revenue at parent Alphabet grew a slower-than-expected 25% to $127.6 billion, disappointing investors. ServiceNow shares dropped 19% after its third-quarter earnings. ServiceNow says adoption of its AI products is continuing to grow, but investors seem to remain wary of the potential threat AI could pose to its business. Here’s what else is going on… Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Chipmaker Marvell Technologies has been in talks to buy data center optics maker Lumentum , The Information and others reported. A deal for Lumentum would rank as one of the largest semiconductor deals, as Lumentum has a market capitalization of more than $80 billion. The status of the deal couldn’t be learned, but Bloomberg reported that a transaction could be announced as soon as next week. Cognition , the AI coding startup behind Devin , is weighing a new funding round before year's end after receiving offers valuing it at $70 billion to $80 billion — up sharply from the $48 billion valuation it announced just weeks earlier, Business Insider reported. FuriosaAI , a South Korean company that designs AI chips for data-center inference, raised $620 million (KRW 820 billion) in a Series D funding round at a $2.9 billion valuation led by South Korea's National Growth Fund. Upwind Security , which provides security around cloud infrastructure and AI agents, raised $400 million in a Series C funding round at a $3.8 billion valuation led by Bessemer Venture Partners. BioGeometry , a Beijing-based AI-native biopharmaceutical company, raised more than $100 million across its Series A financing rounds, led by China Life Capital . Lumaril , which develops AI software for optimizing industrial production, raised $66 million in Series A funding led by Elad Gil . Casap , an AI agent platform for financial services, raised $56 million in a Series B funding round led by Base10 Partners. Fragment , which builds autonomous AI agents for purchasing and payment services, launched with $56 million in total funding: a Series A led by 8VC and an earlier seed round led by General Catalyst and A *. Broccoli AI , which sells AI agents that answer calls and book jobs for plumbing, HVAC and electrical contractors, disclosed $52 million in combined funding: a previously unannounced $22 million Series A and a new $30 million Series B, both led by Khosla Ventures. Easol , an AI platform for businesses like festivals and wellness retreats, raised $30 million in a Series A extension funding round with investors including Y Combinator . Circuit Mind , which uses agentic AI to design circuit boards, raised $25 million in new funding: an $18.5 million Series A led by Norwest and a previously unannounced seed round led by Third Prime. Plato , which builds simulated workplaces where AI models can practice real jobs, raised $16 million in a Series A funding round led by Nava Ventures. Sava , which builds agentic software infrastructure for the US trust and estate industry, raised $10 million in funding led by Gradient Ventures. AvalonX , an AI-powered security startup, emerged from 18 months in stealth with up to $10 million in funding from Ridown Capital . Google unveiled Gemini 4 Carbon , which it said is significantly more capable than the model it released less than a month ago, as the company steps up efforts to contend with the leading frontier labs. Shopify said it has added agentic payment technology created by Visa , Mastercard and American Express for its checkout feature, Shop Pay , a move that runs counter to how Stripe mainly handles agentic shopping and credit cards. Amazon has significantly expanded its Shop Direct program to list more than 250 million products from rivals, up from around 100 million in March, as rival AI agents make it easier to buy across retailers. Anthropic released new reporting tools on Wednesday to show customers a breakdown of the value they’re getting from their token spend. title: Why Publishers Are Adding Invisible Ads for AI Agents
content: For as long as there have been ads on the internet, marketing has targeted human eyeballs. But as AI agents crowd onto the web, advertisers and publishers are beginning to deliver ads only AI can see, sparking consternation among some of the agents’ developers, who fear marketers could try to sway agents to take actions without their users’ knowledge. The first publisher to experiment with these types of invisible ads was venerable Time magazine, which continues to generate a significant portion of its revenue from ads on Time.com. Those ads—for Ally Bank and Project Management Institute, a trade group for project managers—first showed up online in August and were developed in a partnership with Mobian, a New York–based ad tech startup. The ads were designed to give agents information about the institute’s expertise in project management and Ally Bank’s online banking services and ATM network. Following the ads’ debut, Time has had over 30 meetings with brands about doing similar ads for AI agents, and several new advertisers are launching them now, said Time Chief Operating Officer Mark Howard. Since Time launched its ads for agents, 10 more publishers have started running such ads, said Mobian CEO Jonah Goodhart, who previously sold Moat, a data analytics startup, to Oracle for nearly $1 billion in 2017. Those other publishers are mostly niche sites. One is Daily.dev, a news website for developers, which has signed a one-year revenue-sharing deal with Mobian. Its ads for agents launched around September . Goodhart hopes more than two dozen publishers will be running such ads by December. These ads for AI agents exist on a separate, text-only website version designed to be easily read by the agents. A site using these ads, like Time.com , identifies an agent as soon as it arrives and serves it the stripped-down version of the site rather than the one human visitors see. Paul Bannister, chief strategy officer at Raptive, a New York digital ads company, said he is planning to begin pitching ads for AI agents to brands in the next couple of weeks. And over at PMG, roughly a fifth of the Texas-based digital marketing agency’s 60 or so clients plan to run Mobian’s agent ads over the next month, according to a person close to PMG. If those clients go ahead and launch such ads, the agency expects to know by early next year just how successful they are at getting agents to pay attention to those brands. The past year has brought a frenzy of interest around agentic AI—software that can autonomously carry out tasks on behalf of people. Much of the technology’s development has focused on coding and office tasks, but attention has lately turned to agents people can use for everyday tasks like shopping. In September, Meta Platforms launched its Muse agent, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently said shopping is the most popular use of the app. A few weeks after Muse launched, OpenAI debuted a competing tool, Dots. Another competitor is Instinct, from a San Francisco–based startup by the same name that was founded last year and is valued at $10 billion. The enthusiasm around agentic shopping has drawn a mixed reaction from web retailers. Amazon, for instance, has blocked agents from its site. Other companies, including Walmart and Expedia, have struck partnership deals with Meta to allow it access to their sites. Agentic shopping is very much in its infancy. While 80% of consumers in the U.S., Japan, Mexico, Brazil and the U.K. use AI as part of their shopping experience, only 7% feel comfortable letting it place orders without their approval, according to a study published in late October by Riskified, a New York firm that sells software to prevent online fraud. Still, publishers and advertisers are eager to figure out how to push their brands to agents. Many of them have been energized by how AI has overturned the digital ads world, with chatbots replacing internet searches and direct visits to websites, the two main traditional avenues for selling ads online. At the same time, publishers are trying to figure out exactly how to commercialize those ads and how much a brand is willing to pay for ads visible only to agents compared to traditional ads meant for humans. Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have all held informal discussions with publishers about ads aimed at agents, according to two people familiar with these discussions. In those conversations, the companies have expressed their worry that marketers could include hidden instructions with an ad—perhaps telling an agent to ignore a competitor’s product—and they want the content clearly labeled as an advertisement, these people said. (Anthropic, OpenAI and Google wouldn’t comment for this story.) Some advertising executives worry they could be criticized for using agent-targeting ads and have drawn a comparison between such ads and cloaking, a tactic in which a website shows search engines different content than it shows people visiting the site in order to manipulate search results. Google has long treated cloaking as a form of spam. The comparison irks Goodheart, the Mobian CEO, who insists that humans and AI see the same advertising content. Nimrod Kramer, CEO of Daily.dev, thinks brands will self-police themselves and won’t use the agent-targeting ads to deceive consumers and their agents. He believes such deception might lead the companies developing the agents to blacklist those brands, effectively banning them “from one of the most important sources of traffic over the next 10 to 20 years.” Within two weeks of Time’s launch of its agent ads, Perplexity said it began blocking those ads from influencing its AI agents and search results, calling the practice deceptive. After Time began its experiment, the Interactive Advertising Bureau, the chief trade group for online publishers and ad agencies, polled publishers and advertisers about their thoughts on the ads. More than half of the respondents said they felt it was “too early to tell,” while more than a quarter said they viewed the ads as deceptive or manipulative. “The Time experiment struck a nerve,” said John Dawson, vice president of strategy at Jellyfish, a London-based digital marketing company. “We’re at an inflection point where advertisers need to think about messaging to machines in some pretty explicit ways.” To figure out how much traffic comes from agents, four publishers have signed up to use a new tool from Resemble AI, a startup best known for deepfake detection software used by The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times. None of those publishers has started using the tool yet, which will be released on Thursday, said Resemble CEO Zohaib Ahmed. The tool identifies whether a website visitor is a person or an agent based on behavior such as mouse movements and clicks. In internal testing, it caught 98.8% of agents designed to look human, Ahmed said. If the websites see a large amount of AI traffic, it could spur them to add their own ads meant for agents, he said. Right now, publishers that want to include ads for agents aren’t sure exactly when the best moment is to show them to agents. Some ads are shown to an agent when it is carrying out initial shopping research, while others are shown just as it is completing a purchase. While agent ads remain experimental, publishers are feeling pressured to figure out what will work best whenever they look at the numbers of bots visiting their site: It’s a veritable onslaught. When Daily.dev’s Kramer first heard about Time’s experiment with such ads, he checked to see how many bots were crawling his site. “I was shocked,” he said. “It was millions and millions.”

title: How Instacart Ended Up in DoorDash’s Cart
content: That was fast! DoorDash said this morning that it agreed to buy grocery delivery app Instacart for roughly $17 billion, mostly in cash financed by borrowing, just a few days after we reported that Instacart was in talks to sell itself . After our report, DoorDash and Instacart rushed to seal the deal at a roughly 30% premium to where Instacart shares traded before we broke the news of their talks. They wanted to get it signed before both reported quarterly earnings, which were originally scheduled for next week, say people familiar with the matter. Both companies reported earnings today instead. A deal could take a year or longer to close. So how did this deal come together? Over the years, DoorDash’s leaders have thought about buying Instacart to buttress their grocery sales, according to people familiar with the discussions. Uber, a competitor to DoorDash in restaurant deliveries through Uber Eats, had also talked to Instacart about an acquisition before 2026, and it has had a commercial partnership with Instacart for years. Since going public, Instacart’s annual revenue growth has slowed considerably—to 11% in 2025. (In the third quarter, sales increased 17%, according to the earnings report the company released today.) It faces considerable competition from Amazon and Walmart, which both offer grocery deliveries: Walmart accounted for nearly 32% of all online grocery sales in 2025, while Amazon had almost 23%, according to a report from eMarketer, a market research firm. And last year it lost longtime CEO Fidji Simo to OpenAI and Chief Product Officer Daniel Danker to Walmart. So this year, Instacart’s leaders believed it was the right time to sell, according to people familiar with the matter. Instacart leaders also didn’t want to miss a window to merge with a competitor during the Trump administration, which it viewed as being friendlier to such deals, said the people familiar with the deal. Around late August, Instacart leaders shopped the company to Uber, according to people familiar with the matter. Uber executives felt obliged to take a look and started talking. Instacart told Uber that it thought a deal could make it past antitrust regulators by arguing that Walmart and Amazon were larger, formidable competitors, according to a person familiar with the pitch. Instacart brought on Goldman Sachs, which took Instacart public in 2023, to advise them on a deal. (The grocery delivery firm has long been close to the investment bank, and Goldman partner Nick Giovanni served as Instacart’s chief financial officer from 2021 to 2024.) After talking with Uber, Instacart began conversations with DoorDash , people with knowledge of the discussions. Working with boutique bank Centerview Partners, DoorDash sprang to action, the people said. In 2021, DoorDash had considered buying Instacart in a deal that would’ve valued Instacart at more than $40 billion. Nothing happened partly because they thought the acquisition would face antitrust opposition from the Biden administration. While Instacart’s revenue growth has slowed since then, it has started to generate plenty of cash. Uber wasn’t as keen on a deal. It wasn’t necessarily convinced that regulators would sign off, and it had recently announced another big acquisition, a $15 billion deal for Europe-based Delivery Hero, people close to Uber said. Uber ultimately pulled away from the Instacart talks in September. Instacart then moved ahead with DoorDash. A sale to DoorDash could help Instacart compete against Amazon and Walmart by getting in front of relatively well-to-do customers who regularly use the restaurant-delivery app. DoorDash already offers grocery delivery from retailers such as Safeway, in addition to its core restaurant-delivery business. (Some grocers like Kroger already work with both companies, however.) Research firm Bernstein estimated Tuesday that a combination of DoorDash and Instacart would account for 23% of all online grocery sales in the U.S. Wedbush Securities analysts said in a note to investors this week that they expect regulators will be OK with DoorDash buying Instacart. Still, some grocers that work with both companies might not love the deal, so even if U.S. authorities approve it, state attorneys general might review the merger of competitors themselves. It isn’t clear what will happen to Instacart’s partnership with Uber, in which customers can order Uber Eats from the Instacart app. But DoorDash said it’s keeping Instacart as a separate brand after the deal closes. Apoorva Mehta, the founder of Instacart and its former CEO before Simo joined, said in a statement that he and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu “have explored bringing Instacart and DoorDash together on and off over the years. We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear.” Now that “the biggest companies in the world” are moving deeper into grocery delivery, Mehta says “retailers and restaurants need the technology and service to compete,” and Instacart and DoorDash can be their “partner in that fight.” Today on TITV New From Our Reporters Exclusive OpenAI’s Astra Model Becomes Top Distillation Target for China’s AI Labs By Jing Yang, Juro Osawa and Qianer Liu ‘Nobody’s Ready’: AI-Found Bugs Spark a Corporate Security Spending Spree By Aaron Holmes Recommended Newsletter AI Agenda by Stephanie Palazzolo separates hype from reality and explains how AI is transforming industries. title: Everyone’s Using AI But Divisions Are Growing:  WTF Highlights
content: Artificial intelligence has thoroughly infiltrated business and politics, but it’s also starting to divide companies and investors. That was the takeaway from leaders at The Information’s WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women in the technology and finance industries this week. Investors are increasingly picking AI winners and losers, and favoring companies that can train models and control the chips and data centers that undergird them, said Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking Kim Posnett . “What you’re seeing is not a change in AI sentiment,” she said, but “you’re seeing a repositioning and differentiation across the AI trade.” Meanwhile, the largest tech companies are starting to square off over essential policies that govern the progress of the technology, such as chip export control. Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s global head of data center energy, warned that fast-moving cloud upstarts are prompting the need for new industry-wide standards and regulation around data centers’ use of resources. Leaders from these companies as well as NYSE Group, Goldman Sachs spoke at the conference, alongside CBS News Editor In Chief Bari Weiss and Bumble’s co-founder Whitney Wolfe Herd . Anthropic Policy Chief Hopeful ‘Compromise’ on Chip Export Controls Will Pass Anthropic Head of Public Affairs Sarah Heck said the chip export controls the AI lab has been lobbying to include in the U.S. government’s annual defense bill are the best chance to pass such controls before year end, though she emphasized that the legislation passing is “not assured.” The maker of Claude Code has advocated for stronger chip export controls, warning that without them, governments like China could use American technology to “cement authoritarianism .” Heck said Anthropic has been working with Republicans, Democrats and the White House to “get language that people feel they can live with” in the National Defense Authorization Act. Congress is still debating whether to include three bills that would curb the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China. Anthropic Head of Public Affairs Sarah Heck. Photo by Erin Beach. These bills have also divided the tech industry. In September, Anthropic quit a major tech trade group after the organization, which includes Nvidia and OpenAI as members, urged lawmakers not to include the chip export control bills in the NDAA. The group argued that some of the measures could slow the progress of American AI companies and turn some customers toward China because of the country’s relative lack of regulation. “This is an area where there has been a bit of compromise,” Heck added of the bill. “But if something gets passed, it will be the NDAA.” Heck was dismissive of the argument that China would be able to catch up or pass America’s AI lead without using American chips. “If you believe China is somewhere between six and 12 months behind us, they’re not going to be able to build chips fast enough to close that gap,” she said. Heck acknowledged that Anthropic and other U.S. AI companies may need to work with China on AI safety in the future, but said that could be possible even with chip exporting restrictions. “I think we can do both. I think we can walk and chew gum at the same time,” she said. — Jemima McEvoy AI is Accelerating Trading, NYSE President Says New York Stock Exchange President Lynn Martin. Photo by Erin Beach. AI is the latest technology to change the nature of trading itself, New York Stock Exchange President Lynn Martin said. It’s a far cry from when Martin started her career in financial services, when a trader’s physical stature influenced their effectiveness on the trading floor, she recalled. “A guy who was six foot eight could yell a lot louder over a woman who is five four. That actually mattered,” Martin said. That advantage shrank with the rise of electronic trading, which also made markets more liquid and more efficient. She said AI is accelerating that process. NYSE processes 1.2 trillion to 1.3 trillion incoming order messages every single day, according to Martin. She predicts AI will significantly increase the volume of inbound messages the exchange has to process. While technology can help manage that volume, Martin argued the increase will make the role of human intervention more important. “If the model is trading with [other] models, that’s not a good scenario, or if there’s a bug in the model’s code” and the model itself doesn’t have the judgment or discretion to react appropriately, “that’s not good for markets,” Martin said. “Having that human interacting with the AI is, in my mind, the optimal market.” Martin also noted Anthropic’s highly anticipated megalisting has been looming over the broader initial public offering market, holding back other companies gearing up for debuts.— Anita Ramaswamy Google Data Center Power Head: ‘I Live in 2031’ Amanda Peterson Corio. Photo by Erin Beach. The timeline for AI server chip production is much shorter than the time it takes to build out enough power to run AI data centers, said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s Global Head of Data Center Energy. That means Corio is thinking today about data centers that get built and switched on in 2031 or later. It takes five to ten years to build out new power on the grid, but Google churns out new versions of tensor processing units—the company’s AI chips—about once a year. “That inherently doesn’t work with a seven-year build out of power,” Corio said. To solve that mismatch and prevent a potential chip glut, Corio foresees a rise in power sources like gas generators or clean energy sources built directly on or near data center sites and bigger upfront capital commitments to fund the buildout of new grid and transmission infrastructure. Corio said she just returned from a trip to India to explore pumped hydropower solutions. Local community concerns are also a major factor in whether a data center is built and powered on time. Corio pushed back against broader concerns that data centers use too much water, don’t create enough jobs or pay enough in taxes. She also said that some newer entrants into the space are rushing to build data centers and don’t have the same “history or sophistication” as Google, making industry-wide regulation critically important. “We’re very supportive of that for the industry,” she said. — Phoebe Liu Goldman Sachs Investment Banking Co-Head Sees ‘Repositioning’ Amid AI Boom Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett. Photo by Erin Beach. Areas of weakness are emerging within the broader AI market as the cost of capital is set to continue rising, said Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking. Posnett said that while she’s “hugely bullish” on AI overall, investors are growing more discerning. Posnett noted that AI projects won’t drive expected returns should rates stay elevated for a long period. “While AI itself is not a bubble, I think you can have bubbles within that,” she said. Investors are starting to favor vertically integrated companies that produce frontier models, business applications and AI chips, Posnett added. Goldman is playing leading roles in major deals announced this week for some of the biggest AI companies, including SpaceX’s GPU financing , Meta’s stock offering and Anthropic’s planned initial public offering. Asked about circular financing across the AI ecosystem, Posnett said she’s thinking “more about demand” but acknowledged the risk in tech giants like Nvidia funding their own suppliers and customers. “It makes sense that they want to build closer partnerships with each other,” she said. “And I think it creates greater risk. I think both are true.”— Laura Bratton Flock Co-Founder: ‘Not Our Call’ if Police Share Footage With ICE Flock Safety co-founder and chief people officer Paige Todd said the “most challenging” part of running the startup has been navigating an early decision to not restrict law enforcement’s legal use of its technology. “I have a lot of personal beliefs on a lot of legislation out there, as does everyone. We decided it was not our call to actually decide how laws would be implemented with our technology,” said Todd. “If it is legal in a market to work with [U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement], then that is their decision.” Founded nine years ago, venture-backed Flock makes license plate recognition technology designed to help local officials enforce traffic laws and find criminals. As President Donald Trump sent more federal agents across the country to crack down on illegal immigration, some residents warned the cameras were aiding forced deportations. The company does not have a contract with ICE, said Todd, though “local law enforcement may choose to share their footage with Immigration.” “It’s not our call, because at the end of the day, we actually don’t own the footage ourselves,” she said. Todd added that, despite protests against Flock cameras, the company internally has “actually been pretty calm.” The company offered voluntary buyouts to its U.S.-based employees in September because “people were sitting at the dinner table with their family or going out with their friends on a weekend, and people were like, ‘I cannot believe you work there,’” Todd said. “And after a while, no matter how much they believe in what we’re doing, it just hurt.” — Julia Hornstein Arm, Nscale Executives: There is No Chip Glut Arm’s Ami Badani and Nscale’s Nidhi Chappell. Photo by Erin Beach. Some data center developers, market analysts and investors have become increasingly worried about a future glut of specialized AI server chips that don’t have a functional data center to plug into, due to delays in obtaining power, political pushback and technical issues. Ami Badani, chief marketing officer of semiconductor firm Arm, said she is not aware of any Arm-based chips currently sitting idle in warehouses due to a lack of power. Nidhi Chappell, president of AI infrastructure at data center and cloud company Nscale, said Nscale was also monitoring its supply chain to prevent such power and chip mismatches. In recent months, fears that a shortage of data centers connected to power could lead to chip deliveries going unused has prompted Nvidia to obsessively track power supply . Badani also said Arm was seeing more customer interest than ever in designing custom chips, called ASICs. Arm has helped design chips for Nvidia, Apple and all of the largest cloud computing providers. Designing your own chip can have higher up-front cost, but it can afford companies more control, according to Badani. Shifts in how consumers are using AI are also driving changes to chip demand, Chappell and Badani said. One trend is tighter integration between the different hardware components within a datacenter, which can include different types of chips specialized to different purposes, in order to make the best use of all components. Chips are also getting more specialized for specific types of work, such as training or running AI, Chappell said.  — Tiffany Li 23andMe’s Wojcicki: AI Can Find Medical Insights Anne Wojcicki. Photo by Erin Beach. Anne Wojcicki, who heads the 23andMe Research Institute, said she believes AI will help find new medical insights and concrete actions people can take to improve their health by mining the nonprofit’s huge DNA database. “It is the power of scale,” she said. Wojcicki recounted her personal journey co-founding 23andMe, which became a pioneer in the direct-to-consumer DNA testing market but never came up with a sustainable business model. The company ended up filing for bankruptcy in 2025. Wojcicki spent more than $300 million of her own money to buy the company back last year and turned it into a nonprofit research institute. At the summit, Wojcicki cited a recent scientific collaboration that demonstrated the potential for making new discoveries from the 23andMe database, which includes DNA from more than 3.3 million people who have agreed to participate in research. She said that researchers from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston and the 23andMe Research Institute identified a rare genetic mutation that puts people at exceptionally high risk of getting lung cancer. People who have never smoked but have the gene mutation are 60 times more likely to get lung cancer as people without the faulty gene. Wojcicki’s sister, Susan, the former CEO of YouTube, died in 2024 from lung cancer. “I care a lot about this cause,” Wojcicki said. Wojcicki said she met the Dana-Farber researchers at a scientific conference. They told her they were studying the gene mutation but only had 20 people and how difficult it was to find more patients. “Oh, I have 500 of these people with that genetic variant,” she told them. She said 23andMe can now contact the people and suggest they do screening to make sure they do not have cancer. “I can save these lives,” Wojcicki said. The 23andMe Research Institute is working on a new feature called the Health Summary that can use AI to find connections between people’s DNA and all the other health data they share to make health recommendations. “The more information we get,” she said, “we can give you insights.” — Amy Dockser Marcus

title: OpenAI’s Astra Model Becomes Top Distillation Target for China’s AI Labs
content: OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the most powerful model the company has released, has met with strong demand since its release in early September. One growing customer base: Chinese AI labs that look to extract Astra’s capabilities. DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, two of China’s leading AI developers, relied heavily on outputs from Astra when training their own latest models, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. The practice, known in the industry as distillation, continues to be one of the biggest contributors to the progress made by Chinese open-weight models despite repeated criticism of such efforts by OpenAI and rival Anthropic . Moonshot AI distilled Astra during the development of its new model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, which was released last week, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter. Similarly, DeepSeek’s V4.1-Flash 1017, an Oct. 17 upgrade to its V4.1-Flash model that demonstrated substantial improvements from the original version released in September, also benefitted from distilling Astra, according to two other people with direct knowledge of that. Until recently, Anthropic’s Claude models were the biggest target of Chinese distillation efforts. Moonshot didn’t comment. DeepSeek didn’t respond to a request for comment. Anthropic and OpenAI have both repeatedly accused Chinese labs including Moonshot and DeepSeek of distilling their models. Chinese labs haven’t publicly responded to the allegations. Distillation is a common technique in developing AI; Anthropic and OpenAI have said they distill their own models when creating smaller, faster and cheaper versions of them. But the practice becomes controversial when outside companies target proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Both companies have policies barring others from distilling their models and don’t release their models in China. Distillation targeting them requires tricking their models into spewing out the steps taken to complete a user’s query, secrets that the developers don’t willingly share. Distillation isn’t the only reason Chinese models are competitive, though. U.S. export controls on advanced chips and other resource constraints have forced Chinese labs such as DeepSeek to explore innovative techniques to train and run models with fewer chips. But researchers at Chinese labs say the technique has played a critical role in enabling China’s AI sector to closely trail U.S. frontier models at a fraction of what OpenAI and Anthropic spend on compute. How OpenAI and Anthropic Are Fighting Distillation The rising popularity of Astra as a distillation target is due in significant part to Anthropic’s intensifying efforts to crack down on what the company has called an “industrial-scale, covert campaign” to extract the capabilities of its Claude models, the people with direct knowledge of Chinese labs’ efforts said. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it had made “substantial progress” in reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks, with new methods helping reduce the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90% to 99%. The company, for example, made it harder for distillers to use proxy networks to try extracting Claude’s protected reasoning—the hidden thinking process before the model generates an answer. Users who make repeated attempts to extract reasoning face stricter usage limits and account bans, it said. Use of such proxy networks, which violates Anthropic’s policies, is a common set-up underpinning distillation. Anthropic said this week in the prospectus for its planned initial public offering that customers that violated its terms contributed between roughly 5% and 7% of its revenue for the first nine months of this year. One of the operators of such proxy networks in China estimated that their customers have contributed roughly $10 million a month to Anthropic’s revenue, The Information reported . Anthropic’s revenue this year through September totaled more than $33 billion, according to the prospectus and The Information’s reporting . An OpenAI spokesperson said the company is closely tracking distillation attempts by Chinese AI labs and actively working to detect and disrupt them, including by banning or restricting fraudulent accounts, tightening signup and infrastructure controls, and expanding monitoring. It remains unclear to what extent the practice has contributed to OpenAI’s revenue growth. OpenAI’s third-quarter financials haven’t come out, but its annualized revenue neared $50 billion last month , up 70% from the end of June. An OpenAI spokesperson declined to provide an estimate for how distillation affects revenue but said the company takes the issue “extremely seriously” and is continuing to work on it. “As we deploy new defenses, attackers adapt their tactics, requiring continued improvements,” the spokesperson said. OpenAI has stepped up its measures against distillation. In late September, it said it had identified and mitigated a “coordinated model-distillation campaign” in July involving individuals associated with Moonshot. OpenAI said the operators of the campaign tried to extract protected reasoning by interacting with models in ways that could make their reasoning visible. OpenAI’s models remain accessible for distillation, but gathering usable training data from them, which requires more than 10 times as many prompts as normal use, requires distillers to use many accounts to avoid triggering detection, according to two of the people with knowledge of Moonshot and Deepseek’s distillation efforts. Prior to Anthropic’s heightened crackdown in the past two months, Claude was the go-to model for Chinese labs looking for shortcuts as they seek to stay ahead in the fierce AI race. DeepSeek CEO Liang Wenfeng initially didn’t want to resort to distillation when developing the company’s new generation V4 model, according to the two people with direct knowledge of DeepSeek’s model development. But he had to succumb to competitive pressure after seeing the success of domestic rivals such as Z.ai , whose GLM models, also developed with distillation, were gaining traction, the people said.

title: Google Cloud Closes In on Azure, but Microsoft Wins the Day With Investors
content: There was a lot to digest from Wednesday’s earnings reports from Microsoft and Google, long the No. 2 and 3 players in cloud computing, respectively. But let’s start with the most interesting takeaway: Google’s cloud unit revenues are now within spitting distance of Microsoft’s Azure cloud revenues, thanks in part to Google’s sales of its AI chips, known as tensor processing units. For those of us who remember the days not long ago when Google was an also-ran in cloud, that’s a pretty stunning development. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves. The stellar third-quarter growth in Google’s cloud computing business was overshadowed by other financial results that disappointed Wall Street analysts, particularly weak growth in Google’s search advertising revenues. Google’s stock dropped nearly 10% in after-hours trading. Microsoft’s growth, meanwhile, played better with investors, sending its stock up about 3% in after-hours trading (Microsoft shares are up 12% for the year, compared to 2% for Google). First, let’s look at Google’s numbers. Alphabet, the search giant’s parent company, reported a 25% jump in revenue to $127.58 billion, which fell slightly short of Wall Street forecasts. Due to its enormous spending on AI, the company showed negative free cash flow of over $9 billion compared to positive free cash flow of over $24 billion in the same period a year ago. The figures that seemed to alarm some investors the most were Google’s search revenues, which grew 12% to $63.35 billion—the softest growth in the business since the second quarter of 2025. Those results seemed discordant with the fact that people are using Google search more than ever. Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said Google’s year-over-year search query growth rate is the highest it has been in five years, which he attributed to the company’s AI investments. But for the moment, Google isn’t showing as many ads in AI Mode, its AI-powered search results, as it typically does. “It’s worth noting the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on a call with analysts, in explaining the disconnect. Still, there were those Google Cloud results to admire. Revenue from that business more than doubled in the quarter to over $30 billion, while the unit’s operating income tripled to $11.12 billion. That revenue figure was just shy of Microsoft’s $33 billion in Azure revenues for the period, which grew 48%. If Google Cloud keeps up its superior growth rate, it won’t be long before the business is bigger than Azure. Of course, the comparison isn’t totally apples-to-apples. Google Cloud revenues include a burgeoning server hardware business , through which the unit sells TPU systems to customers that put the chips in their own data centers. Google didn’t disclose exactly what its TPU sales were in the quarter, though it did say they were a “meaningful contributor to revenue growth.” Google executives primed analysts to expect TPU sales to have an even bigger impact on Google Cloud next year. “We’re seeing extraordinary demand,” Thomas Kurian, Google Cloud’s CEO, told them. Less is More at Microsoft Last month, when Microsoft announced it was overhauling how it reports its business segments’ quarterly results, CEO Satya Nadella promised “increased transparency.” Today though, one figure they had disclosed in the prior quarters—the number of paying users of its flagship Copilot AI software—was conspicuously absent. Previously, the company had said it had 30 million paying users of Copilot as of the end of June, up from 15 million at the end of 2025. Those customers each pay a $30 per month fee to use Copilot in its Office and Teams software, on top of fees they pay separately for those applications. That solid growth planted Microsoft’s flag as the second-biggest seller of AI software after OpenAI , and helped assuage some investors’ concerns about whether Microsoft’s core enterprise software business was getting returns from its ballooning AI spending. The company’s decision to stop disclosing the figure raises the question of whether Copilot subscriptions are growing as robustly as they had in the past. The good news for Microsoft is that its AI-infused software business still seems to be strong . Revenue in its 365 Commercial Cloud unit—which includes Copilot as well as sales of its broader suite of Office software—rose 17% to $27.7 billion, a slight acceleration from the June quarter. Overall revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion in the September quarter, 1 percentage point faster than the growth it reported in the prior quarter. There are other reasons Microsoft might want to get investors to pay less attention to the growth of per-seat subscriptions of Copilot. The company overhauled its Copilot software late last month to combine various features under one application; part of the reason for the change was to steer Copilot users towards newer features like agents that compete with Meta’s Muse and vibe-coding tools, which are billed on a pay-as-you-go basis. In other words, Microsoft is now trying to get more Copilot revenue growth to come from people using the software more, rather than just from selling additional seats. Nadella hammered this point during Wednesday’s call with analysts, stating that the number of customers paying for usage-based features in Copilot grew 75% in the September quarter, and CFO Amy Hood said average revenue per user grew thanks to increased use of the pay-as-you-go AI tools. Whether Microsoft can keep its AI software revenue growth going will be more telling, especially as it starts to offer steeper per-seat discounts on the software in a broader pricing war with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. —Aaron Holmes In Other News Apple launched its first touchscreen computer, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, which will start at $2,899. That’s a steep premium to its latest MacBook Pro without a touchscreen, which starts at $1,999. Oracle provided a roadmap for when its capital expenditures will begin to slow, describing fiscal 2028 and 2029 as a “period of peak capex.” The company’s free cash flow will turn positive in fiscal 2028 and exceed $30 billion in fiscal 2029, it said. Oracle’s shares rose 10%. Google launched Gemini 4 Carbon, the company’s second major model release in a month. Marvell is in advanced talks to buy data center optics maker Lumentum.
