title: “Nearly Everybody Had Given Up” – Scientists Finally Solve a 60-Year Chemistry Mystery
content:
Chemistry
Structure, bonding and electronic aspects of a newly-prepared oxoborane. Credit: Lukas Lubczyk, Christian Markl, Dr. Thomas Kupfer, Dr. Rian Dewhurst / University of Wuerzburg)
After more than six decades of failed attempts, chemists have achieved a breakthrough involving a class of molecules long considered too unstable to isolate.
Chemists have succeeded in isolating a group of molecules that researchers have struggled to capture for more than 60 years. Known as oxoboranes, these compounds contain an unusual triple bond between boron and oxygen, a combination long considered too unstable to isolate in a lasting form.
Researchers led by Professor Holger Braunschweig at the University of Würzburg have now developed a method that produces three surprisingly stable oxoboranes. Published in
Nature Chemistry
, the work was supported by computational research from Professor Ashwini K. Phukan’s team at Tezpur University in India.
An Unexpected Reaction Produces Elusive Molecules
The breakthrough began when Würzburg doctoral students Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl independently reacted a compound called a diboracumulene with different ketones, chemicals commonly used in organic synthesis. Instead of the anticipated products, they obtained unusual orange or yellow solids. The reactions had unexpectedly produced oxoboranes as their main products.
“The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something,” says Lukas Lubczyk.
Solving a 60-Year Challenge in Chemistry
Boron has a strong tendency to avoid forming triple bonds, making these molecules particularly difficult to synthesize. Braunschweig has spent more than 15 years investigating this type of chemical bonding. His team created the first molecule containing a boron-boron triple bond in 2012, followed by the first neutral molecule with a boron-carbon triple bond in 2025. Organic oxoboranes represented the remaining challenge involving triple bonds between boron and other elements in the first row of the periodic table’s p-block.
Chemists have pursued oxoboranes since at least the early 1960s. Although previous experiments detected or trapped them under extreme conditions, inferred their presence from chemical reactions, or produced related derivatives, researchers had been unable to isolate stable examples.
“Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them,” says Holger Braunschweig.
The successful preparation of three oxoboranes suggests that the new approach could provide access to additional members of this difficult-to-synthesize molecular family. The researchers are now investigating whether the method can be extended to produce other elusive compounds involving elements across the periodic table.
Reference: “Synthesis and isolation of stable oxoboranes” by Lukas Lubczyk, Christian Markl, Mudit Jain, Sourav Kar, Thomas Kupfer, Rian D. Dewhurst, Ashwini K. Phukan and Holger Braunschweig, 27 October 2026,
Nature Chemistry
DOI: 10.1038/s41557-026-02272-w
The work was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

title: Flexell Space and Satoro plan two in-orbit demonstrations of space solar cells
content:
Flexell Space and Satoro plan two in-orbit demonstrations of space solar cells
Flexell Space
and Singapore-based Satoro have agreed to pursue two in-orbit demonstrations of Flexell’s solar cells, one planned for 2027 and the other for 2028, each aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Under the plan, Satoro will build the CubeSat satellites, while Flexell will provide the solar cells and test modules. The companies say they will coordinate the satellite-platform and payload requirements. The demonstrations are intended to compare ground-test results with operating data collected in orbit, assessing the cells’ power output and how their performance changes over time.
Flexell is developing solar cells based on both CIGS (copper indium gallium selenide) and perovskites, including perovskite/CIGS tandem designs for space. The reported plan does not assign either technology to a specific mission.

title: 中电联发布《2026年三季度全国电力供需形势分析预测报告》-索比光伏网
content:
10月29日，中国电力企业联合会对外发布《2026年三季度全国电力供需形势分析预测报告》(以下简称《报告》)。《报告》指出，今年前三季度全国电力消费呈现总量稳增、结构调优、动能焕新、韧性增强的特征，全国电力系统安全稳定运行，电力供应结构持续绿色低碳转型，电力供需总体平衡。
《报告》显示，前三季度，全国全社会用电量8.07万亿千瓦时，同比增长3.9%。全国新增发电装机容量2.5亿千瓦，其中风电和太阳能发电合计新增装机1.7亿千瓦，占新增发电装机总容量的67.8%。
截至9月底，全国全口径发电装机容量达41.3亿千瓦，同比增长11.2%，其中非化石能源发电装机容量25.9亿千瓦，同比增长14.4%，占总装机容量比重为62.6%;太阳能发电装机规模历史性超过煤电成为国内第一大电源，风光发电装机合计已超20亿千瓦，新能源发电成为我国主体电源，发电装机延续绿色低碳发展趋势。
前三季度，全国规上口径发电量7.49万亿千瓦时，同比增长2.2%，非化石能源发电量增量占全社会用电量增量的比重为87.2%。
《报告》预测，四季度全国电力消费增速较三季度明显回升，全年全社会用电量10.8万亿千瓦时左右，同比增长4%-4.5%。迎峰度冬期间，预计全国电力供需形势总体平衡，若出现大面积寒潮天气、一次能源供应紧张等极端情况，局地高峰时段可能出现电力供需偏紧。
预计2026年全年新增发电装机有望超过3.5亿千瓦，到2026年底，全国发电装机容量将达到43亿千瓦左右，其中非化石能源发电装机约27亿千瓦，占总装机的63%左右;风电和太阳能发电装机规模达到总发电装机的一半;煤电装机占总装机的比重将降至31%左右。

title: 河北：大力推进港口“风光储充”一体化建设，加快绿色港口创建-索比光伏网
content:
10月29日，从省政府新闻办召开的《“绿动渤海”行动方案（2026—2030年）河北篇》政策解读新闻发布会获悉，河北围绕加快航运绿色低碳转型、推进港口低碳智能建设、赋能临港绿色产业升级、强化全域污染协同防治、健全要素支撑保障机制”五大板块，提出20项具体任务，着力打造绿色港航示范区，赋能经济强省、美丽河北建设。
加快航运绿色低碳转型
优化运输结构体系
方案从船舶、燃料、运输组织、航线网络四个维度系统推进：
01推动船舶绿色低碳转型
加快老旧营运船舶报废更新，引导新建改造船舶应用新能源清洁能源，聚焦沿海短途货船、港作拖轮、旅游游艇推广电池动力等清洁动力，支持秦皇岛山船重工等企业强化绿色船舶研发制造。
02推进船舶绿色燃料应用
研究推进港口绿色燃料加注基础设施建设，支持曹妃甸LNG码头加注改造等绿色燃料加注产业发展，有序落地绿色燃料加注示范项目。
03优化交通运输组织模式
纵深推进“公转铁”“公转水”，深入实施多式联运，建立绿色船舶库，实行绿色船舶“一船一策”、绿色航线“一线一策”、绿色走廊“一廊一策”，推广船舶“四直”绿通和“八优”快线模式，提升港口作业效率、减少船舶待港时间。
04打造绿色示范航线网络
推动唐山港至山东博兴港海河联运等绿色航线建设，探索构建国际绿色航运走廊，全面提升航运绿色化、集约化水平。
推进港口低碳智能建设
夯实绿色发展根基
01深化港口清洁能源使用
全面推进岸电设施提档升级，组建渤海“岸电使用绿色联盟”，有序推动港口作业装备新能源替代，大力推进港口“风光储充”一体化项目建设。
02加快绿色低碳港口创建
支持建设“近零碳港区”“零碳码头”“零碳运输线路试点”，聚焦黄骅港煤炭港区打造近零碳港区，到2030年专业化散货码头全部建成星级绿色港口。
03提升港口智慧绿色运营水平
依托数字化智能化技术升级运营管控体系，强化能耗排放实时监测，推进港区绿化美化和生态缓冲带建设，实现港口生产与生态保护协同发展。
赋能临港绿色产业升级
培育低碳发展动能
01有序推进海上风电光伏项目建设
加快秦皇岛、唐山、沧州海上清洁能源项目建设，推进海上风电与海洋石油、海洋牧场、海水制氢、海洋算力融合发展，结合唐秦负荷中心需求实施“海上风电+绿电直连”实施项目。
02加快推动油田绿色发展
鼓励绿电就近接入油田生产系统，推动秦皇岛—曹妃甸油田群岸电扩容，支持秦皇岛27-3油田建成“低碳零碳作业区”。
03壮大海洋绿色新兴产业
大力发展新能源船舶、高端海工装备等绿色制造产业，谋划实施秦皇岛无人船制造、智能港口设备制造等项目，有序布局海水制氢等前沿产业，培育临港经济新的绿色增长极。
强化全域污染协同防治
提升海洋生态环境
01从严管控船舶污染排放
综合运用卫星遥感、无人机巡查等科技手段构建立体化监管体系，严格船舶排放控制区监管，常态化开展燃油硫含量和尾气处理装置检查。
02系统提升港口污染治理水平
严格落实环保设施“三同时”制度，完善船舶污染物接收转运处置闭环管控，打造煤炭码头“无废港口”示范港，到2030年煤炭本质抑尘技术全面应用，干散货码头绿色化水平国际领先。
03提升海上污染应急能力
充分发挥环渤海区域海上污染应急协同机制作用，加强溢油应急队伍建设，常态化开展应急演练。
04深化海洋生态环境风险防范
动态排查涉海环境风险隐患，编制海湾生态环境风险“一湾一图”，巩固提升秦皇岛湾等美丽海湾建设成效，与天津市协同加强入海排污口监管，促进津冀区域海洋环境规范管理水平共同提升。
健全要素支撑保障机制
夯实绿色发展根基
方案从法规、金融、体系、人才、数智、履约六个方面强化保障：
01完善法规标准政策体系
修订完善《河北省防治船舶污染海洋环境管理办法》等法规，推动水运领域绿色低碳标准制修订。
02发挥蓝色金融支撑作用
创新蓝色信贷产品，探索海域使用权、海洋碳汇等非传统抵押品信贷模式，推广EOD模式，鼓励研发清洁能源船舶专项保险。
03推动降碳减污动态监测和科学评价体系建设
探索建立港航和海洋产业碳排放统计核算评价体系。
04加强人才队伍建设
深化校企合作产教融合，布局双燃料船舶船员培养见习点。
05提升数智化管控能力
加快智慧航道、智慧交管建设，在秦皇岛、沧州开展低能见度通航技术研究应用，建设海上搜救智能化辅助决策系统。
06强化国际海事履约与涉外航运治理
严格落实国际防止船舶污染公约等国际公约，提升河北港口国际化服务能力和对外开放水平。

title: 宁夏新能源完成三次转型 风光资源变身新型生产要素-索比光伏网
content:
31日，记者从国网宁夏电力有限公司获悉，前三季度宁夏回族自治区新能源装机达到6079万千瓦，占总装机比重64.94%，稳居区内第一大电源。区内售电量811亿千瓦时，同比增长5.05%;外送电量815亿千瓦时，同比增长7.01%。塞上风光资源正实现三次转身，从发电资源变为外销商品，最终成长为可调度、可交易的新型生产要素。
高比例新能源并网，最大难题是风光出力的波动性。宁夏以储能+调峰火电+坚强电网协同托举，破解“靠天吃饭”困境。截至9月底，宁夏储能装机1125万千瓦，规模位居全国第四。当地对电网侧储能实行清单化管控，明确下半年33个储能项目、1004万千瓦并网计划，工期逾期将予以清退。中卫电厂机组作为全国首个“沙戈荒”大基地配套调峰电源，灵活调节出力，为新能源腾出消纳空间。
市场化机制进一步盘活储能收益。随着宁夏电力现货市场V2.0连续结算试运行，独立储能可自主报价参与交易，“低充高放”收益更加稳定。储能配套电网工程同步提速，前三季度新开工55项电网工程、投运61项基建工程，骨干网架承载力持续增强。储能的规模化应用，直接将宁夏新能源利用率稳定维持在96%以上。
绿电就地消纳通道持续拓宽。宁东煤化工园区、硅基、铝锰基工业企业纷纷签订绿电协议，清洁电力走进厂房车间。依托源网荷储一体化建设，工业柔性负荷主动参与电网平衡，供需联动更加紧密。
算力产业成为绿电就地转化的核心载体。前三季度，宁夏算力用电量达20.31亿千瓦时，同比大增85.92%，其中绿电占比56%。中卫依托“算电协同”模式，把大漠风光直接转化为AI算力。当地出台八项举措保障算力用电，搭建多层次电力市场，推行小时级绿电交易，引导非实时算力任务在光伏大发时段集中运行。目前中卫已投运17家数据中心，绿电占比最高突破80%，为“东数西算”提供可复制经验。
如今，宁夏形成“就地转化+跨区外送”双轮并行格局，戈壁风光不再只是并网发电的资源，已然成为支撑产业升级、服务全国双碳转型的新型生产要素。

title: 2026“光能杯”光伏评选持续进行中｜缩量之年，谁在逆风换挡？-索比光伏网
content:
2026年的光伏，
关键词不是“更大”，而是“换挡”。
上半年新增并网71.77GW，累计装机突破1271GW，但增速明显回落；组件出口同比下降，价格在历史低位震荡。与此同时，BC、THBC、钙钛矿的技术迭代没有减速。行业不再奖励“谁做得更大”，而是在筛选“谁换挡更快、谁在低价环境里守住了质量与口碑”。
一年一度的“光能杯”光伏评选，要做的就是把这个分化年份里逆风换挡的企业找出来，让它们被行业看见、被市场记住。
一年一度的“年终奥斯卡”
2012年，索比光伏网发起“光能杯”，迄今已连续举办十四年，被业内称为光伏行业的“年终奥斯卡”。上一届评选共有300余家光伏企业参与报名，颁奖盛典在苏州举行。
2026年，光能杯官方对行业阶段的判断很明确：光储产业告别规模竞速，迈向价值化、场景化、市场化高质量转型。这意味着今年的评选，比的不是谁的增长曲线最陡，而是谁在调整期展现了穿越周期的能力——技术切换的执行力、产品在低价环境中的品质底线、供应链上的履约责任、细分场景里的真实落地。
为什么今年的“光能杯”
值得你认真填一张申报表
因为在这个年份，“被看见”本身正在变成一种稀缺资源。
一面是，行业信息噪声前所未有地大。价格每天在变，产能每天在出清，企业的真实进展很容易被淹没在“内卷”叙事里。另一面是，客户、渠道、资本在当下做判断时，比任何时候都更需要一个超出企业自我陈述的第三方参照。
“光能杯”的价值不在奖杯本身，而在于它提供的是一个有十四年连续记录、有评审流程约束、有行业公开可见度的信任凭证。对于在逆风中完成了技术切换、守住了产品口碑、打开了新场景的企业，这个凭证的意义远大于顺境时的一次曝光。
而且，申报本身就有可见回报。根据2026年光能杯的申报权益安排，申报企业即纳入公示展示，获得索比平台基础稿件传播和颁奖典礼同期大会免费门票1张；入围企业额外获得专属海报、专题页独立卡片、直播间独家盘点；获奖企业颁发荣誉奖牌并受邀出席颁奖晚宴。
█ 奖项怎么设，谁在评？
2026年光能杯光伏评选设置三大奖项层级：
光能杯最高荣誉，每届每个奖项仅授予1家企业，采用定向邀约与行业机构推荐机制，不开放自主申报。获奖者代表行业顶尖水准，须经专家委员会严格审核，企业高层亲临现场领奖。包括年度企业、年度人物、年度产品、年度特色大奖。
特色专项奖，表彰在产品实力、创新性、可持续发展、行业前瞻探索等方面表现突出的主体：Solarbe Test 评测大奖、ESG 实质性披露奖等。
覆盖光伏产业链各环节，综合考量企业综合实力、核心产品质量与体量、品牌影响力，是申报覆盖面最广的奖项层级，适合绝大多数参评企业作为主攻方向。
评审依据企业主动申报，结合组委会年度内走近企业所获取的一线信息、企业公开传播内容，以及公众投票、年度经营表现、受众口碑、奖项匹配度等要素，由权威专家与权威媒体联合评审，公开、公平、公正产生归属。
█ 哪些企业可以申报
从硅料、硅片、电池、组件，到辅材、支架、逆变器、EPC与运维，再到认证检测、系统解决方案、光储融合、光电建筑等各环节，全产业链皆可登台。
基本条件清晰直接：具有独立法人资格，无重大违法违规行为，对核心产品（服务）的核心技术拥有自主知识产权，在所处产业链环节处于领先地位，具备第三方检测认证机构出具的产品或系统认证证书，具备质量管理体系、安全生产、职业健康安全等相关证明文件。
不看“规模排名”，看你在过去一年有没有值得被行业记住的实绩——效率爬坡的进度、成本控制的真实水平、交付履约的记录、场景落地的案例，都算。
█ 怎么报，现在就报
申报通道一：扫描下方二维码，直接进入光能杯申报页面。
扫描下方二维码，直接进入光能杯申报页面。
点击文末“阅读原文”，跳转索比光伏网光能杯官方申报入口。
申报时间:9月23日-11月30日
名额与展示位置随报名进度推进。早一步提交材料，早一步进入评审视野，也早一步进入申报公示与传播序列。
光伏行业从来不缺在逆风里把事做成的企业。缺的是让这些事被行业看见、被记住、被兑现为下一程信任的窗口。
2026年度“光能杯”已经启程，缩量之年，换挡者值得一个被看见的位置。

title: Cadeler's Wind Mover to install 72 wind turbine generators at Inch Cape
content:
Cadeler's Wind Mover to install 72 wind turbine generators at Inch Cape TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Cadeler's Wind Mover to install 72 wind turbine generators at Inch Cape
Vestas Wind Systems A/S is set to begin the installation and commissioning
of 72 wind turbine generators (WTGs) at the 1.1GW Inch
Cape offshore wind farm,
with Cadeler's construction jack-up vessel Wind Mover leading the installation
campaign.
Turbine components will be loaded at the Port of Dundee before being transported
to the project site offshore. Ahead of the first load-out operations, Wind
Mover is expected to arrive at Inch Cape on or around 30 October.
Commissioning activities will be carried out from the service operations
vessel Acta Hercules. Technicians will access the turbines using a walk-to-work
system during the commissioning phase.
Additionally, the campaign will be supported by the crew transfer vessels
NOS Exceller and NOS Empowerer. Installation and commissioning of all 72
turbines are expected to continue through to September 2027.

title: LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution sign Taean Wind Farm agreement
content:
LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution sign Taean Wind Farm agreement TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution sign Taean Wind Farm agreement
LS Cable & System and LS Marine Solution have signed a Capacity Reservation
Agreement (CRA) with Taean Wind Power Co. to supply and install submarine
cables for the 504 MW Taean
offshore wind farm.
The agreement secures production facilities and construction vessel availability
needed to support cable manufacturing and installation. The announcement
follows the selection of the companies as preferred bidders in 2024.
The Taean offshore wind farm is located off Taean-gun in Chungcheongnam-do
and is being developed by Korea Western Power, Vena Energy and Copenhagen
Infrastructure Partners.
“Due to the unique offshore construction environment, it is crucial to
closely link cable production and installation to enhance on-site responsiveness
and accountability,” an LS Cable & System official said.
Adding, “We will proceed with the main contract without any setbacks to
expand our penetration of the domestic offshore wind market.”
The offshore wind farm is currently expected to be completed by 2030.

title: Nordlicht I has Installed all 68 foundations
content:
One of Germany’s largest offshore wind farm has reached a major milestone,
with all 68 foundations installed in the German North Sea ahead of schedule.
Once completed, the Nordlicht
I offshore wind farm
will have an installed capacity of 980 MW. The project forms part of the
Nordlicht cluster, which consists of two offshore wind farms with a combined
capacity of 1.6 GW.
“Nordlicht is far more than just an offshore wind project. It is a significant
investment in Germany’s energy future and an important contribution to
the transition of Europe’s electricity supply to renewable energies,”
said David Flood, head of offshore at Vattenfall.
The milestone follows an installation update in September that confirmed
all monopiles had been installed. Since then, transition pieces have also
been successfully fitted.
The foundations were manufactured by EEW Special Pipe Constructions and
CS WIND Offshore, while DEME was responsible for transporting and installing
both the monopiles and transition pieces.
The company highlighted several environmental measures implemented during
the installation phase, including the use of turbine towers made from reduced
emissions steel, continuous environmental monitoring, and bird and marine
mammal observation programs.

title: All 52 turbines installed at 760 MW Ecowende offshore wind farm
content:
The final turbine has been installed at the 760 MW Ecowende
offshore wind farm,
marking the project's final construction phase, with all 52 turbines installed
over the past five months.
The installation was completed through a joint effort between Van Oord
and Vestas. Van Oord was responsible for the transportation and installation
of the turbines and other wind farm components, while Vestas supplied the
V236-15.0 turbines.
Ecowende, a joint venture between Shell, Eneco and Chubu, is located 53
kilometres off the Dutch coast and is expected to meet around 3% of the
Netherlands' electricity demand.
“Ecowende is designed to gain knowledge on how to build and operate a
wind park in harmony with nature. We will share that knowledge, so that
researchers, governments and wind park developers can build on it,” said
Ecowende CEO Tjalling de Bruin.
According to the company, the project aims to be the most ecologically
focused offshore wind farm developed to date. The wind farm will test
measures designed to protect birds and bats while supporting underwater
biodiversity.

title: New T5 Terminal opens in Gdańsk to support Poland’s offshore wind expansion
content:
New T5 Terminal opens in Gdańsk to support Poland’s offshore wind expansion TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
New T5 Terminal opens in Gdańsk to support Poland’s offshore wind expansion
The Polish Development Fund (PFR) has completed construction of the T5
Terminal at the Port Gdansk.
The milestone follows a gross investment of PLN 1.2 billion.
The new terminal is expected to strengthen Poland’s energy security while
increasing opportunities for suppliers and contractors to participate in
the country’s energy transition.
“Energy security is the foundation of a strong Poland. That's why we are
investing in new energy sources, modern infrastructure, and the development
of domestic industry,” said Andrzej Domañski, Poland’s minister of finance
and economy.
Following the completion of construction, the terminal will support the
2 offshore wind project.
A lease agreement for the facility has already been signed back in 2024
with Elektrownia Wiatrowa Baltica 2.
“This is a breakthrough moment for the development of the domestic offshore
sector and proof that a complete ecosystem for implementing this type of
investment is being created in Poland,” said Dariusz Lubera, CEO of PGE
Polska Grupa Energetyczna.
The terminal was developed by Istrana, with an 85% stake currently held
general contractor.

title: N-Sea Group announces completion of Vattenfall’s 2026 seabed survey campaign
content:
N-Sea Group has announced the completion of the 2026 Vattenfall seabed
survey campaign. The project aimed to gather valuable data to support the
monitoring and management of offshore assets.
N-Sea supported the campaign by providing seabed monitoring services, deploying
a range of vessels and nearshore assets, as well as offshore and nearshore
teams, to complete the work.
The campaign covered several major offshore wind farms, including Hollandse
Kust Zuid,
Vesterhav
North and South,
and Kriegers
in Denmark. In total, the survey encompassed 253 wind turbine locations,
inter-array cable corridors, export cable routes, and offshore substations.
According to the company, high-resolution survey data was successfully
collected with no recorded incidents.

title: It’s Contract Renewal Season, But Some Customers Aren’t Biting
content: My colleagues and I have been hearing a lot of stories about big enterprise customers renegotiating their annual contracts with model developers. Traditionally, software sellers use this time as an opportunity to convince customers to increase their annual commit by, for instance, reminding them how they exceeded their usage limits this year or highlighting new features they’ve released. In the past, model developers have had success using that playbook. This year has been a different story, though, some customers tell me. For instance, one executive at a major financial services firm said their company was hesitant to increase their spending commitment with Anthropic , OpenAI or any other model provider for a couple reasons. First, this executive said, the rapid pace of model releases means enterprises want flexibility to quickly switch to whatever the best new model is, something that can change week to week. Switching the models that power a company’s application is much easier now than it used to be. We previously reported that AI coding startup Replit took just mere hours to make the code changes to switch their product from primarily using Anthropic’s models to OpenAI’s. The second reason is that these model providers keep releasing cheaper, “good-enough” AI, such as OpenAI’s Terra and Luna versions or Anthropic’s Haiku , the exec said. When the model providers do so, companies move as many workloads to these cheaper models as they can, which can sometimes quickly cut their bills to a fraction of what they used to be, the exec said. (Over time, though, their overall spending could increase because they might use more AI.) In doing so, the model providers are essentially cannibalizing their more expensive models with cheaper ones. We’re not trying to argue that revenue growth at Anthropic and OpenAI will fall off a cliff. The potential market is enormous, and both are growing pretty well right now. It’s also not lost on us that Anthropic says that in the third quarter, its net retention rate was 900%, meaning existing customers spent many more times what they were spending a year earlier. And Anthropic’s inference margins were crazy good in the first half of the year. Still, anecdotes like the one involving the major financial services firm raise the perennial question of whether models will eventually be commoditized. Such a scenario would crush trillions of dollars in market caps, and we aren’t ready to buy into the idea. A more realistic framework to hold is that the rapid improvement in models, and their capabilities frequently leapfrogging each other, has caused some decision paralysis among some enterprise customers. That could explain why, instead, they are turning to model routers like OpenRouter —where they can access nearly any model from a single application programming interface—or platforms that offer multiple models, such as Snowflake . That puts the model providers in an awkward position. Anthropic said in its prospectus that it wants more enterprise customers to sign non-cancelable, multiyear contracts with minimum spending commitments, just as some of those customers are trying to avoid getting locked in. Meanwhile, both Anthropic and OpenAI have committed to spending hundreds of billions of dollars on computing over the next decade. If big customers keep their options open, the model providers could end up being the only ones locked into long-term commitments. You can expect that subject to come up during Anthropic's first quarterly earnings call early next year. The company has since cut its target to roughly $20 billion at a reduced $1.25 trillion valuation, the FT reported Friday. title: Inside Apple’s Slog to Create Its First Robot
content: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots, but judging by Apple’s plodding progress on the first one it hopes to sell—a device with a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp—he could face an uphill battle. Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it. The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get off a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it. Much of the hardware needed for the robot has been finished for around two years, but the software team has found it difficult to keep pace, people who have worked on the project said. The hardware team responsible for J595 has pushed to hurry up and release the product. Meanwhile, the software team has advocated for delaying its release, and for the past year, it has attempted to strip back some proposed features and focus the product on a few capabilities related to FaceTime and automating home tasks, like switching on a light. Apple hopes to sell the robot for around $1,000. It could cost even more—depending on the market prices for the robot’s components. Several former employees said they expect Apple may call the device HomeView Ultra, borrowing the name from HomeView, the stationary tabletop device that Apple unveiled last month. Right now, Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though. (The hardware team behind the robot had initially planned to release it this year.) Apple’s struggles to get the robot ready highlight the challenges the company faces as Ternus’ reign begins. While Apple is a finely tuned machine at cranking out new, incremental updates to iPhones and Macs every year, it is less adept at developing entirely new products, and the company has a long-standing tendency to move at a placid pace. For instance, it took around eight years for Apple to complete work on its Vision Pro headset, which it released two years ago to muted fanfare. (If the J595 robot does come out next year, it will have taken roughly the same amount of time.) Apple has appeared particularly sluggish in the AI era. Its overhaul of Siri took years to complete, and even with new AI features rolled out earlier this year, the assistant is still seen as a laggard behind what AI agents like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots can do. As a gesture to Ternus, Tim Cook, his predecessor, delayed the release of some new products so that their debuts coincided with Ternus’s start in September. Since then, Apple has unveiled HomeView, the foldable iPhone Duo and a touchscreen MacBook. But those products have received a mixed reaction from consumers. The $2,899 MacBook is seen as expensive. The Duo has genuine buzz around it but has also attracted complaints about cracked screens. And HomeView has been critiqued as just a giant repurposed Apple Watch, one that relies heavily on a still disappointing Siri. Ternus arrives in the top job at a moment when many other fierce competitors are working on AI-powered devices and robots. A year ago, OpenAI acquired a hardware startup co-founded by Jony Ive, the former Apple design chief. Since then, Ive has been devoted to creating a line of AI devices for OpenAI, which has hired more than 400 ex-Apple engineers to work on those devices. Next year, OpenAI hopes to release a doughnut-shaped smart speaker that will have moving parts and a camera that allows it to gather information about its user and environment. New Apple CEO John Ternus unveils the new $2,800 touchscreen MacBook Pro in October. (Getty Images) Meta has been rolling out a slew of its own devices, including AI glasses and virtual reality headsets. Compared with Apple, Meta has been able in some cases to move rapidly from concept to product: It has said it took less than a year to develop Charm, a pocket-sized AI device that it plans to ship in December. Tesla is working on a humanoid robot, Optimus, that CEO Elon Musk has said will help with household tasks. And then there are a slew of startups trying to compete with the established tech giants, including robotics startup 1X, which had hoped to have its humanoid robot in homes this year. 1X’s robot, Neo, caught a moment of virality when it was first unveiled last year in videos showing it washing dishes and folding clothes. In addition to the J595 robot, Apple’s robotics team, which is led by Kevin Lynch, a longtime company executive, has explored other types of robots, such as one that follows a user around the home on wheels and another that flies inside the home. There is also an Apple project focused on robots that can complete specific everyday tasks, such as folding clothes. Robots devoted only to a few specific chores are, theoretically, much easier to develop than humanoid robots made to do many different things. Ternus has been particularly enthusiastic about discussions around robots that focused on household tasks, people familiar with the meetings said. As one former engineer who worked on the J595 robot put it, Apple “is tearing itself apart at the seams trying to get on this AI bandwagon.” An ‘iPad on a Stick’ The creation of the J595 robot has unfolded over nearly a decade, with responsibilities for the robot falling to a slew of Apple executives, some of whom were working on multiple projects at once and never had an opportunity to focus solely on the device. (Bloomberg has previously reported some details about the robot.) Early prototypes of the robot were done in 2018. A year later, Cook received a demo of a prototype and gave the green light to continue working on it. The prototypes were bigger than the one currently being envisioned, and the initial designs drew jokes from some Apple engineers, who remarked that it looked like “an iPad on a stick.” The robot’s hardware was developed by a team led by Matthew Costello, who’d previously worked on Beats, the headphones brand acquired by Apple in 2014. Software development fell to employees within Apple’s Special Projects Group, which was then primarily working on Project Titan, Apple’s autonomous car initiative. For a time, Brian Lynch, a veteran Apple engineer whose time stretched back to the iPod, was working on both the car’s interior and the J595 robot: He envisioned the robot being able to sit not only inside people’s homes but on the front console of the Apple car too. Apple may call its new robot the HomeView Ultra, making it expansion from its stationary tabletop device, HomeView, that it unveiled in September. (Getty Images) In 2021, leadership of the Special Projects Group shifted from Doug Field, who departed for Ford, to Kevin Lynch, who got credit for saving the Apple Watch by developing its health-tracking features. But most of Lynch’s attention was on the car, and much of the robotics effort fell to Chris Saari, who had led efforts to develop the Apple Watch’s software. Even at these early stages, the people working on the J595 robot knew it had to be more than a fancy way to make FaceTime calls if Apple wanted to justify a high price tag on it. After the ChatGPT’s launch in 2022 ignited the AI boom, they began to develop AI features to make it more sophisticated. Employees working on the robot began pushing for a wide range of proactive agentic AI capabilities, envisioning a device that could accomplish a variety of tasks. There was even an agentic AI research arm opened up inside the robotics group, led by Vladlen Koltun, who joined Apple in 2021 after leading AI at Intel. But Apple’s in-house AI technology was meager compared with what competitors were creating. As a result, the robotics team was given permission to use any available AI models, including open-source models and licensed models from Google. They hoped to eventually integrate the J595 robot with Siri, but during the robot’s early development, the Siri team was kept separate from the robotics squad and was overwhelmed in its own work in trying to improve Siri itself. Apple’s Kevin Lynch, who is created with saving the Apple Watch, had advocated for developing the new robot slowly and to release an early version with limited features. (Getty Images) When Apple shuttered its work on its autonomous car in 2024, Lynch moved all of his focus to robots that would be used within a home, redeploying many of the people who’d been working on the car with him to work on robots. Some of the Apple employees who had been working on robots before Lynch shifted his attention were disappointed with his leadership and felt he rarely talked to or consulted with them, three people involved in the project said. Lynch tried to pull back on some expectations for what a debut version of the J595 robot would be able to do. He wanted to slowly add features to it after it launched—a similar approach to what had been done with the Apple Watch. While the initial Apple Watch came out in 2015, Apple later added the sensors for tracking someone’s health and fitness that made the wearable more popular. Ternus Takes Command Prior to becoming CEO, Ternus, then the company’s hardware chief, was skeptical of many new products, like the failed autonomous car project and the Vision Pro headset. But he has been more enthusiastic about Apple’s potential robots, three people familiar with the company’s robot projects said. Last year, oversight of Lynch and the Special Projects Group was taken away from Senior Vice President John Giannandrea and put under Ternus. (Giannandrea, who’d been responsible for Apple’s AI efforts, left Apple earlier this year.) In April, Apple announced it would promote Ternus to CEO later in the year. But even as he was preparing to take the job, Ternus made an effort to be at every demonstration and product planning meeting for J595 and Apple’s other robots, people involved in those projects said. Much of the development of the J595 robot has fallen to a team that reported to John Giannandrea until last year. Giannandrea departed Apple earlier this year. (Getty Images) Across the company, Ternus has been advocating for Apple to run faster with leaner teams, people familiar with his strategy said. And the team working on the robots remains relatively small. Apple has very few employees with deep backgrounds devoted to robotics; one person estimated the company has only 10 or so “true roboticists.” Under Lynch, the team working on software is around 300—with around 30 of them focused on research, said people familiar with the team. The employees dedicated to the J595 robot have already been talking about a second-generation version of the robot that would have some of the proposed features they’ve discarded. Meanwhile, many of the engineers who initially worked on the robot have since departed, including hardware leader Brian Lynch, who joined fitness device maker Oura, and robotics research head Jian Zhang, who joined Meta. While many J595 employees want the robot to come out as soon as possible, some employees worry it could face the same lack of enthusiasm that has greeted HomeView. But they fear the longer Apple waits to release the robot, the higher expectations will be for it as AI capabilities grow more sophisticated across the industry.

title: Apple, Uber and Elections Headline Week
content: Can Apple, Uber and Palantir turn this stock market around? It sure needs it. Worries about excessive AI spending tanked Google’s stock last week and sent the Nasdaq Composite to its worst month since March 2025. While the major indexes are still in the green for the year, a few more days like Friday’s could change that. Fortunately, we have a handful of earnings that might temper the gloom. Palantir Technologies, which reports Monday, has told investors to expect an 83% jump in the third quarter from the year-ago period. That’s a slowdown from the second quarter’s blistering 93% growth . But at least investors will get a reprieve from enormous capital expenditures. Palantir only spent $22 million in capex in the first half. As for Apple, it’s already warned investors that supply constraints for advanced chip manufacturing would contribute to slower revenue growth, to a range of  9% to 11% in the September quarter from a year ago, slower than its 16% growth in the June quarter. Apple has also forecast iPhone revenue growth in the mid-teens versus 22% in the June quarter. An improvement on that outlook could buoy the mood. On the other hand, a sharper slowdown in growth from either companies could give investors another reason to sell tech stocks. Here’s what else is going on… Ternus’ Turn When the iPhone maker reports results late Monday, it will be the first time new CEO John Ternus will lead the conference call. Ternus, Apple’s former senior vice president of hardware engineering, got off to a fast start after he took the torch from Tim Cook, Apple’s long-running CEO, who is now executive chair. In just the last two months, Apple announced three notable new products—an iPhone with a folding screen , a MacBook with a touchscreen and the HomeView, a tabletlike smart home device . The first two products, which followed designs popular with competitors like smartphone maker Samsung and laptop maker Lenovo, were a sign of a new Apple adventurousness under Ternus (though the products were almost certainly greenlit some time ago under his predecessor). But brand-new products have a habit of glitching at the start, even for a company with superlative manufacturing processes (anyone remember Antennagate or Bendgate?). In recent weeks, media reports have highlighted cracks in the Duo’s wide folding screen and other operational issues. Apple’s announcement last week that the new MacBook Pro with a touchscreen would cost at least $2,899 —a whopping $900 more than the version without a touchscreen—will likely hold some buyers back. As for the HomeView, I’ll be curious if enough households think a $299 standing tablet is really that necessary—or if they can get by with how most people use FaceTime, change songs and watch videos while they putter in the kitchen: by propping the phone against the mayonnaise jar (additional cost: zero). • Uber reports quarterly results Wednesday. Uber has already been in the news recently, thanks to Instacart’s agreement to sell to DoorDash for $17 billion in cash and stock. As Valida reported last week , Instacart leaders had shopped the company to Uber. But those talks fizzled, in part because Uber had just recently announced another big acquisition, a $15 billion deal for Europe-based Delivery Hero, and was also worried that an acquisition would hit antitrust hurdles. Uber has forecast that gross bookings—the value of dollars spent on its various apps—will rise in a range from $58.25 billion to $60.25 billion, with the median up 19% from the same period last year. • Tuesday midterm elections. Tech heads to the polls in a variety of ways Tuesday. As Shane reported this morning , in 21 of the 36 states electing a governor on Tuesday, at least one major-party nominee backs a data center moratorium. And that’s not all. An expected return to a Democratic majority in Congress could increase headaches for large tech companies like Meta Platforms, Nvidia and Amazon if Democrats decide to hold oversight hearings into their executives’ work with the Trump administration, as this Politico article details . Even a blue sweep wouldn’t overcome Trump’s veto power, meaning any potential AI legislative pushes next term will likely still need his support. We’ll also be watching the outcome of California’s Proposition 40, the so-called billionaire’s tax. Several well-known tech CEOs have lambasted the proposition—or protested by moving their zip code out of state—but probably more notably, the measure has lost ground after a number of large groups like the state teachers’ union have also criticized it. Abe has more here . In Other News The Federal Bureau of Investigation said Saturday that North Korea was r esponsible for the $6.3 billion theft from crypto exchange Binance, the largest crypto hack in history. S&P Global Ratings lowered its credit rating outlook on Meta from stable to negative, citing limits on the company’s ability to monetize its AI investments. OpenAI lowered the target for its fundraising to $20 billion from $30 billion, at a $1.25 trillion valuation, the Financial Times reported. Amazon disclosed a new loan facility up to $80 billion to purchase technology infrastructure assets. Cyera, a five-year-old cybersecurity startup focused on protecting corporate data against AI-powered attacks, has discussed nearly doubling its valuation to $20 billion. title: Exclusive: How the Embattled CEO of Our Next Energy Plotted a Comeback
content: A few years ago, Mujeeb Ijaz was one of the most prominent startup CEOs in what was then a go-go next-generation U.S. battery industry. Previously, he had headed the battery program in Apple’s secret electric vehicle development program, and before that was an executive at Ford. In early 2023, the startup he founded, Our Next Energy, was flush with $300 million in cash, raised in February of that year in a Series B round with a $1.2 billion valuation. The company appeared to be on its way to its first commercial revenue. By the end of the year, however, ONE was in freefall and Ijaz was out as its CEO. The main culprit was a sudden reversal in the EV industry, which had been going gangbusters but then stalled. But the company had also been overly ambitious in diving into costly projects, according to former employees, splashing around cash, full of confidence that it could raise another round. Today, an apparently humbler Ijaz is back as CEO of ONE. The Novi, Mich., startup has abandoned trying to make batteries for EVs and is instead producing them to power less sexy technologies, like locomotives and maritime drones. And Ijaz says he’s no longer chasing quick hockey-stick, off-the-charts profit. Instead, he’s doing what he says he should have been doing all along—trying to build up ONE slowly, block by block and using cash sparingly. He projects $30 million in revenue this year, which he said will be triple last year’s amount. In 2027, he expects revenue to double to $60 million. “We don’t see the world in hockey sticks anymore,” Ijaz told me. “We see it in building our customer base, in making sure we deliver our results and then keeping the capital intensity low where we’re not overcapitalizing ahead of where we see the demand.” Ijaz’s argument for low-key management is understandable given his own recent trajectory and that of ONE (more on that below). But it also applies to the rest of the industry, which is seeing its first modest revenue, almost all of it tied to the revolutions in flying drones, AI data centers and robots. As we have written, startups like Enovix and Nyobolt have reported initial revenue from contracts for drone and robot batteries, respectively. Amprius Technologies and Unusual Machines have reported even larger drone battery contracts. Sodium-ion startup Peak Energy has $1.1 billion in contracts, but last week we reported that it has adopted a go-slow approach to scaling up its business. Ijaz has said ONE’s batteries power more than 100 locomotives in the U.S. and Canada. But the market for drones, robots and locomotives is far smaller than the potential one for EVs, and the revenue from these use cases will fall well short of the billions of dollars in sales to EV makers that some of the startups forecast when they went public in 2020 and 2021. For now, at least, the U.S. battery industry is still in search of business that will drive big revenue, even though some battery startups seem likely to eke out profits. ONE’s troubles startled industry veterans, who had regarded the company—which was developing a novel dual-battery pack that would power an EV at least 600 miles, along with a lithium-iron-phosphate pack for the grid—as one of the next-generation battery startups most likely to reach large-volume commercial production. Ijaz himself was one of the industry’s most respected startup CEOs. He had founded ONE in 2020 after running the battery division of Apple’s EV development program for five years. In addition to working at Ford, he had also been an executive at lithium-ion battery pioneer A123 Systems. The success of the February 2023 round aligned with investor and industry ebullience around EVs and battery startups with ambitions to power them; EV sales soared 60% year on year in 2022 and another 60% year on year in the first half of 2023. ONE, buoyed by the boom, burned through nearly all the new cash in just months in what employees said was an almost devil-may-care spending spree on new projects and lavish marketing. On the tail of that Series B round, Ijaz began raising a Series C for another $300 million. A U.K. firm, Just Climate, emerged as the lead investor with a pledge for a $100 million investment. Ijaz said he would use the funds to build a gigafactory in Michigan with 2.7 gigawatt-hours of capacity, enough to make 40,000 batteries for trucks per year or enough grid batteries to power 250,000 homes. By 2027, Ijaz had plans to expand the plant almost tenfold. But in the third quarter of 2023, the first signs of consumer fatigue in the EV market surfaced. Affluent early adopters already had EVs in their driveways. While EVs were still selling , they began to pile up just a bit in dealer lots. The slight slowdown spooked Ford and General Motors, along with investors. The venture capital industry began a substantial retreat from new investments in battery startups. Just Climate also became concerned about the EV industry downturn, and did not believe that ONE could produce batteries nearly as fast as it predicted, as we reported at the time . In November 2023, the VC firm backed out of the investment. ONE had to close out the year with a sudden layoff of most of its employees. Ijaz  himself was forced out as CEO, though he managed to stay on as chief technology officer. Ijaz’s description of the last three years sounds like a roller coaster. For most of 2024, ONE’s board attempted to sell the company without luck. The board considered bankruptcy. But in March 2025, Phillip Sarofim, CEO of Trousdale Ventures, co-led a new investment round with Ijaz’s brother, Mansoor Ijaz, who ran Crescent Global Partners, a family investment office. The amount of the investment was not disclosed. Mansoor Ijaz joined the ONE board, which restored Mujeeb Ijaz as CEO. Ijaz said he spent the entirety of last year visiting potential customers and recalibrating what ONE might do with its existing assets, which included a cell production factory in Van Buren Township, Mich., and a pack assembly factory at its headquarters in Novi. In January this year, ONE announced a new product line: It would no longer make EV batteries but would power locomotives, drones and the grid. Ijaz said ONE is selling nine different batteries to more than 20 customers. Almost all the business, he said, is tied to demand for U.S.-made batteries, as the Trump administration has issued import controls and bans on Chinese-made batteries and components. The company has also developed a battery that can charge to 85% of capacity in just 12 minutes. I asked Ijaz where ONE would be right now if the Series C had not fallen apart. He said the investors in that round had “lost an opportunity,” since the AI boom has created massive demand for grid batteries of the type ONE was manufacturing. Either way, a quieter Ijaz is going at it again. “We have a second chance to retool a healthy birth,” he said. ---- Noteworthy Exclusive: Caterpillar-backed battery startup Lithos Energy has shut down. The Hayward, Calif., company stopped operations and let go all of its employees on Oct. 5, according to three former executives, though it hasn’t announced the shutdown. Lithos was founded in 2015 by former Tesla employee James Meredith to make batteries for off-road and marine electric vehicles, along with industrial uses. In 2023, Caterpillar invested $38 million in the company with the objective of developing batteries for its construction vehicles. Lithos used the cash to build a pilot factory in Hayward and hire personnel. But last year, when President Donald Trump pulled the plug on EV programs, Caterpillar shelved the Lithos battery programs it was backing, according to Rob Sweney, who had been Lithos’ vice president of engineering. Absent any other big customers, Lithos ran out of money. After the initial investment, “we bit the hook hard—recruited a large team, moved into a shiny pilot facility etc. [and] chewed through the investment rapidly,” Sweney told me. Meredith and Caterpillar did not respond to emails. Electric construction equipment maker Bedrock Robotics raised $600 million in a Series C round at a $4.1 billion valuation. The raise and valuation illustrates investor enthusiasm for electric startups outside mainstream consumer EVs. For now, San Francisco–based Bedrock, founded by former Waymo executives, is making electric excavators, as we reported last year . KoBold Metals says China is blocking its use of surveying technology to mine lithium in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The company has asked the U.S. to step in and help clear the way. Berkeley, Calif.–based KoBold says it uses AI to explore for metals. It wants to use aerial surveying technology to assess a lithium deposit in the DRC, but that will require a United Nations exemption because the equipment has possible military use as well, the Financial Times reported. KoBold claims China has stalled this exemption, and the firm has asked the U.S. Department of State to intervene. --- Recommended Newsletter Start your day with Applied AI, the newsletter that uncovers how leading businesses are leveraging AI to automate tasks. title: The Information’s WTF Summit in Pictures
content: At The Information’s annual WTF Summit a few days ago, women leaders from Anthropic, Google, Goldman Sachs and dozens of other companies across technology and media gathered to discuss the forces remaking those industries. Conversation topics ranged from on the state of tech M&A to chip financing to the geopolitics between America and China. Across all of those talks, the VIPs had their eyes fixed on what lies ahead—perhaps no one more so than Amanda Peterson Corio, Google’s global head of data center energy. “I live in 2031,” she told attendees. Below, some scenes from one of our favorite events of the year. Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett, the bank’s global co-head of investment banking. (Erin Beach) Bari Weiss, editor in chief of CBS News. title: Google Energy Chief: Space Data Centers Cost Up to 100 Times More Than Those on Earth
content: Data centers in space could cost up to 100 times as much as those on Earth, Google's head of data center energy said this week, a reality check from a company that itself is testing AI server chips in orbit. “Let’s explore all the terrestrial options before we go extraterrestrial,” Amanda Peterson Corio said at The Information’s WTF summit, a gathering of senior women in the technology and finance industries. The comments came as SpaceX’s orbital data center plans underpin part of its roughly $1.8 trillion market capitalization. Peterson Corio also said that rising public opposition to data centers here on Earth is largely the fault of younger, less experienced companies that should be subject to higher standards. Before the recent boom, she said, companies that had been building data centers for years “were doing it the right way,” and the facilities rarely drew controversy. Launch costs for sending computing hardware into orbit are “incredibly, incredibly expensive, up to 100 times more expensive than building on earth,” Peterson Corio said. Beyond cost, operators would also need to figure out how to maintain and upgrade equipment in orbit. On Earth, data center staff constantly swap out computers and rewire systems, she said. ( Watch an interview with Peterson Corio here .) Peterson Corio’s cautious comments about space come even as Google's own researchers said this month they will partner with satellite imaging firm Planet Labs to use satellites to explore the potential of larger-scale data center clusters in space. As part of a project it calls Suncatcher, Google has already launched a smaller space server prototype carrying tensor processing units, the AI server chips it codesigns with Broadcom, to space. (On Friday, Google said those first TPUs in orbit processed their first AI workloads: writing a haiku.) In a research paper last fall, Google employees working on Suncatcher and the company’s research chief James Manyika said that if a launch costs hit $200 per kilogram or less, the “cost per unit of power in space could be approximately comparable to terrestrial spend.” The company’s researchers said it could potentially reach that threshold by 2035, though the timing might depend on SpaceX’s ability to launch Starship and rev up the rocket’s launch frequency. (Starship promises to lower launch costs and increase the amount of payload capacity, compared to the company’s current flagship rockets.) Others have been more bullish. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that his company will have data centers in space as soon as next year, and Jeff Bezos, Amazon’s founder and the owner of SpaceX rival Blue Origin, has said that there will be data centers consuming a gigawatt of power in space in a decade. Google and SpaceX have also reportedly explored working together on data centers in orbit. (Alphabet also owns a sizable stake in SpaceX.) Peterson Corio didn’t dismiss the concept, saying it’s “really fascinating” and that Google invests in long-shot ideas because it is “always thinking 10, 20, 30 years down the line.” But such technology is “not tomorrow,” she said. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has gone further, calling the idea of putting data centers in space under current conditions “ridiculous” and criticizing Musk’s speedy timeline. The Real Bottleneck: Permits, Not Power On Earth, Peterson Corio pushed back on the idea—also espoused by Musk—that the U.S. lacks enough electricity for the AI buildout. “Is there enough power? Sure, absolutely,” she said. The bottlenecks, she said, are permitting and the lengthy studies required to connect new projects to the public energy grid. Alphabet's X unit has a project, Tapestry, which is working with PJM, the largest grid operator on the East Coast, to use AI to speed up those studies. In Texas, the state utilities regulator has slowed down some data center projects as it boosts reviews to make sure new facilities don’t burden the grid or spike prices. The grid itself also isn’t properly utilized the way it ought to be, other executives in the field say. Brian Janous, co-founder of data center land and power developer Cloverleaf Infrastructure, recently told The Information that about 45% of the grid’s capacity goes unused on average because it has to accommodate peaks in usage. For most hours of the day, there's enough spare capacity in the grid to meet data centers’ needs, he said. (Startups like Cloverleaf as well as Nvidia are trying to figure out how to use such capacity.) Notably, Google appears to have a power-related advantage over its cloud rivals , in terms of squeezing as much computing capacity as possible from its data centers, a metric known as power usage effectiveness. As for the data center backlash in the U.S., Peterson Corio blamed it on “a lot of new entrants that are selling or building and maybe don't have that history or sophistication,” though she didn’t name names. While numerous first-time developers have rushed to enter the AI data center market in recent years, well-known firms such as Oracle, not just the newcomers, have also faced local resistance. Higher Standards In any case, she said she supports regulation and higher standards for the industry. She didn’t propose specific rules but pointed to Google’s rising financial contribution to the communities where it operates, and efforts to limit risks if facilities can’t be completed. Those include committing to pay for grid upgrades over 15 to 20 years so no one else is “left holding the bill” if a project stalls. Such arrangements, under which Google commits up front to pay for grid infrastructure, are now happening in more than nine U.S. states and “growing really, really quickly,” she said. The standards also include Google paying its full power bills and property taxes; posting bonds to cover the restoration of land if the company ever abandons a site; and ending nondisclosure agreements with local governments. (On the latter point, Google only this month agreed to end such NDAs, which activists had decried, following similar moves from Microsoft and Amazon.) Her comments follow rising investor scrutiny of the valuations or viability of young AI cloud providers, often heavily backed by Nvidia, that are racing to build data centers using a lot of borrowed cash and a short track record. While such firms appear to be among the companies Peterson Corio thinks need tighter standards, Google also said it is going to increasingly rely on “third‑party compute capacity” for its own computing needs, though it didn’t specify which providers it will use. (SpaceX is one of them.) Google needs them because it can’t build its own facilities fast enough! New From Our Reporters AI Agenda How Is Anthropic So Efficient? title: Candidates Backing Data Center Pauses Could Win in Up to 15 Governor’s Races
content: As data centers have gone from obscurity to the top of voters’ minds, midterm candidates are taking a stance on the issue. The fight is most heated in races for governor, the office that has shown the most power to limit data centers on a broad scale. Whichever candidates win, more doors are likely to close on the industry, leaving it with fewer places to build and higher costs where it still can. In 21 of the 36 states electing a governor on Tuesday, at least one major-party nominee backs a data center moratorium, according to The Information’s analysis of candidate platforms and public statements. Both nominees back pauses in five states (Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio, Oregon and Texas), and a candidate promising a pause is likely to win in three (Maine, New Mexico and New York), based on recent polls. In seven more, it could be a close race between a candidate who backs a pause and one who doesn’t (Alaska, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Wisconsin and Vermont). Those 15 states are home to more than a third of the U.S. population. They are also home to some of the country’s biggest data center projects. OpenAI’s Stargate project with Oracle has massive sites in Texas, Michigan and New Mexico. SoftBank’s SB Energy plans to build an 8-gigawatt campus for OpenAI in Ohio. Microsoft, Amazon and Nvidia have lined up Texas sites . In Georgia, the Atlanta metro area has overtaken Northern Virginia as the busiest market for data center construction, according to real estate firm CBRE. In three of the states holding gubernatorial elections next week, sitting governors have already paused new large-scale data center projects: Kathy Hochul in New York, Greg Abbott in Texas and Tina Kotek in Oregon. Hochul’s opponent, Bruce Blakeman, calls her pause “ crazy ” but trails far behind her in the polls. Abbott’s opponent, Gina Hinojosa, who wants an even broader pause of any new approvals, calls Abbott’s pause “an election-year stunt” on her campaign website, saying, “We know that goes away on November 4.” Democrats make up most of the bloc backing moratoriums, but it’s not a clean partisan split. In Maryland and Iowa, the Republican candidates support moratoriums while their opponents don’t, though these two candidates trail in their races. Even if candidates aren’t pushing data center pauses, some of them hope to rein in the industry in other ways. Of the 46 top nominees not calling for moratoriums, 38 back at least one restriction on data centers. One of the most common alternatives to pauses is ratepayer protections—policies that make sure the costs of powering giant AI campuses don’t raise household electricity bills. That option echoes the voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge President Donald Trump asked tech companies to sign in March, as well as a bipartisan bill passed in the House and blocked in the Senate that would have pushed state regulators to make data centers cover their power costs. Because the bill would not actually require states to adopt standards, Senate Democrats spiked it, calling it “ toothless .” Other candidates want to end tax breaks for builders, add environmental and water protections, require union labor or ban nondisclosure agreements in public deals. Hawaii is the only state where neither candidate for governor is campaigning on data center restrictions. Data centers are on everyone’s lips, but in some places, other tech issues are also on the ballot. Some candidates are calling for AI legislation mandating model safety reviews and child safety protections. At least a dozen candidates have weighed in on the presence of Flock Safety cameras after privacy concerns and police misuse drew backlash from some communities. A couple of candidates have plans for crypto and prediction markets. Whether hopefuls will actually follow through on their promises is another question. Our tally takes the candidates at their word. Nationwide Drama Opposition to data centers bubbled up quickly from the local level, as shown by The Information’s ban tracker . At the year’s start, only about 40 towns and counties had bans in place. By August, there were over 500 bans, driven by worries about power bills, water usage, noise and blight. In the court of public opinion, data centers are losing. In an August poll from Pew Research Center, six in 10 U.S. adults said they would be uncomfortable with a new one operating in their area, with more than half calling them bad for the environment and half considering them bad for home energy costs. Few saw a bright side: Less than a quarter agreed they would be good for local jobs or tax revenue. Association with the industry has become a liability, prompting candidates to brand their opponents with derisive nicknames. In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford dubbed his opponent, Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo, “Data Center Joe”—and the state Democratic Party set up a website to match. In Wisconsin, Republican Tom Tiffany called his rival, David Crowley, “Data Center David” (though Crowley backs a “de facto moratorium” and Tiffany doesn’t.) In Oregon, the state Democrats dubbed Christine Drazan, their opponent, “Data Center Drazan.” In Alaska, Republican Bernadette Wilson called Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who goes by JKT, “ Chat JKT ,” based on donations to his campaign from Anthropic employees. However, he backs a moratorium and she doesn’t, though she said she’d never “allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands.” In Michigan, which is at the center of both the build-out and the backlash, Republican John James has gone after Democratic candidate Jocelyn Benson’s husband, an executive at a firm involved in the state’s Stargate site. Benson’s campaign says he has recused himself from any state-related work and points to money the James campaign has taken from data center developers. For what it’s worth, both candidates say they back a moratorium. Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms and Ohio’s Amy Acton have asked their opponents to divest from tech and data center investments. Even some of the industry’s biggest backers are recalibrating. In July, Alabama’s likely winner, Tommy Tuberville, called data center concerns “bull crap.” Now his ads say, “Politicians get the headlines, big tech gets the tax break, and working families get stuck with the bill.” Donors with a stake in data centers are writing big checks to favored candidates. Since July 2025, Abbott has raised about $9 million from people and companies the Texas Tribune links to data centers . In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds and his PAC have taken at least $1.5 million from data center developers and others in the industry, Politico reported . Feuding AI PACs have aligned behind Donalds, too: Both Leading the Future, supported by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Andreessen Horowitz, and Anthropic-backed Public First Action have spent $2 million each on ads backing the candidate, Bloomberg reported . Same Name, Different Policies The word “moratorium” has become popular enough for candidates to attach it to very different policies. But not all are equal. They vary in duration: Some locales have paused building for just 45 days, others for three years. Many moratoriums are in place to buy time while lawmakers decide on more permanent standards for data centers. They vary in scope, too. Some moratoriums apply only to facilities above a certain size, usually measured in electricity use. New York’s 50-megawatt cutoff rejects larger campuses that train frontier AI models but lets smaller projects through. Most candidates pledging pauses haven’t said where they’d draw the line, but many are aiming at the biggest projects. And some moratoriums look more like a list of guardrails going by a trendier name. Ohio’s Acton backs a “conditional moratorium,” which would approve data centers meeting certain labor and siting conditions, according to her campaign website. Wisconsin gubernatorial candidates David Crowley (left) and Tom Tiffany (right). Crowley supports a “de facto moratorium.” Getty Images. Each statewide ban so far has leaned on the same lever: halting new environmental permits. Abbott has also frozen new electric grid hookups, while Kotek has stopped deals on state land. Not every governor thinks they can do that. New Hampshire incumbent Kelly Ayotte says she can’t act alone and would need to pass a pause with the state’s budget for next July. Her opponent, Cinde Warmington, says she’d sign an executive order on day one. Whatever happens Tuesday, the AI and data center industries are already readying themselves to navigate narrower paths. In the initial public offering filing Anthropic released last week, the company identified moratoriums and other restrictive measures as a business risk, naming measures by New York and Texas. Anthropic said regulatory challenges are part of why it’s expanding its international data center footprint. SB Energy and neocloud Nscale named the same risks in their filings to go public.

title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
content:
Provided by
When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive.
The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits.
Gartner predicts
that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028.
The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap.
Measure the software that ships
A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality.
If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces.
Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work.
Match the model to the task
Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself.
A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload.
Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work.
Change the economics of repeated use
Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows.
The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request.
Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting.
Test the operating model
At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%.
That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work.
Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it.
HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships.
Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice.
Build for adoption, not rationing
Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code.
As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them.

title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
content:
The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
Plus: A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The agentic web is here
In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.
At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process.
—Grace Huckins
Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths
Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes.
Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign.
Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths.
—Sara Kiley Watson
This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Subscribe to read the other five instalments in our new Impossible issue.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble
Big AI bills and weak earnings have spooked investors. (BBC)
+ The Nasdaq 100 had its worst day since June on Friday. (NBC News)
+ OpenAI has cut its funding target by $10 billion. (CNBC)
+ What even is the AI bubble? (MIT Technology Review)
2 Hackers have hit Ukraine and Russia’s emergency alert apps
Kyiv residents were warned of “nuclear danger.” (NBC News)
+ Russia’s app said nuclear warheads had been launched. (CNN)
+ Ukraine has blamed Russia, which hasn’t yet accused anyone. (BI)
+ AI will transform cyber warfare. (MIT Technology Review)
3 Binance users withdrew $3.6 billion after the largest ever crypto hack
The funds moved when the exchange reopened on Sunday. (Guardian)
+ Binance says it’s covered $6 billion of the stolen $6.3 billion. (Reuters $)
+ But the industry’s response has undermined its “decentralized” image. (Gizmodo)
4 An AI agent injected drugs into a live mouse’s brain
It chose the gene therapy and controlled the needle itself. (Wired $)
+ We need real-time tracking of AI agents. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Data centres have made utilities a flashpoint in the midterms
Americans are angry over rising electricity bills. (Reuters $)
+ Virtual power plants could help. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Apple has overtaken Nvidia as the world’s most valuable company
Investors are favouring its restraint on AI spending. (Bloomberg $)
+ But critics say it’s entering its “slop era.” (404 Media)
7 Supermarket fridges have overheated in a new wave of cyberattacks
Stores in Belgium, Sweden, and Luxembourg were hit. (Politico)
8 The first chocolate bars made from lab-grown cocoa are here
Startups are cultivating chocolate to tackle a cocoa shortage. (WSJ $)
9 Hackers hijacked digital billboards in multiple countries to show porn
They also criticized security flaws and Egypt’s government.(Gizmodo)
10 A new 3D map reveals instability in interstellar space
The discovery could help explain why stars form so inefficiently. (Quanta)
Quote of the day
“It would be great if all this was just a house of cards.”
—Kevin Roose, a technology columnist at the New York Times, tells NPR that an AI investment crash would be preferable to the technology permanently upending work and society.
One more thing
Useful quantum computing is inevitable—and increasingly imminent
Last year, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang jolted the stock market by saying that practical quantum computing is still 15 to 30 years away. He also suggested that those computers would need Nvidia GPUs to function. But Huang’s predictions miss the mark—both on the timeline and the role his company’s technology will play.
Quantum computing is rapidly converging on utility. And that’s good news, because the hope is that they will be able to perform calculations that no amount of AI or classical computation could ever achieve. Read the full story.
—Peter Barrett
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ A miniaturist has built a delightful diorama of the world's creepiest living room.
+ The year's best dog photos have been announced, and they're very good boys and girls.
+ At the Green Zone golf club, you tee off in Sweden and putt in Finland, an hour in the future.
+ Astronomers say they’ve found the real celestial arrangement that inspired van Gogh’s The Starry Night.
